**Setting Aside Adjudication Decision (s.15):** Limited grounds — (a) the adjudication decision was improperly procured through fraud or bribery; (b) there has been a denial of natural justice; (c) the adjudicator has not acted independently or impartially; (d) the adjudicator has acted in excess of jurisdiction. WRP Asia Pacific Sdn Bhd v NS Bluescope Lysaght Malaysia Sdn Bhd [2018] 1 MLJ 1 FC.

**PART 2: STANDARD FORM CONTRACTS**

**PAM 2018 Contract (Malaysian Institute of Architects):**
- Architect has certification function — Interim Certificates (monthly), Final Certificate.
- LAD (Liquidated and Ascertained Damages): Payable by contractor for delay at rate specified in Appendix.
- EOT (Extension of Time): Contractor's right to apply for EOT upon occurrence of Relevant Events (inclement weather, employer delay, etc.).
- Dispute resolution: Adjudication → Arbitration → Court (in that sequence).

**PWD 203/203A (Government contracts):**
- S.O. (Superintending Officer) performs certification function.
- Disputes go to CIPAA adjudication; then arbitration under Government Contract provisions.

**PART 3: COMMON CONSTRUCTION DISPUTES**

**Payment disputes:** Most common — non-payment of progress claims, disputed interim certificates, set-off and abatement.

**Delay disputes:** Who caused the delay? Critical Path Analysis (CPA) and delay analysis methods (as-planned v as-built, time impact analysis) are key. Concurrent delay apportionment.

**Defects claims:** Employer's right to withhold retention sum and LAD for defective work. Contractor's right to cure defects during Defects Liability Period (DLP).

**Variations:** Contractor's right to additional payment for variations instructed by the Architect/S.O. Oral variations — disputed but may be enforced under contract or quantum meruit (Fasda Heights Sdn Bhd v Soon Ee Sing Construction Sdn Bhd [2013]).

**LAD (Liquidated Damages) disputes:** Is the LAD clause a genuine pre-estimate (valid) or a penalty (void and unenforceable)? Cavendish Square Holding BV v El Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67 (partially adopted in Malaysia).

**PART 4: ARBITRATION IN CONSTRUCTION**

Most standard form contracts provide for arbitration as the final dispute resolution mechanism. The Arbitration Act 2005 (Act 646) governs arbitration in Malaysia. Key principles:
- Kompetenz-Kompetenz: Tribunal has power to rule on its own jurisdiction.
- Minimal court intervention (s.8 AA 2005).
- AIAC Arbitration Rules are widely used.
- Awards are final and binding; enforcement under the New York Convention if international.

**PRACTICAL NOTES**
— CIPAA timelines are strict and jurisdictional. Failure to respond to a payment claim within the prescribed time is extremely disadvantageous.
— In CIPAA adjudication, the decision is interim binding — respondent must pay even if challenging the decision by way of setting aside. Challenge does not automatically stay enforcement.
— To challenge a CIPAA decision, apply to the High Court under s.15 CIPAA — grounds are narrow. Courts have consistently upheld CIPAA decisions to give effect to the legislation's pay-now-argue-later philosophy.
— Always obtain independent expert evidence (delay analyst, QS, structural engineer) for construction disputes going to arbitration or court. Technical experts are critical.
— Construction contracts often contain multi-tier dispute resolution clauses — negotiation, adjudication, then arbitration. Compliance with each tier is a condition precedent to commencing the next step.
legislation: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012 (Act 746)
relatedCases: WRP Asia Pacific Sdn Bhd v NS Bluescope Lysaght Malaysia Sdn Bhd [2018] 1 MLJ 1 FC (CIPAA — interim binding, setting aside grounds)
Martego Sdn Bhd v Arkitek Meor & Chew [2018] 7 MLJ 219 (CIPAA — natural justice)
Bauer (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd v Jack-In-Pile (M) Sdn Bhd [2018] 10 MLJ 60 (sub-contractor disputes)
Fasda Heights Sdn Bhd v Soon Ee Sing Construction Sdn Bhd [2013] 8 MLJ 149 (variations — oral instructions)
Renoflex Systems (M) Sdn Bhd v Batu Kawan Berhad [2019] (CIPAA — payment response failure)
keyPrinciples: CIPAA operates on a 'pay now, argue later' philosophy. Even if you believe the adjudicator was wrong, you must pay the adjudicated sum and then pursue your remedies (arbitration or litigation) to recover it. Non-payment entitles the claimant to enforce as a judgment debt.

In construction delay disputes, prepare a contemporaneous record of events. The project site diary, weather records, RFI logs, and correspondence are critical evidence. Reconstruction of events after the fact is always less convincing.

LAD (Liquidated Damages): If the LAD rate is commercially justifiable as a genuine pre-estimate of loss at the time the contract was made, it will be enforced. Courts are now more willing to enforce commercial LAD clauses (Cavendish approach). Advise clients to document the rationale for the LAD rate when the contract is negotiated.
For government contracts (PWD 203), disputes may not be directly referable to arbitration until after the S.O.'s decision under the contract. Follow the contract's dispute resolution ladder strictly.

Adjudication under CIPAA: The adjudicator must give a decision within 45 working days. If the adjudicator exceeds this time without an extension agreed by parties, the decision may be challenged as made without jurisdiction.

theory_topics.title: Probate & Administration of Estates in Malaysia
theory_topics.overview: The law relating to probate and administration of deceased estates in Malaysia is governed by the Probate and Administration Act 1959 (Act 97) and the Distribution Act 1958 (Act 300), which applies to non-Muslims. Muslim estates are governed by Islamic inheritance law (Faraid). The High Court has jurisdiction to grant probate and letters of administration.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: TESTATE AND INTESTATE SUCCESSION**

**Testate Succession (with a valid will):** The estate of a deceased person who left a valid will is distributed according to the terms of the will. The executor named in the will applies for a **Grant of Probate** from the High Court.

**Intestate Succession (without a valid will):** The estate is distributed according to the **Distribution Act 1958 (Act 300)** for non-Muslims. An administrator (appointed by the court) applies for **Letters of Administration**.

**Distribution Act 1958 — Intestate Distribution Rules:**
- Surviving spouse + children: Spouse (1/3) + Children (2/3) equally.
- Surviving spouse only (no children): Spouse (1/2) + Parents (1/2).
- Children only (no spouse): Children equally.
- Parents only: Parents equally.
- Surviving spouse + parents (no children): Spouse (1/2) + Parents (1/2).

**PART 2: REQUIREMENTS FOR A VALID WILL**

Under the Wills Act 1959 (Act 346):
1. Testator must be at least 18 years old (or married).
2. The will must be in writing.
3. Signed at the foot or end of the will by the testator (or by another person in the testator's presence and direction).
4. Witnessed by at least two witnesses present at the same time.
5. Witnesses cannot be beneficiaries (their gifts will be void — s.9 Wills Act 1959).

**Testamentary Capacity:** The testator must: know the nature of making a will, know the extent of the property disposed of, know the claims of those who might expect to benefit, and not be suffering from any disorder of mind affecting the will — Banks v Goodfellow test, adopted in Malaysia.

**PART 3: GRANT OF PROBATE — PROCEDURE**

**Non-Contentious Probate:**
1. Executor files **Originating Summons** (Form 1, PAA 1959) in the High Court together with the original will, death certificate, affidavit of scripts, and schedule of assets.
2. **Advertisement in Government Gazette** for 14 days.
3. If no caveat or challenge, the Registrar grants probate — issue of **Grant of Probate** (sealed by the court).
4. Executor can then collect assets, pay debts, and distribute the estate.

**Letters of Administration (Intestate):**
1. Administrator (usually spouse, parent, or adult child) files OS together with death certificate, affidavit verifying family tree, and proposed schedule of assets.
2. Sureties (guarantors) may be required to ensure due administration.
3. Grant of Letters of Administration issued by court.
4. For estates below RM2 million, amanah saham, EPF, insurance — small estates may be administered through the **Amanah Raya Berhad** (trustee corporation).

**PART 4: CONTENTIOUS PROBATE**

A challenge to a will or to a grant of probate/administration is called a **probate action**. Grounds of challenge:
- **Lack of testamentary capacity** — testator was of unsound mind or undue influence.
- **Undue influence** — testator's will was overborne by another person's dominance.
- **Fraud** — the will was forged or the testator was deceived as to its contents.
- **Failure to comply with formal requirements** — not witnessed properly, not signed correctly.

**Procedure in Contentious Probate:**
Proceedings are commenced by filing a **Probate Action (Writ)** in the High Court. The contentious proceedings follow normal writ action procedure (pleadings, discovery, trial).

**Caveats in Probate:** A person who believes they have a legitimate interest in opposing a grant may lodge a caveat at the Probate Registry. A caveat prevents a grant from being issued without the caveator being notified and given an opportunity to appear.

**PART 5: TRUST LAW — BASIC PRINCIPLES**

The Civil Law Act 1956 imports English trust law. A trust is an equitable obligation binding a person (trustee) to deal with property (trust property) for the benefit of another (beneficiary) or for charitable purposes.

**Express Trusts:** Created by the settlor's intention, ascertainable beneficiaries (or charitable purpose), and identified subject matter (the three certainties — Morice v Bishop of Durham).

**Constructive Trusts:** Imposed by equity regardless of intention — to prevent unjust enrichment, fraud, or unconscionable conduct. Important in family property disputes and vendor-purchaser relationships.

**PART 6: EXECUTOR AND ADMINISTRATOR DUTIES**

- Collect and preserve all assets of the estate.
- Pay all valid debts, funeral expenses, and estate administration costs.
- Pay estate duty (if applicable — currently abolished in Malaysia, but prior to 1991 applicable).
- Distribute the residue to beneficiaries/entitled persons in accordance with the will or Distribution Act 1958.
- Maintain proper accounts — beneficiaries have the right to inspect estate accounts.

**PRACTICAL NOTES**
— Application for grant of probate: Check whether the estate includes property in other states/jurisdictions — may require resealing or separate applications.
— EPF and insurance nominations do not form part of the estate and pass directly to the nominee — advise clients to update nominations whenever a will is made or circumstances change.
— For small estates (below RM2 million excluding immovable property): Amanah Raya has simplified procedures. For larger estates, always go through the High Court Probate Registry.
— Limitation for estate claims: 12 years from the date the right accrues (Limitation Act 1953, s.8) for recovery of property from the estate. Claims against the estate for debts: 6 years.
— In contentious probate, obtain medical records of the deceased to assess testamentary capacity. Specialist psychiatric or geriatric expert evidence is often required.
relatedCases: Banks v Goodfellow (1870) LR 5 QB 549 (testamentary capacity — widely applied in Malaysia)
Wong Ah Ngoh v Lim Kooi Hean [1998] 5 MLJ 209 (undue influence in wills)
Re Estate of Syed Abdullah bin Omar Syed Ja'far Al Mashor [2000] 5 MLJ 349 (contentious probate procedure)
Rajah Hamid bin Raja Majid v Tan Sri Datuk Lim Goh Tong [1987] 2 MLJ 484 (constructive trust)
Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (trust — historical, applied in Malaysia for constructive trust principles)
keyPrinciples: Always ensure the original will is kept safely. A will that cannot be produced will need to be proved by secondary evidence — a difficult task. Advise clients to deposit wills with their solicitors or with the Probate Registry.
EPF, insurance, and Tabung Haji savings with valid nominations pass outside the estate — they do not form part of the testator's estate for distribution. This is frequently misunderstood by clients.

If you suspect testamentary capacity is in issue, obtain the deceased's medical records from hospitals and GPs immediately. Medical evidence of cognitive decline or mental illness near the time of will-making is crucial for a capacity challenge.

In contentious probate proceedings, the burden of proving the will is on the propounder (executor). Once the will is proved, the burden shifts to the challenger to prove the specific vitiating factor (undue influence, fraud, etc.).

For estates with immovable property in multiple states in Malaysia, a Grant of Probate from one state High Court may need to be resealed in the land registry of the state where the property is situated (NLC, s.347).

theory_topics.title: Interlocutory Applications, Interim Orders & Applications in Chambers
theory_topics.overview: Interlocutory and interim applications are the procedural tools used between commencement of an action and final judgment. They are typically heard 'in chambers' before a Judge or Senior Assistant Registrar (SAR) of the High Court. These applications are governed primarily by Order 32 (Applications and Proceedings in Chambers), Order 29 (Injunctions, Interim Preservation of Property, Interim Payments), and various other Orders of the Rules of Court 2012. Mastery of chamber practice is fundamental to Malaysian civil litigation — the great bulk of pre-trial work happens in chambers, not in open court.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: WHAT IS AN INTERLOCUTORY APPLICATION?**

An **interlocutory application** is any application made to the court between the commencement of proceedings and final judgment. It does not finally dispose of the substantive rights of the parties; rather, it deals with procedural, evidential, or interim matters incidental to the main action. Common examples include applications for summary judgment, striking out, discovery, amendment of pleadings, and interim injunctions.

**Interim orders** are orders that are temporary in nature, designed to preserve the status quo, protect rights, or hold the ring pending the full hearing of the dispute. Interim orders include interim injunctions, Mareva (freezing) orders, Anton Piller (search) orders, interim payment orders, and orders for the preservation or detention of property.

**Applications in chambers** is the procedural mode by which most interlocutory applications are heard. Under **Order 32 r 1 ROC 2012**, "every application in chambers shall be made by summons" except where the rules expressly provide otherwise. Chambers proceedings are conducted in private (not open court), before a Judge in Chambers or before a Senior Assistant Registrar (SAR), depending on the nature of the application.

**PART 2: STATUTORY AND PROCEDURAL FRAMEWORK**

The principal sources of law and procedure are:
- **Rules of Court 2012 (PU(A) 205/2012)** — particularly Order 32 (Applications in Chambers), Order 29 (Injunctions, Interim Preservation, Interim Payments), Order 14 (Summary Judgment), Order 18 r 19 (Striking Out), Order 24 (Discovery), Order 26 (Interrogatories), Order 33 (Mode of Trial / Preliminary Issues), Order 34 (Pre-Trial Case Management), Order 41 (Affidavits), Order 56 (Appeals from the Registrar), Order 92 r 4 (inherent jurisdiction).
- **Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (Act 91), s. 25(2) and the Schedule** — the additional powers of the High Court, including the power to grant injunctions in any case in which it appears just or convenient.
- **Specific Relief Act 1950 (Act 137), Part III (ss. 50–55)** — preventive relief by injunction; perpetual and temporary injunctions; mandatory injunctions; injunctions to perform negative agreements.
- **Civil Law Act 1956 (Act 67), s. 24** — saving for the rules of equity.
- **Subordinate Courts Rules 1980** for Sessions and Magistrates Courts (where relevant; though most chamber practice now follows ROC 2012 forms).

**PART 3: TYPES OF INTERLOCUTORY APPLICATIONS**

**(A) Procedural / Pleading Stage Applications**
- Striking out of pleadings or endorsement (Order 18 r 19) — on grounds of (a) no reasonable cause of action or defence; (b) scandalous, frivolous or vexatious; (c) prejudice or embarrassment to fair trial; (d) abuse of court process.
- Amendment of pleadings (Order 20) — adding or substituting parties, amending the writ or pleadings.
- Further and better particulars (Order 18 r 12).
- Striking out for want of prosecution (Order 25 r 1).
- Setting aside default judgment (Order 13 r 8 / Order 19 r 9).
- Application to enter appearance / extend time (Order 12).

**(B) Summary Disposal Applications**
- **Summary Judgment under Order 14** — Plaintiff applies for judgment on the basis that the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim.
- **Order 14A** (determination of question of law) — court may, on application or its own motion, determine any question of law or construction of any document where (a) the question is suitable for summary determination without a full trial; (b) the determination will finally determine the entire cause or matter or any claim or issue.
- **Order 81** (Specific Performance, etc. by summary procedure).

**(C) Discovery and Evidence-Gathering Applications**
- General discovery and inspection (Order 24).
- Specific discovery (Order 24 r 7).
- Interrogatories (Order 26).
- Pre-action discovery and discovery against non-parties (Order 24 r 7A) — including Norwich Pharmacal-type orders.
- Subpoena ad testificandum / duces tecum (Order 38).

**(D) Interim Injunctive and Preservation Relief**
- **Prohibitory injunction** (interim) — restraining the defendant from doing some act pending trial.
- **Mandatory injunction** (interim) — compelling the defendant to do some act pending trial.
- **Quia timet injunction** — restraining an apprehended (not yet committed) wrong.
- **Mareva (freezing) injunction** — restraining the defendant from disposing of or dissipating assets pending judgment.
- **Anton Piller (search) order** — permitting the plaintiff to enter the defendant's premises to search for and preserve evidence.
- **Erinford injunction** — preserving the status quo pending an appeal.
- Orders for preservation, detention, custody, sale, inspection, sampling, or experimentation upon property (Order 29 r 2).
- **Interim payments** (Order 29 rr 10–18) — interim payment by a defendant on account of damages or debt likely to be recovered.

**(E) Procedural Management Applications**
- Pre-trial case management directions (Order 34).
- Consolidation of actions (Order 4 r 1).
- Trial of preliminary issues (Order 33).
- Security for costs (Order 23).
- Stay of proceedings — pending arbitration (s.10 Arbitration Act 2005), pending appeal, or on case-management grounds.
- Transfer of proceedings between courts (Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.27; Subordinate Courts Act 1948, s.31).

**(F) Enforcement-Related Interlocutory Applications**
- Garnishee order nisi / absolute (Order 49).
- Charging orders (Order 50).
- Judgment debtor summons (Order 48).
- Committal for contempt (Order 52).

**PART 4: APPLICATIONS IN CHAMBERS — PROCEDURE AND FORMS**

**Mode of Application** — **Order 32 r 1**: Every application in chambers is made by **Notice of Application** (Form 57 ROC 2012) supported by an **Affidavit** (Form 65 ROC 2012). Until the 2012 Rules, the equivalent was a "Summons in Chambers" — practitioners still commonly use that terminology. The Notice of Application:
- Identifies the parties and the action;
- States the relief sought (the orders prayed for);
- Specifies the date, time and place of hearing;
- Is supported by one or more affidavits exhibiting documentary evidence.

**Inter Partes vs Ex Parte:**
- **Inter partes** (the default): both sides appear and are heard. Applies to most interlocutory applications.
- **Ex parte**: only the applicant appears, without notice to the other side. Reserved for cases of urgency or where notice would defeat the purpose of the order (e.g., Mareva injunctions, Anton Piller orders, freezing of bank accounts). Ex parte orders are by their nature time-limited and must come back inter partes for a return date — **Order 29 r 1(2A)** requires an ex parte injunction to be inter partes within 14 days unless the court otherwise orders.

**Hearing in Chambers** — Hearings before a Judge in Chambers or SAR are private (not open to the public). The procedure is informal: counsel make oral submissions, often with skeleton submissions filed beforehand. Formal evidence-in-chief is by affidavit; cross-examination on affidavits is rare and requires leave (Order 38 r 2(3)).

**Affidavit Requirements (Order 41):**
- Affidavits must be sworn or affirmed before a Commissioner for Oaths.
- Must state the deponent's full name, NRIC, occupation and address.
- Must be confined to facts within the deponent's personal knowledge, save for interlocutory proceedings where statements based on information and belief are admissible — provided the source is identified (Order 41 r 5).
- Exhibits must be marked, paginated, and identified by an exhibit slip signed by the Commissioner for Oaths.

**Sequence of Affidavits:**
1. **Affidavit in Support** — filed with the Notice of Application by the applicant.
2. **Affidavit in Reply / Opposition** — filed by the respondent.
3. **Affidavit in Rejoinder** — filed by the applicant in response.
4. Further affidavits only with leave of court.

**PART 5: INTERIM INJUNCTIONS — PRINCIPLES**

The leading test is **American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396** (HL), adopted in Malaysia in **Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah & Ors [1995] 1 MLJ 193** (CA). The court asks:
1. **Is there a serious question to be tried?** — not a high threshold; the claim must not be frivolous or vexatious.
2. **Are damages an adequate remedy?** — for either party. If damages would adequately compensate the plaintiff and the defendant can pay, no injunction.
3. **Where does the balance of convenience lie?** — including: status quo, irreparable harm, comparative hardship, public interest, the strength of each party's case if obvious.

For **mandatory** interim injunctions, the test is stricter: a high degree of assurance that at trial it will appear the injunction was rightly granted (**Films Rover International Ltd v Cannon Film Sales Ltd [1987] 1 WLR 670**, applied locally).

**Undertaking as to Damages:** Every applicant for an interim injunction must give an undertaking to pay damages to the respondent if the injunction is later found to have been wrongly granted (Order 29 r 2A). Failure to give the undertaking is fatal.

**Mareva Injunction** — Additional requirements:
1. A good arguable case on the merits.
2. Real risk of dissipation or removal of assets.
3. Balance of convenience favouring the order.
4. Full and frank disclosure on the ex parte application — failure is grounds for immediate discharge (**Bank Mellat v Nikpour [1985] FSR 87**; locally applied in **Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 97**).

**Anton Piller Order** — A draconian remedy. Three essential conditions (per Ormrod LJ in **Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55**, applied in **Lian Keow Sdn Bhd v Paramjothy [1982] 1 MLJ 217**):
1. An extremely strong prima facie case.
2. The damage, potential or actual, must be very serious.
3. Clear evidence that the defendant has incriminating documents/items and a real possibility of their destruction before an inter partes application.

**PART 6: HEARING, ORDERS AND COSTS**

**The Order:** The Registrar (or Judge) records the order made and issues a sealed order. Drafting the order is the responsibility of the successful party's solicitor — submitted for sealing within 14 days. The order takes effect from the date of pronouncement, not the date of sealing, unless the court directs otherwise.

**Penal Notice:** Injunctions and orders requiring a person to do or refrain from an act must carry a **penal notice** — a warning that disobedience may result in committal for contempt, sequestration of assets or fine. Without a penal notice, contempt proceedings cannot be founded on the order (**RHB Bank Bhd v Tan Sweet Bee [2009]**).

**Costs in Chambers:** The court has wide discretion over costs of an interlocutory application (Order 59). Common orders:
- "Costs in the cause" — costs follow the event of the main action.
- "Costs in any event" — fixed for one party regardless of trial outcome.
- "Costs reserved" — to be decided at a later stage or at trial.
- "No order as to costs" — each party bears own costs.
- "Costs thrown away" — costs wasted because of the other party's amendment, adjournment, etc.

**PART 7: APPEALS FROM CHAMBER DECISIONS**

- **Appeal from SAR to Judge in Chambers** — by Notice of Appeal (Form 110) filed within 14 days; reheard de novo by the Judge (Order 56 ROC 2012).
- **Appeal from Judge in Chambers to Court of Appeal** — by Notice of Appeal filed in the High Court Registry within 30 days from the date the order was sealed, with leave required for non-final orders that fall within s.68 Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (the so-called "leave-required" categories).
- **Stay of execution pending appeal** — must be applied for separately under Order 55 r 16 ROC 2012; not automatic upon filing the appeal.

**PART 8: PRACTICAL POINTS AND COMMON PITFALLS**

— **Use the correct form**: Notice of Application (Form 57) for chamber applications. Originating Summons (Form 5) is for commencing an action where there is no substantial dispute of fact.
— **Affidavits must be sworn before filing** — unsigned or unsworn affidavits cannot be used and will be struck out.
— **Hearsay in interlocutory affidavits** is permitted (Order 41 r 5(2)) but the source of information and belief MUST be identified — a "bare assertion" affidavit is liable to be given little weight.
— **Service:** Notice of Application must be served at least **2 clear days** before the hearing (Order 32 r 3) — except for urgent ex parte applications.
— **Bundle of documents:** A small chambers bundle (typically the Notice of Application, all affidavits, sealed order/cause papers, written submissions, list of authorities) should be prepared and filed/submitted in advance for the convenience of the court.
— **Skeleton submissions:** Increasingly expected — file at least 2 days before hearing. Bundle of authorities (cases marked at relevant passages) should accompany.
— **Full and frank disclosure** in ex parte applications is a sacred duty — material non-disclosure (whether deliberate or innocent) almost invariably leads to discharge of the order with costs on an indemnity basis.
— **Drafting the prayer**: Be precise. Vague or omnibus prayers ("such other relief as the court deems fit" alone is insufficient) lead to unenforceable orders.
— **Time limits are strict**: Many interlocutory applications have rigid time bars (e.g., setting aside default judgment within reasonable time; appeal from Registrar within 14 days). Late applications require leave to extend time and are not always granted.

**PART 9: INTERLOCUTORY vs FINAL ORDERS — WHY IT MATTERS**

The distinction is crucial for appeal purposes. **Section 68 of the Courts of Judicature Act 1964** restricts appeals to the Court of Appeal in certain categories of "interlocutory" decisions to those made with leave. The leading test for whether an order is interlocutory or final is the **"order test"** affirmed by the Federal Court in **Asia Commercial Finance (M) Bhd v Kawal Teliti Sdn Bhd [1995] 3 MLJ 189** — does the order, as actually made, finally dispose of the rights of the parties? If yes, it is final; if no, interlocutory. Striking out and summary judgment, when granted, are final orders (the action is disposed of); refusal of striking out or summary judgment is interlocutory.
legislation: Rules of Court 2012, Order 32 (Applications and Proceedings in Chambers)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 (Injunctions, Interim Preservation of Property, Interim Payments)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 18 r 19 (Striking Out)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 56 (Appeals from the Registrar)
Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (Act 91), s. 25(2) and Schedule
Specific Relief Act 1950 (Act 137), Part III, ss. 50–55
relatedCases: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 (HL) — adopted in Malaysia for interim injunction principles
Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah & Ors [1995] 1 MLJ 193 (CA) — the leading Malaysian formulation of the interim injunction test
Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA [1975] 2 Lloyd's Rep 509 — origin of the Mareva (freezing) injunction
Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55 — three-condition test for search orders
Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 97 (SC) — full and frank disclosure in Mareva applications
Lian Keow Sdn Bhd v Paramjothy [1982] 1 MLJ 217 — Anton Piller in Malaysia
Asia Commercial Finance (M) Bhd v Kawal Teliti Sdn Bhd [1995] 3 MLJ 189 (FC) — order test for distinguishing interlocutory and final orders
Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v United Malayan Banking Corporation Bhd [1993] 3 MLJ 36 — striking out under Order 18 r 19
National Company for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya Sdn Bhd [1984] 2 MLJ 300 (FC) — Order 14 summary judgment principles
keyPrinciples: Master the Notice of Application + Affidavit format (Forms 57 and 65 ROC 2012). The vast majority of pre-trial work in Malaysian civil litigation is done by way of chamber applications — clean, well-drafted, and properly supported applications save weeks of court time.

On any ex parte application, full and frank disclosure of all material facts (including those adverse to the applicant's case) is mandatory. Material non-disclosure is the single most common reason for discharge of ex parte orders, with costs on an indemnity basis.

Always check whether the order sought is interlocutory or final — this determines the appellate route under s.68 Courts of Judicature Act 1964 and whether leave to appeal is required. Apply the Asia Commercial Finance 'order test'.

An undertaking as to damages is a non-negotiable precondition for any interim injunction. The undertaking must be expressly recorded in the order. Where the plaintiff is impecunious or foreign, the court may require the undertaking to be fortified by security or a bank guarantee.
Never proceed with enforcement of an injunction without a properly endorsed penal notice. Without it, no contempt proceeding for breach can succeed.

theory_topics.title: Mareva Injunctions (Freezing Orders) — Deep Dive
theory_topics.overview: The Mareva injunction (now commonly called a 'freezing order') is one of the most powerful weapons in the civil litigator's armoury. It restrains a defendant from disposing of, dealing with, or removing assets pending judgment, so that the eventual judgment is not rendered worthless by asset dissipation. Originating in the English Court of Appeal decision in Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA [1975] 2 Lloyd's Rep 509, the jurisdiction was received into Malaysian law via s.25(2) and the Schedule to the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 and is regularly granted by the Malaysian High Court — most prominently affirmed in Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 97. This topic is a deep dive into the principles, procedure, drafting, ancillary orders, defences, and pitfalls of Mareva practice.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: ORIGIN, JURISDICTION AND CHARACTER**

The Mareva injunction is an in personam equitable remedy. It does not give the plaintiff a proprietary right over the frozen assets — the defendant remains the legal owner. Its purpose is purely protective: to prevent the defendant from frustrating the eventual judgment.

**Jurisdictional source in Malaysia:**
- **Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (Act 91), s. 25(2) and the Schedule** — High Court has power to grant an injunction in any case in which it appears just or convenient.
- **Specific Relief Act 1950 (Act 137), Part III, ss. 50–55** — preventive relief by injunction.
- **Rules of Court 2012, Order 29** — procedural framework for injunction applications.
- **Civil Law Act 1956 (Act 67), s. 24** — saving for the rules of equity.

**Foundational Malaysian authorities:**
- **Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 97 (SC)** — confirmed Mareva is part of Malaysian law; emphasised duty of full and frank disclosure.
- **Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd v Lorrain Osman [1985] 2 MLJ 236** — first Malaysian recognition of Mareva.
- **Eng Mee Yong v V Letchumanan [1979] 2 MLJ 212 (FC)** — though decided on caveats, articulated equitable injunction principles.
- **Creative Furnishing Sdn Bhd v Wong Koi [1989] 2 MLJ 153** — application in the construction debt context.

**PART 2: SUBSTANTIVE TEST**

The applicant must satisfy each of the following:

**(1) Good arguable case on the merits.** Higher than a "serious question to be tried" (the Cyanamid threshold) but lower than balance of probabilities. Per Mustill J in Ninemia Maritime Corp v Trave Schiffahrtsgesellschaft GmbH [1983] 1 WLR 1412 — adopted locally — the applicant must show "a case which is more than barely capable of serious argument and yet not necessarily one which the judge believes to have a better than 50 per cent chance of success".

**(2) Real risk of dissipation, removal or concealment of assets.** This is the heart of the Mareva. Mere assertion is insufficient — concrete evidence is required. Indicia commonly accepted by Malaysian courts:
- Pattern of recent unexplained large transfers.
- Defendant's commercial dishonesty, fraud, or concealment in dealings with the plaintiff.
- Defendant resident or with assets in non-cooperative jurisdictions.
- Defendant a foreign company with no physical presence in Malaysia.
- Recent attempts to put assets beyond reach of creditors (e.g., transfer to family members, trusts).
- Pending or imminent insolvency of defendant.

**(3) Balance of convenience.** Weigh the prejudice to the plaintiff if no order is made (judgment may be unenforceable) against the prejudice to the defendant of having assets frozen.

**(4) Identifiable assets within the court's jurisdiction (or, for worldwide Marevas, abroad).** The applicant should identify, so far as possible, the specific assets to be frozen — bank accounts, real property, shares, vehicles. A general "all assets" formula is permissible but the affidavit must justify the breadth.

**(5) Undertaking as to damages.** Mandatory under Order 29 r 2A. The undertaking may need to be **fortified** by security, bank guarantee, or payment into court — particularly where the applicant is impecunious or foreign.

**PART 3: EX PARTE PROCEDURE — FULL AND FRANK DISCLOSURE**

A Mareva is almost invariably sought ex parte (without notice) because notice would defeat the order's purpose. The applicant therefore owes the court a strict duty of **full and frank disclosure**:

- All material facts within the applicant's knowledge — including those adverse to the application.
- Any potential defences known to the applicant.
- Any previous unsuccessful application or any reason the application might be refused.
- The respondent's likely answer if it had been heard.

**Consequences of breach:** The standard remedy is discharge of the order with costs on the **indemnity basis**, and possible dismissal of any later renewed application — see Bank Mellat v Nikpour [1985] FSR 87 and Aspatra (above).

**PART 4: ANCILLARY ORDERS COMMONLY GRANTED WITH A MAREVA**

A bare freezing order is often inadequate. The court will commonly grant ancillary orders to make the freeze effective:

- **Disclosure of assets order** — defendant ordered to identify all assets above a value within (or worldwide), confirm by affidavit. Failure = contempt.
- **Order against banks (notice to third parties)** — banks served with the order are bound and must freeze the defendant's accounts; banks may be heard for variation.
- **Restraint on encumbering or transferring real property** — registration of the order against title.
- **Order for delivery up** — of specific assets (e.g., a specific car, jewellery) into the custody of the court or the plaintiff's solicitors.
- **Cross-examination on assets affidavit** — where the asset affidavit is suspected to be false or incomplete.
- **Living expenses and legal expenses exceptions** — defendant permitted to draw a specified sum from frozen funds for ordinary living expenses, and legal fees in the action.
- **Worldwide Mareva** — restraining dealings with assets anywhere in the world; Malaysian courts will grant only on strong evidence and with reciprocal undertakings (Babanaft v Bassatne carve-out).

**PART 5: STANDARD FORM — STRUCTURE OF A MAREVA ORDER**

A typical Mareva order (drawn from English Commercial Court precedent and adapted to Malaysian practice) contains:
1. **Penal notice** at the head — warning of consequences of breach.
2. **Recitals** — undertaking as to damages, undertaking to issue substantive proceedings, undertaking re. service.
3. **Operative restraints** — defendant restrained from disposing of, dealing with or diminishing assets up to the value of [RM amount].
4. **Identified assets** (where known) — bank accounts (number/branch), real property (title/lot), shares, vehicles.
5. **Ancillary disclosure order** — defendant to swear and serve an affidavit identifying all assets above [RM threshold] within [N days].
6. **Living expenses / legal expenses provisos** — defendant permitted to spend up to [RM] per week on ordinary living expenses, and reasonable legal expenses on this and any other action.
7. **Notice to third parties** — banks and others on notice are bound; may apply to vary.
8. **Return date** for inter partes hearing.
9. **Liberty to apply** to vary or discharge.

**PART 6: DEFENCES AND APPLICATIONS TO DISCHARGE**

A defendant served with a Mareva should consider:
- **Material non-disclosure** — usually the first and best ground.
- **No good arguable case** on the merits.
- **No real risk of dissipation** — produce evidence of legitimate business and absence of suspicious transfers.
- **Order too widely drawn** — apply to narrow.
- **Ordinary course of business** — exceptions for paying ordinary trading debts, taxes, salaries, mortgage instalments.
- **Inadequate undertaking** — apply for fortification.
- **Living and legal expenses** — apply for proviso.
- **Variation** of identified assets — to release particular accounts not needed for the freeze.

**PART 7: ENFORCEMENT — COMMITTAL FOR CONTEMPT**

Breach of a Mareva is contempt of court. The procedure (Order 52 ROC 2012):
1. **Application for leave** to issue committal proceedings — by Notice of Application + Affidavit of breach.
2. If leave granted, **Notice of Motion for Committal** (Form 109).
3. Service personally on the contemnor.
4. Hearing — court may impose imprisonment (up to the maximum recognised), fine, or sequestration of assets.

The **penal notice** must have been endorsed on the order and the order personally served before contempt proceedings can be founded (Order 45 r 7).

**PART 8: WORLDWIDE MAREVAS AND CROSS-BORDER CONSIDERATIONS**

The Malaysian High Court has jurisdiction to grant a worldwide Mareva but will do so cautiously. Practical considerations:
- Standard Babanaft and Derby & Co carve-outs to protect third parties and ensure the order is not penal extraterritorially.
- Coordination with proceedings in other jurisdictions (Singapore, Hong Kong, England) where mirror orders may be needed.
- Norwich Pharmacal-type orders to identify assets held by third parties (banks, trustees).
- Asset tracing experts may be retained to identify and locate hidden assets.

**PART 9: PRACTICAL POINTS FOR PRACTITIONERS**

— **Investigate before applying.** Engage forensic accountants or asset tracers if necessary. Speculative Mareva applications fail and result in indemnity costs against the applicant.
— **Draft narrowly.** A precisely drawn order is harder to discharge than a broad sweep. Identify accounts and assets if you can.
— **Prepare for the return date.** Material non-disclosure may emerge from the defendant's reply affidavit; have evidence ready.
— **Always include living and legal expenses provisos.** Failure to do so often leads to the order being varied or discharged on humanitarian grounds.
— **Consider the 'commercial damage' exception.** A Mareva should not paralyse a legitimate business. Plan for ordinary trading exceptions if the defendant is a going concern.
— **Watch the limitation issue.** If the substantive cause of action is close to time-barring, file the writ first; the Mareva is parasitic on the main action.
— **Costs.** Successful Mareva: costs in the cause or against the defendant. Discharged Mareva for non-disclosure: indemnity costs against the applicant.
legislation: Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (Act 91), s.25(2) and Schedule
Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 (Injunctions, Interim Preservation, Interim Payments)
Specific Relief Act 1950 (Act 137), Part III, ss.50–55
Rules of Court 2012, Order 45 r 7 (Personal service of orders)
relatedCases: Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA [1975] 2 Lloyd's Rep 509 (CA) — origin of the freezing order
Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 97 (SC) — Malaysian leading case
Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd v Lorrain Osman [1985] 2 MLJ 236 — first Malaysian Mareva
Ninemia Maritime Corp v Trave Schiffahrtsgesellschaft GmbH [1983] 1 WLR 1412 — 'good arguable case' threshold
Bank Mellat v Nikpour [1985] FSR 87 (CA) — full and frank disclosure
Babanaft International Co SA v Bassatne [1990] Ch 13 — worldwide Mareva carve-outs
Derby & Co Ltd v Weldon (No 1) [1990] Ch 48 — worldwide Mareva principles
Eng Mee Yong v V Letchumanan [1979] 2 MLJ 212 (FC) — equitable injunction principles
keyPrinciples: A Mareva is a discretionary equitable remedy granted to prevent dissipation of assets — not as a means of obtaining security for an unsecured debt. The applicant must show real risk of dissipation, not mere convenience.

On any ex parte Mareva application, full and frank disclosure of all material facts is mandatory and absolute. Material non-disclosure is the most common ground for discharge — followed by indemnity costs.

Always include living-expense and legal-expense provisos. The Mareva is meant to preserve, not to suffocate. Courts will discharge or vary orders that leave the defendant unable to live or defend the action.
The undertaking as to damages must be expressly recorded. For impecunious or foreign applicants, expect the court to require fortification by bank guarantee, security, or payment into court.
Endorse the order with a clear penal notice and effect personal service before any thought of contempt proceedings. Without these, breach is unenforceable.

theory_topics.title: Anton Piller Orders (Search Orders) — Deep Dive
theory_topics.overview: The Anton Piller order — sometimes called a 'search order' — is among the most draconian remedies in civil practice. It permits the applicant (with a supervising solicitor) to enter the respondent's premises without prior notice to search for, inspect, copy and preserve specified evidence. Originating in Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55, the order was received into Malaysian law in Lian Keow Sdn Bhd (in liquidation) v Paramjothy [1982] 1 MLJ 217 (FC) and is granted only in the rarest cases of fraud, breach of confidence, IP infringement, or similar conduct where there is clear evidence of incriminating items and a real risk of destruction.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: NATURE OF THE ORDER**

An Anton Piller order is not a search warrant — it does not authorise forcible entry. It operates *in personam*: it commands the respondent, on pain of contempt, to permit the applicant's representatives to enter and search. Refusal is contempt and may give rise to adverse inferences at trial. The order is invariably ex parte (without notice); the whole point is surprise.

**Jurisdictional source in Malaysia:**
- **Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (Act 91), s.25(2) and Schedule** — additional powers of the High Court.
- **Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 r 2** — preservation of property pending trial.
- **Specific Relief Act 1950, ss.50–55**.
- **Inherent jurisdiction** under Order 92 r 4.

**PART 2: THE THREE-CONDITION TEST**

Per Ormrod LJ in **Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55**, adopted in **Lian Keow v Paramjothy [1982] 1 MLJ 217**:

**(1) An extremely strong prima facie case.** Far higher than the *Keet Gerald* "serious question". Effectively, near-certainty of success at trial.

**(2) Very serious actual or potential damage.** Damage that monetary judgment cannot adequately compensate — typically destruction of unique evidence or trade secrets.

**(3) Clear evidence that the respondent has incriminating documents/items in possession** AND **a real possibility of destruction** before any inter partes application.

The court additionally considers:
- Whether the order is necessary in the interests of justice.
- Whether the prejudice to the respondent is proportionate.
- The capacity and probity of the supervising solicitor.

**PART 3: SUPERVISING SOLICITOR**

The order is executed under the supervision of an independent solicitor (the **supervising solicitor**) who is not the applicant's regular solicitor. The supervising solicitor:
- Explains the order to the respondent in plain language.
- Advises the respondent of the right to seek legal advice (and may delay execution for a short period to allow this).
- Supervises the search — present at all times, ensures only items within the order are taken/imaged.
- Lists everything taken.
- Ensures female respondents are afforded appropriate dignity (a female member of the search party where possible).
- Reports to the court on the conduct of the search by affidavit.

The supervising solicitor's role is the principal safeguard against abuse.

**PART 4: TYPICAL TERMS OF AN ANTON PILLER ORDER**

A standard order includes:
- **Penal notice** at the head.
- **Undertakings** by the applicant: as to damages; to issue substantive proceedings; to serve respondent immediately; to abide by the supervising solicitor's instructions; to compensate the respondent if items are damaged or removed wrongfully.
- **Permission to enter** specified premises during specified hours (typically business hours on a working day).
- **Right to search** for specified categories of documents/items.
- **Right to inspect, photograph, image (forensically clone), and seize** specified items.
- **Restrictions** — no removal of items beyond a specified value without the supervising solicitor's permission; items returned within a specified period unless the court orders otherwise.
- **Imaging of computers/digital media** by an independent computer expert.
- **List and receipt** for everything taken.
- **Restraints on respondent** — not to inform third parties for 72 hours (to allow related searches); not to destroy or remove evidence.
- **Permission to apply** by respondent for variation/discharge on short notice.

**PART 5: EXECUTION ON THE GROUND**

Practical sequence:
1. **Plan the execution** — the search team typically comprises: supervising solicitor, applicant's solicitor (1–2), independent computer expert, applicant's representative familiar with the items sought.
2. **Arrive** at the premises during the permitted hours. Usually 9:30–10:00 a.m.
3. **Identify yourselves** and present the order to the most senior person present. The supervising solicitor reads and explains.
4. **Wait for legal advice** — typically up to 2 hours for the respondent to obtain solicitor's advice.
5. **Execute the search** — methodically, room by room, in the supervising solicitor's presence.
6. **Image computers** — original drives untouched; forensic clone taken with verifiable hash.
7. **List and receipt** every item taken or imaged.
8. **Depart** within the permitted hours.
9. **Lodge** seized originals with the supervising solicitor or court within 24–48 hours.
10. **File** the supervising solicitor's report with the court.

**PART 6: RESPONDENT'S RESPONSES**

A respondent served with an Anton Piller may:
- **Comply** — but consult solicitor as soon as possible.
- **Apply to discharge** on the return date (typically 14 days).
- **Apply for early variation** — e.g., to limit the scope of imaging, to exclude legally privileged material.
- **Claim privilege against self-incrimination** — particularly where the order touches matters of criminal liability (e.g., copyright piracy, fraud).
- **Claim legal professional privilege** — privileged documents must be excluded from inspection.
- **Refuse to comply** — but at the very serious risk of contempt; raise objection in court instead.

**PART 7: COMMON USE CASES IN MALAYSIA**

- **Trade secrets misappropriation** — former employee or business partner suspected of taking confidential customer lists, technical know-how, source code.
- **IP infringement** — counterfeiting, software piracy, trade mark infringement (often in tandem with police-assisted seizures under the Trade Marks Act 2019 or Copyright Act 1987).
- **Fraud** — to preserve documents demonstrating embezzlement, accounting irregularities, undisclosed commissions.
- **Breach of confidence** — in technology, pharmaceutical, and financial-services disputes.
- **Pre-action discovery** — rare; usually attached to the substantive action.

**PART 8: PRIVILEGES AND PROTECTIONS**

- **Legal professional privilege** — items covered by LPP cannot be inspected; supervising solicitor segregates and seals such items pending court ruling.
- **Privilege against self-incrimination** — under Malaysian law, the privilege is narrower than in English law (Tan Boon Bak & Sons Ltd v RHB Bank [2001]); but where genuine criminal exposure exists, items relating to that risk may be protected.
- **Without prejudice communications** — protected from inspection.
- **Confidential information of unrelated third parties** — supervising solicitor will not allow inspection of materials clearly belonging to unconnected business of the respondent.

**PART 9: CONSEQUENCES OF ABUSE**

The court takes a serious view of abuse of the Anton Piller jurisdiction. Where the order has been wrongly obtained or wrongly executed:
- **Discharge of the order** with **indemnity costs** to the applicant.
- **Damages** under the cross-undertaking — sometimes substantial (loss of business, reputation damage).
- **Striking out** of the substantive action in egregious cases.
- **Disciplinary referral** of the applicant's solicitor or supervising solicitor for professional misconduct.

**PART 10: PRACTICAL POINTS**

— **Use sparingly.** Anton Pillers are not for ordinary disputes. The bar is intentionally high.
— **Independent supervising solicitor is non-negotiable.** Reputable, experienced, available on the day. Brief them thoroughly.
— **Forensic computer expert.** Engage one before applying. Hash-verified imaging is standard practice.
— **Penal notice and personal service.** Standard requirements.
— **Plan for delays.** The respondent may take 1–2 hours to obtain legal advice; the search may take a full day for complex premises.
— **Document everything.** Photograph the premises before, during, after. Keep a contemporaneous log. Both supervising and applicant's solicitors must be ready to give evidence on the conduct of the search.
— **Confidentiality.** The applicant's team must observe strict confidentiality regarding material seen in the course of execution that is not relevant to the action.
legislation: Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (Act 91), s.25(2) and Schedule
Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 r 2 (Preservation of Property)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 92 r 4 (Inherent Jurisdiction)
relatedCases: Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55 (CA) — origin of the search order
Lian Keow Sdn Bhd v Paramjothy [1982] 1 MLJ 217 (FC) — Anton Piller in Malaysia
Universal Thermosensors Ltd v Hibben [1992] 1 WLR 840 — guidelines for execution
Columbia Picture Industries Inc v Robinson [1987] Ch 38 — abuse of Anton Piller
Petrofina (UK) Ltd v Magnaload Ltd [1984] QB 127 — discharge for non-disclosure
Tan Boon Bak & Sons Ltd v RHB Bank [2001] — privilege against self-incrimination in Malaysia
keyPrinciples: The Anton Piller is exceptional. The three Ormrod conditions are stringent — extremely strong prima facie case, very serious damage, clear evidence of items and real risk of destruction. Marginal cases will be refused.
An independent supervising solicitor is the principal safeguard against abuse. Engage a solicitor of standing and experience, brief them thoroughly, and respect their authority on the day.

Document the search exhaustively — contemporaneous logs, photographs, lists, receipts, hash-verified forensic images. The supervising solicitor's report will be the primary evidence on the conduct of execution.
Respect privileges. Legal professional privilege is sacrosanct; segregate and seal LPP items pending court ruling. Do not inspect unrelated business confidential materials.
A wrongly obtained or wrongly executed Anton Piller results in indemnity costs and substantial damages under the cross-undertaking. Use the remedy only when truly justified.

theory_topics.title: Summary Judgment under Order 14 — Deep Dive
theory_topics.overview: Order 14 of the Rules of Court 2012 provides a procedure by which a plaintiff (and, less commonly, a defendant on a counterclaim) can obtain judgment without a full trial where the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim and there is no other compelling reason why the case should go to trial. It is the workhorse procedure in Malaysian banking litigation — the typical route by which banks obtain judgment for liquidated loan debts. The procedure is governed by Order 14 ROC 2012, the leading Federal Court authority National Co for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya Sdn Bhd [1984] 2 MLJ 300, and a substantial body of subsequent case law on what constitutes a 'triable issue'.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: SCOPE OF ORDER 14**

Order 14 is available where:
- The plaintiff has filed a Writ and Statement of Claim.
- The defendant has entered Memorandum of Appearance.
- The plaintiff believes the defendant has no defence to the claim or any part of it (or no defence except as to amount).

Order 14 covers all causes of action **except**:
- Claims for libel, slander, malicious prosecution, false imprisonment, or seduction (Order 14 r 1(2)).
- Claims based on an allegation of fraud (Order 14 r 1(2)) — but note: the bar is on claims *in* fraud, not claims that incidentally mention fraud. Banking debt claims with allegations of fraudulent transactions can still proceed under Order 14 if the substantive claim is for the debt.
- Probate actions.
- Admiralty actions in rem.

**Companion procedures:**
- **Order 14A** — court may, on application or its own motion, determine any question of law or construction of any document where suitable for summary determination and the determination will dispose of the entire cause/matter or any claim/issue.
- **Order 81** — summary procedure for specific performance, recovery of land, etc.

**PART 2: THE TEST — TWO-STAGE BURDEN**

The leading Malaysian authority is **National Co for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya Sdn Bhd [1984] 2 MLJ 300 (FC)**, supplemented by **Bank Negara Malaysia v Mohd Ismail [1992] 1 MLJ 400 (FC)** and **Voo Min En v Leong Chung Fatt [1982] 2 MLJ 241 (FC)**:

**Stage 1 — Plaintiff's burden:** Establish a prima facie case: the writ and statement of claim disclose a sufficient cause of action; the affidavit verifies the facts and exhibits the supporting documents (loan agreement, statement of account, demand letter, notices).

**Stage 2 — Defendant's burden:** "Show cause" — by affidavit, demonstrate either:
- A **bona fide triable issue** of fact requiring trial — not a 'shadowy' or 'sham' defence; or
- An **arguable point of law** requiring full argument; or
- "Some other reason" why the case should go to trial — e.g., complex factual matrix requiring oral evidence and cross-examination.

The defendant must **condescend to particulars**: a bare assertion is insufficient. Where the defence is shadowy or attended by suspicion, the court may give leave to defend only on terms — typically payment into court of all or part of the claimed sum (Bank Negara v Mohd Ismail).

**PART 3: COMMON ISSUES RAISED IN ORDER 14 BANKING APPLICATIONS**

**Defences raising triable issues (often defeating summary judgment):**
- Misrepresentation inducing the loan agreement.
- Undue influence (especially in spousal/guarantor contexts — Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge applied locally).
- Non est factum — defendant did not understand the nature of the document signed.
- Forgery of signature.
- Fraud in the procurement of the loan.
- Variation of contract or waiver/estoppel.
- Compounding or settlement agreement post-default.
- Statute of limitation (where on the face of the documents the claim may be time-barred).
- Set-off or counterclaim of equivalent or greater value.

**Defences typically NOT raising a triable issue:**
- Mere denial without particulars.
- "I don't owe the bank that amount" without specifying what is disputed.
- Generalised hardship arguments.
- Disputes as to interest computation alone (court can give judgment for principal and direct accounts inquiry on interest).
- Claims of unconscionability without supporting facts.

**PART 4: PROCEDURE STEP-BY-STEP**

1. **Wait for appearance.** Order 14 cannot be filed before the defendant enters Memorandum of Appearance.
2. **File Notice of Application** (Form 57) — within reasonable time of appearance, typically before defence is due.
3. **Affidavit in Support** — by an officer of the plaintiff with personal knowledge, exhibiting:
   - Loan/facility agreement.
   - Statement of account showing computation of debt.
   - Letter of demand.
   - Any pre-action notices.
   - Memorandum of charge or other security documents.
4. **Service** of Notice of Application + affidavit on defendant — at least 4 clear days before hearing (Order 14 r 2(2)).
5. **Defendant's Affidavit in Reply** — typically within 7–14 days of service.
6. **Plaintiff's Affidavit in Rejoinder** (if needed).
7. **Hearing in chambers** — before SAR or Judge in Chambers. Each side argues whether triable issue exists.
8. **Order:**
   - **Judgment for plaintiff** (in whole or in part).
   - **Conditional leave to defend** — defendant may defend on payment of [RM amount] into court within [N days].
   - **Unconditional leave to defend** — full trial.
   - **Adjourned for further evidence** — rare.

**PART 5: ORDER 14 IN BANKING — LIQUIDATED DEBT**

Banks routinely use Order 14 for:
- Recovery of loan principal and accrued interest.
- Judgment on guarantor liability (typically separate from primary debtor).
- Hire purchase deficiency claims after sale of repossessed vehicle.
- Trade finance debts (LC, BG calls).
- Credit card debt.
- Personal loan debt.

**Form of judgment:**
- Liquidated sum (principal).
- Interest at the agreed contractual rate to date of judgment.
- Post-judgment interest (typically 5% pa under court order, or contractual rate if higher and reasonable).
- Costs on the agreed basis (often solicitor-and-client basis under the loan agreement).

**PART 6: ORDER 14A — SUMMARY DETERMINATION OF LAW**

Where the dispute turns on a pure question of law or construction of a document (e.g., interpretation of an indemnity clause), Order 14A provides a faster route than full trial. The court may, on application or own motion, summarily determine the question if:
- The question is suitable for summary determination without full trial of the action; AND
- The determination will dispose of the entire cause or matter or any substantial claim/issue.

**PART 7: APPEAL FROM ORDER 14 DECISIONS**

- Decision by SAR — appeal to Judge in Chambers under Order 56 r 1, within 14 days, by Notice of Appeal (Form 110); reheard de novo.
- Decision by Judge in Chambers granting summary judgment — appeal to Court of Appeal as of right (final order).
- Decision by Judge in Chambers refusing summary judgment / giving leave to defend — appeal to Court of Appeal requires leave under s.68 CJA 1964 (interlocutory order).
- Decision granting **conditional** leave to defend (payment into court) — generally treated as interlocutory; leave required.

**PART 8: STRATEGIC AND PRACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS**

— **Timing.** File Order 14 promptly after appearance. Delay beyond filing of defence may attract objection that the application is premature or that the defendant's defence has crystallised.
— **Affidavit deponent.** Must have personal knowledge of the facts (or identify the source of information and belief). Generic affidavits by junior officers without personal knowledge are vulnerable.
— **Exhibits.** Be exhaustive: every document the plaintiff would rely on at trial. Court will not give summary judgment on inadequate documentary support.
— **Anticipate defences.** Address known defences in the supporting affidavit pre-emptively where possible.
— **Conditional leave.** Where the defence is shadowy but not entirely sham, conditional leave (payment into court) is a useful intermediate result — it tests the bona fides of the defendant.
— **Costs.** On grant of summary judgment: costs in the plaintiff's favour, typically on the agreed contractual basis. On dismissal: costs to defendant in the cause.
— **Banking practice.** Some banks combine Order 14 with simultaneous Order 81 (specific performance) or Order 83 (foreclosure) where appropriate — careful pleading allows multiple summary remedies.
legislation: Rules of Court 2012, Order 14A (Determination of Question of Law)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 81 (Summary Procedure for Specific Performance)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 56 (Appeals from the Registrar)
Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.68 (Restrictions on Appeals)
relatedCases: National Co for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya Sdn Bhd [1984] 2 MLJ 300 (FC) — leading authority on Order 14
Bank Negara Malaysia v Mohd Ismail [1992] 1 MLJ 400 (FC) — conditional leave / payment into court
Voo Min En v Leong Chung Fatt [1982] 2 MLJ 241 (FC) — 'show cause' burden
Esso Standard Malaya Bhd v Southern Cross Airways (Malaya) Bhd [1972] 1 MLJ 168 (FC) — triable issue test
Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd v Esah binti Abdul Ghani [1986] 1 MLJ 16 — banking summary judgment
Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2002] 2 AC 773 (HL) — guarantor undue influence (applied locally)
keyPrinciples: Order 14 is a powerful tool in banking litigation but is not a substitute for trial where genuine triable issues exist. The defendant's burden is to condescend to particulars — bare denial is not enough.
Affidavit evidence must come from a deponent with personal knowledge, exhibit every document the plaintiff would need at trial, and pre-emptively address known defences.
Conditional leave to defend (payment into court) is a useful intermediate result for shadowy defences. It separates bona fide disputes from delaying tactics.
Order 14A is under-used. Where the dispute turns on a pure question of law or document construction, summary determination can save months of trial preparation.
Appellate route: SAR → Judge in Chambers (de novo, 14 days). Judge in Chambers → Court of Appeal (30 days; leave required if interlocutory under Asia Commercial Finance order test).

theory_topics.title: Striking Out, Discovery & Other Common Chamber Applications
theory_topics.overview: Beyond the dramatic interim injunctions and summary judgments, the daily diet of chamber practice in the Malaysian High Court consists of a host of routine but vital applications: striking out under Order 18 r 19, specific discovery under Order 24, interrogatories under Order 26, security for costs under Order 23, amendment of pleadings under Order 20, setting aside default judgment under Order 13/19, stay of proceedings, and pre-trial directions under Order 34. Mastery of these applications — their tests, procedures, drafting conventions, and tactical uses — is the mark of a competent civil litigator. This topic surveys each in turn.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: STRIKING OUT — ORDER 18 r 19**

**Grounds (Order 18 r 19(1)):**
(a) No reasonable cause of action or defence;
(b) Scandalous, frivolous or vexatious;
(c) May prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial;
(d) Otherwise an abuse of the process of the court.

**The threshold — Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v UMBC Bhd [1993] 3 MLJ 36 (SC):** "Plain and obvious" cases only. The court will not embark on a "minute examination" of the case. Striking out is reserved for claims that are obviously unsustainable on a reasonable view of the facts and law.

**Limb (a) — no reasonable cause of action:** No evidence is admissible (Order 18 r 19(2)). The court considers only the pleading itself. Question: assuming everything in the pleading is true, does it disclose any cause of action known to law?

**Limb (b)–(d) — wider grounds:** Evidence is admissible. Examples:
- **Frivolous/vexatious:** claim brought to harass or for ulterior motive; collateral attack on a final judgment.
- **Abuse of process:** *Henderson v Henderson* extended res judicata — claims that should have been raised in earlier proceedings; multiple actions on the same matter.
- **Prejudice/embarrassment:** pleading so prolix or obscure that the defendant cannot fairly meet it.

**Inherent jurisdiction (Order 92 r 4):** Supplementary jurisdiction to strike out. Particularly used for:
- Statute-barred claims patent on face of pleading.
- Want of locus standi.
- Issue estoppel.
- Forum non conveniens (combined with stay).
- Unenforceable agreements (e.g., illegal contracts).

**Procedure:** Notice of Application + Affidavit (for limbs (b)–(d)); Notice of Application alone (for limb (a)). Heard in chambers.

**Outcome:** If granted on the whole pleading, the action is dismissed. If granted in part, the offending parts are struck out and the action proceeds on what remains. Costs typically follow the event.

**PART 2: DISCOVERY AND INSPECTION — ORDER 24**

**General discovery (Order 24 r 3):** Triggered automatically post-pleadings or by court direction. Each party serves a List of Documents in two parts: documents currently in possession/custody/power; documents formerly in possession/custody/power. Privilege claimed where applicable.

**Specific discovery (Order 24 r 7):** Where general discovery is incomplete or inadequate. Notice of Application + Affidavit identifying documents (or class of documents), grounds to believe they exist and are in the respondent's possession/custody/power, and relevance.

**Test for relevance — Compagnie Financiere v Peruvian Guano (1882) 11 QBD 55** (applied in Malaysia): documents that may, either directly or indirectly, enable the requesting party to advance its own case or damage the case of the adversary. The test is broad — even documents that may lead to a chain of inquiry are discoverable.

**Privilege:** Common heads:
- **Legal professional privilege** (legal advice + litigation privilege) — client-solicitor and litigation-anticipation communications.
- **Without prejudice** privilege — settlement communications.
- **Public interest immunity** — government documents on national security/diplomatic grounds.
- **Privilege against self-incrimination** — documents tending to expose criminal liability.

**Pre-action discovery and discovery against non-parties (Order 24 r 7A):** Allows discovery from non-parties where: (a) the documents are likely to be in possession of the non-party; (b) likely to be relevant to an issue in proceedings; (c) disclosure is necessary fairly to dispose of or save costs.

**Norwich Pharmacal-type orders:** Compelling a non-party who is innocently caught up in wrongdoing to disclose information identifying the wrongdoer (e.g., bank disclosing identity of customer who received misappropriated funds).

**PART 3: INTERROGATORIES — ORDER 26**

A formal written question requiring a sworn answer. Used where deposing the answer pre-trial will narrow the issues.

**Test:** Necessary to dispose fairly of the action or save costs (Order 26 r 1).

**Restrictions:**
- Must be relevant.
- Must not be oppressive.
- Cannot be used to inquire into evidence as opposed to facts.
- Privilege may be claimed.

**Procedure:** Notice of Application + Affidavit attaching the proposed interrogatories. Court approves, modifies, or refuses. Answers given by sworn affidavit.

In modern Malaysian practice, interrogatories are relatively rare — most matters resolve via discovery and exchange of witness statements.

**PART 4: SECURITY FOR COSTS — ORDER 23**

A defendant may seek an order requiring the plaintiff to provide security (cash deposit, bank guarantee) for the defendant's likely costs of defending the action. If not provided, the action is stayed.

**Grounds (Order 23 r 1):**
(a) Plaintiff ordinarily resident outside Malaysia;
(b) Plaintiff is a nominal plaintiff suing for the benefit of another;
(c) Plaintiff's address misstated or not stated in the writ;
(d) Plaintiff has changed address with view to evading consequences of litigation.

Additionally, **s.351 Companies Act 2016** (formerly s.351 of the Companies Act 1965) — security for costs against a corporate plaintiff where credible testimony indicates the plaintiff cannot pay the defendant's costs if defending the action.

**Court's discretion:** Even where grounds are made out, the court considers all the circumstances — including the merits of the claim, the defendant's bona fides, and whether the order would stifle a genuine claim.

**Quantum:** Security typically reflects 50–80% of the defendant's anticipated party-party costs to a particular stage (e.g., to close of pleadings; to trial).

**PART 5: AMENDMENT OF PLEADINGS — ORDER 20**

**Order 20 r 5(1):** Amendment by leave at any stage of proceedings. The court has wide discretion.

**Test (Yamaha Motor Co Ltd v Yamaha Malaysia Sdn Bhd [1983] 1 MLJ 213 (FC)):**
- Amendment should be allowed unless it would cause real prejudice to the other party that cannot be compensated by costs or adjournment.
- Amendments to introduce a new cause of action after the limitation period has expired are subject to special rules (Order 20 r 5(2)–(5)).

**Amendment of writ:** Adding/substituting parties (Order 15), correcting names, expanding claim.

**Amendment of statement of claim/defence:** Adding new causes of action, defences, particulars.

**Late amendment:** Permitted but the closer to trial, the heavier the costs and the higher the threshold.

**PART 6: SETTING ASIDE DEFAULT JUDGMENT — ORDER 13 r 8 / ORDER 19 r 9**

**Two categories:**
1. **Regular default judgment (procedural irregularity):** e.g., judgment entered before proper service. Set aside as of right (Order 13 r 8).
2. **Irregular default judgment (substantive defence):** Set aside on the discretionary test (Evans v Bartlam [1937] AC 473, applied in Mageswari v United Asian Bank [1985] 1 MLJ 145):
   - Defendant must show a defence on the merits (a triable issue);
   - Reasonable explanation for the failure to enter appearance/defence;
   - Promptness in applying to set aside.

**Terms:** Setting aside often on conditions — payment into court, costs to the plaintiff in the cause, expedited timetable.

**PART 7: STAY OF PROCEEDINGS**

Common grounds:
- **Pending arbitration** (s.10 Arbitration Act 2005) — mandatory stay if arbitration agreement valid and dispute within scope.
- **Pending appeal** in related proceedings.
- **Forum non conveniens** — Malaysia not the appropriate forum (rare; weighty considerations).
- **Lis alibi pendens** — same dispute pending elsewhere.
- **Case management** — to allow ADR or to await preliminary determination.

**PART 8: PRE-TRIAL CASE MANAGEMENT — ORDER 34**

After close of pleadings, the court convenes a Pre-Trial Case Management (PTCM) conference before the SAR. Directions typically given:
- Filing and exchange of List of Documents and copies.
- Filing of witness statements (evidence-in-chief).
- Filing of expert reports.
- Filing of bundle of documents (agreed/disputed).
- Filing of issues to be tried.
- Setting trial date.

Subsequent PTCMs monitor compliance. Default in compliance may attract costs orders, "unless orders" (compliance by date or claim/defence struck out), or even striking out for want of prosecution.

**PART 9: PRELIMINARY ISSUES — ORDER 33**

The court may direct the trial of any question of fact or law arising in any cause or matter to be tried before, at, or after the trial. Useful where:
- A preliminary point of law (e.g., limitation, jurisdiction) may dispose of the entire action.
- A preliminary issue of fact (e.g., date of breach) is foundational to all other issues.

Procedure: Notice of Application + Affidavit (or court's own motion). If granted, the issue is listed for trial separately.

**PART 10: PRACTICAL POINTS**

— **Choose the right application.** Striking out is for hopeless cases; summary judgment is for indefensible cases; security for costs is for impecunious foreign plaintiffs. Don't conflate them.
— **Always plead in the alternative.** A striking-out application can be combined with summary judgment in the alternative — give the court a graduated set of options.
— **Discovery applications need precision.** Identify documents (or class) with particularity; show relevance; show possession/custody/power.
— **Time is precious in case management.** Comply with PTCM directions; delay attracts costs and worse.
— **Costs in chambers matter.** Cumulatively, interlocutory costs in a contested case can equal the substantive costs. Track them carefully.
— **Always update the case management bundle.** A clean, organised bundle materially affects how a SAR or Judge engages with your application.
legislation: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18 r 19 (Striking Out)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 24 (Discovery and Inspection)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 23 (Security for Costs)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 13 r 8 / Order 19 r 9 (Setting Aside Default Judgment)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 33 (Mode of Trial)
Rules of Court 2012, Order 34 (Pre-Trial Case Management)
Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), s.351 (Security for Costs against Corporate Plaintiff)
relatedCases: Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v UMBC Bhd [1993] 3 MLJ 36 (SC) — striking out threshold
Tractors Malaysia Bhd v Tio Chee Hing [1975] 2 MLJ 1 — limb (a) striking out
Compagnie Financiere v Peruvian Guano (1882) 11 QBD 55 — discovery test
Norwich Pharmacal Co v Customs and Excise [1974] AC 133 (HL) — third-party discovery
Yamaha Motor Co Ltd v Yamaha Malaysia Sdn Bhd [1983] 1 MLJ 213 (FC) — amendment principles
Evans v Bartlam [1937] AC 473 (HL) — setting aside default judgment
Mageswari v United Asian Bank [1985] 1 MLJ 145 — Malaysian application of Evans v Bartlam
Henderson v Henderson (1843) 3 Hare 100 — abuse of process / extended res judicata
keyPrinciples: Striking out under Order 18 r 19 is reserved for plain and obvious cases. Bandar Builder remains the threshold authority — courts will not embark on minute examination of the merits at this stage.
Discovery is broad. The Peruvian Guano test (documents that may advance one's case or damage the adversary's, even via a chain of inquiry) governs. Privilege claims must be specific and supported.
Setting aside default judgment requires (1) a defence on the merits, (2) reasonable explanation for default, and (3) prompt application. Conditional terms (payment into court, costs) are the norm.
Pre-trial case management compliance is non-negotiable. 'Unless orders' and adverse costs orders are real consequences of slippage. Treat PTCM dates as trial dates.
Choose the correct application — striking out, summary judgment, security for costs, discovery — and consider pleading them in the alternative where appropriate.

theory_topics.title: Tort of Negligence — Duty, Breach, Causation, Damage
theory_topics.overview: The tort of negligence is the most frequently litigated tort in Malaysian civil practice. It requires proof of a duty of care, breach, causation and recoverable damage. Governed by common law as received under the Civil Law Act 1956.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: ELEMENTS OF NEGLIGENCE**

To succeed in negligence the plaintiff must prove on the balance of probabilities: (1) the defendant owed a duty of care; (2) the defendant breached that duty; (3) the breach caused the plaintiff's loss (causation in fact and in law / remoteness); and (4) recoverable damage of a kind recognised by law.

**PART 2: DUTY OF CARE**

The neighbour principle was laid down in **Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562** (Lord Atkin): you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour. The modern three-stage test is in **Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605**: (i) reasonable foreseeability of harm; (ii) sufficient proximity; and (iii) whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.

In Malaysia, the Federal Court has applied Caparo in **Majlis Perbandaran Ampang Jaya v Steven Phoa Cheng Loon [2006] 2 MLJ 389** (the Highland Towers case) — local authorities can owe a duty in respect of statutory powers exercised negligently.

**PART 3: BREACH OF DUTY**

The standard is that of the reasonable person in the defendant's position (objective test). For professionals, the **Bolam v Friern Hospital [1957] 1 WLR 583** test applies: a doctor is not negligent if acting in accordance with a practice accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion. The Federal Court in **Foo Fio Na v Dr Soo Fook Mun [2007] 1 MLJ 593** modified this for medical advice/disclosure of risks — the **Rogers v Whitaker** approach now applies (court decides the standard for advice; Bolam survives only for diagnosis and treatment).

**PART 4: CAUSATION AND REMOTENESS**

Causation in fact is tested by the 'but for' test (**Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital [1969] 1 QB 428**). Causation in law (remoteness) is tested by reasonable foreseeability of the kind of damage (**The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] AC 388**), not the precise manner or extent.

Novus actus interveniens — an intervening cause may break the chain of causation if it is unforeseeable, voluntary, and the sole effective cause of the loss.

**PART 5: DEFENCES AND DAMAGES**

Defences include: (i) contributory negligence under the Civil Law Act 1956, s. 12 (apportionment); (ii) volenti non fit injuria; (iii) ex turpi causa; (iv) limitation under the Limitation Act 1953 (6 years from accrual for tort generally, including personal injury — Malaysia has no separate 3-year personal-injury period; s.6A gives a date-of-knowledge extension only for latent non-personal-injury damage). Damages: special (quantifiable past loss), general (pain and suffering, loss of amenities, future loss), aggravated, and exemplary (rarely awarded).
keyPrinciples: Donoghue v Stevenson neighbour principle is the foundation of duty of care.
Caparo three-stage test (foreseeability, proximity, fair/just/reasonable) is the modern test for novel duty situations.
