The Bolam test still applies to medical diagnosis/treatment but not to advice/disclosure of risks (Foo Fio Na).
Causation has two limbs: factual ('but for') and legal (reasonable foreseeability of the kind of damage).
practicalNotes: Plead each element of negligence with particulars in the Statement of Claim. Generic pleading invites striking out under Order 18 r 19.

For personal injury actions, the limitation period is 6 years from accrual under s. 6(1) Limitation Act 1953 — Malaysia has no shorter personal-injury period. Where the defendant is the Government or a public authority, the much shorter 36-month period under the Public Authorities Protection Act 1948 applies.
Always obtain a medical report before filing a personal injury action; quantum schedules from the Compendium of Personal Injury Awards (Malaysia) guide quantum.
Plead contributory negligence in the Defence with full particulars; courts apportion under s. 12(1) Civil Law Act 1956.
relatedCases: Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562
Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605
Foo Fio Na v Dr Soo Fook Mun [2007] 1 MLJ 593
Majlis Perbandaran Ampang Jaya v Steven Phoa Cheng Loon [2006] 2 MLJ 389

theory_topics.title: Defamation — Libel, Slander, Defences
theory_topics.overview: Defamation in Malaysia is governed by the Defamation Act 1957 (Act 286) supplemented by common law. It protects reputation against false statements that lower the claimant in the estimation of right-thinking members of society.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: LIBEL AND SLANDER**

Libel is defamation in permanent form (writing, print, broadcasting under s. 3 Defamation Act 1957) and is actionable per se. Slander is defamation in transient form (spoken word) and generally requires proof of special damage, except in four cases actionable per se: (i) imputation of crime punishable by imprisonment; (ii) imputation of contagious disease; (iii) imputation affecting professional/business reputation (s. 5 Defamation Act 1957); (iv) imputation of unchastity in a woman (s. 4 Defamation Act 1957).

**PART 2: ELEMENTS OF DEFAMATION**

The plaintiff must prove: (i) the words are defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning or by innuendo; (ii) the words refer to the plaintiff (identification); (iii) publication to a third party; (iv) for slander not actionable per se, special damage.

The test for what is defamatory: words that tend to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally (**Sim v Stretch [1936] 2 All ER 1237**), or expose to hatred, ridicule or contempt, or cause to be shunned and avoided.

**PART 3: DEFENCES**

(1) **Justification** (truth): a complete defence at common law if the defendant proves the words are substantially true (s. 8 Defamation Act 1957). Partial truth — s. 8 allows truth defence to stand even if not every charge is proved, if the unproven charges do not materially injure reputation given the truth of the rest.

(2) **Fair Comment**: defence to honest opinion on a matter of public interest based on true facts (s. 9 Defamation Act 1957). Defeated by malice.

(3) **Absolute Privilege**: statements in Parliament (Federal Constitution, Art 63), in court proceedings by judges/counsel/witnesses/parties, official state communications. Cannot be defeated by malice.

(4) **Qualified Privilege**: communications made in performance of a legal/social/moral duty to a person with a corresponding interest in receiving them. Defeated by malice. Statutory qualified privilege under Schedule to the Defamation Act 1957.

(5) **Reynolds Defence** (responsible journalism): adopted from **Reynolds v Times Newspapers [2001] 2 AC 127**; recognised in Malaysia in **Dato' Seri Anwar bin Ibrahim v Dato' Seri Dr Mahathir bin Mohamad** and applied in defamation cases involving the press.

**PART 4: REMEDIES**

Damages: general (presumed in libel and slander per se), aggravated (where defendant's conduct made matters worse), exemplary (rare; only in narrow categories per Rookes v Barnard). Injunctions to restrain publication. Apology — a statutory mitigating factor under s. 10 Defamation Act 1957.
keyPrinciples: Libel is in permanent form and actionable per se; slander generally requires special damage subject to four exceptions.
Defamatory words must lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society.
Justification, fair comment, absolute privilege, qualified privilege, and Reynolds are the principal defences.
Innuendo must be specifically pleaded with the extrinsic facts that give rise to the defamatory meaning.
practicalNotes: Limitation: 6 years under the Limitation Act 1953 — but defendant may rely on continuing republication.
Always demand a retraction and apology before filing — may serve as mitigating evidence and reduce damages.
For online defamation, identify the publisher: ISPs have safe-harbour defences but website operators may be liable.
Consider summary disposal under Order 14 if the defence is plainly bad (e.g. justification with no factual basis).
relatedCases: Sim v Stretch [1936] 2 All ER 1237
Reynolds v Times Newspapers Ltd [2001] 2 AC 127
Tun Datuk Patinggi Abdul Rahman Ya'kub v Bre Sdn Bhd [1996] 1 MLJ 393

theory_topics.title: Land Law: Indefeasibility, Caveats & Adverse Possession
theory_topics.overview: Malaysia operates a Torrens system under the National Land Code 1965 (Act 56). Title is by registration; the register is everything. Caveats and equitable interests temper the principle of indefeasibility.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: INDEFEASIBILITY OF TITLE**

Section 340 NLC 1965 provides that title or interest of any person registered under the Code is indefeasible — i.e. immune from challenge — except in cases of (a) fraud or misrepresentation; (b) forgery, or insufficient or void instrument; (c) acquisition by means of an unlawful instrument; or (d) where the title was unlawfully acquired by the person registered.

The Federal Court in **Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit [2001] 1 MLJ 241** held that even a bona fide purchaser for value from a forger acquires indefeasible title under s. 340(3) — this caused alarm. The Federal Court in **Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1** overruled Adorna Properties, restoring the proper construction: the proviso in s. 340(3) only protects subsequent purchasers, not the immediate transferee from the forger. Indefeasibility under Tan Ying Hong is **deferred indefeasibility**.

**PART 2: CAVEATS**

Three types of caveats under the NLC 1965:

(1) **Private Caveat** (ss. 322–331): lodged by a person claiming title or interest in land. Effect: prevents registration of dealings (s. 322(2)). Lapses after 6 years unless extended by court order. Wrongful caveat — caveator liable in damages under s. 329.

(2) **Lien-holder's Caveat** (ss. 281, 330): protects the holder of a lien (deposit of issue document of title as security under s. 281).

(3) **Registrar's Caveat** (ss. 319–321): entered by the Registrar to protect the public interest, prevent fraud, or protect the title of an incapable person.

The leading case on private caveats is **Damodaran v Choe Kuan Him [1979] 2 MLJ 267** — the caveator must show a 'caveatable interest' i.e. a registrable interest in the land.

**PART 3: ADVERSE POSSESSION (NOT RECOGNISED)**

Adverse possession is **not** recognised under the NLC 1965. Section 341 NLC 1965 provides that no title to State land can be acquired by adverse possession, and **Sidek bin Haji Muhamad v Government of the State of Perak [1982] 1 MLJ 313** confirmed this. Long occupation does not ripen into title — distinguishing Malaysia from common-law jurisdictions retaining adverse possession.

**PART 4: TRANSFER, CHARGE AND LEASE**

Dealings in land must be in the prescribed form and registered:
- **Transfer**: Memorandum of Transfer (Form 14A NLC 1965)
- **Charge**: Charge document (Form 16A) — see Topic on Foreclosure
- **Lease**: Form 15A (lease > 3 years) or registered tenancy
- **Easement**: Form 17A

Unregistered dealings create only equitable interests, protectable by caveat.
keyPrinciples: Indefeasibility under s. 340 NLC is deferred (Tan Ying Hong overruled Adorna Properties).
Adverse possession is NOT recognised under the NLC 1965.
Caveats protect equitable/inchoate interests pending registration; lodged without caveatable interest, the caveator is liable in damages.
The Torrens register is conclusive — title is by registration, not by deeds.
practicalNotes: When acting for a buyer, conduct a land search at the relevant Land Office immediately before completion to confirm no caveat or charge.
When entering a private caveat for a client, ensure caveatable interest is properly identified — a wrongful caveat under s. 329 invites a damages action.
On notice of a private caveat, application to remove may be made under s. 327 (caveator must show cause) or s. 326 (lapse).
For forged instruments, sue the forger in personam and seek rectification of the register; the immediate transferee does not enjoy indefeasibility post Tan Ying Hong.
relatedCases: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1
Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit [2001] 1 MLJ 241
Damodaran v Choe Kuan Him [1979] 2 MLJ 267
Sidek bin Haji Muhamad v Government of the State of Perak [1982] 1 MLJ 313

theory_topics.title: Contract Law: Formation, Breach & Remedies (Contracts Act 1950)
theory_topics.overview: Civil contractual disputes in Malaysia are governed by the Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), supplemented by common law. The Act codifies offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, free consent, and remedies for breach.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: FORMATION**

A valid contract requires offer (s. 2(a)), acceptance (s. 2(b)), consideration (s. 2(d) — note that under s. 26 consideration need not move from the promisee), capacity (s. 11 — age of majority is 18 under the Age of Majority Act 1971), free consent (ss. 13–22, vitiated by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake), and lawful object (ss. 23–24).

**Past consideration** is good consideration in Malaysia — s. 2(d) says 'has done or abstained from doing' — unlike English law (Eastwood v Kenyon).

**Privity** is largely preserved but s. 2(d) expressly allows consideration to move from a third party.

**PART 2: TERMS AND VITIATING FACTORS**

Terms are conditions, warranties, or innominate. Breach of condition entitles repudiation; breach of warranty only damages. **Photo Production Ltd v Securicor Transport Ltd [1980] AC 827** held that exclusion clauses can cover even fundamental breach if clearly worded. The doctrine of fundamental breach is one of construction, not of law.

Misrepresentation: under ss. 18–19, an innocent or fraudulent misrepresentation rendering consent unfree allows rescission and (for fraud under s. 19A) damages. The Misrepresentation Act 1967 (UK) does not apply.

Mistake: s. 21 (mistake of fact essential to the agreement renders it void); s. 22 (unilateral mistake does not, unless known to the other party).

**PART 3: BREACH AND REMEDIES**

(1) **Damages** (s. 74): compensation for loss naturally arising or in the contemplation of the parties at the time of contracting (the **Hadley v Baxendale [1854] 9 Exch 341** rule, codified). Liquidated damages clauses — s. 75 allows recovery of the stipulated sum (with no requirement to prove actual loss after **Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 6 MLJ 15**, FC).

(2) **Specific Performance**: under the Specific Relief Act 1950 (ss. 11–22). Discretionary; not granted where damages are adequate; commonly granted for sale of land (s. 11 illustrates).

(3) **Rescission**: termination of the contract restoring parties to original position (ss. 35, 65–66; SRA 1950, ss. 34–35).

(4) **Injunction**: SRA 1950, ss. 50–55 — interim and perpetual.

(5) **Quantum Meruit**: restitutionary relief for work done where contract is discharged or void.

**PART 4: DISCHARGE**

Discharge by performance (s. 38), agreement (ss. 63–67), breach (s. 40), or frustration (s. 57(2) — supervening impossibility/illegality renders the contract void).
keyPrinciples: Contract law in Malaysia is codified in the Contracts Act 1950; resort to common law only where the Act is silent.
Past consideration is good consideration in Malaysia (s. 2(d) Contracts Act 1950).
Damages under s. 74 follow Hadley v Baxendale; liquidated damages under s. 75 do not require proof of actual loss (Cubic Electronics).
Specific performance is governed by the Specific Relief Act 1950, not the Contracts Act.
practicalNotes: When pleading breach, identify whether the term is condition or warranty — the choice determines repudiation rights.
For liquidated damages, plead s. 75 Contracts Act 1950 and Cubic Electronics; the burden is on the defendant to show the clause is extravagant.
Always preserve the right to rescission with a clear notice — affirmation may bar later rescission.
Frustration is narrow — commercial difficulty or increased cost is not enough; supervening impossibility or illegality is required.
relatedCases: Photo Production Ltd v Securicor Transport Ltd [1980] AC 827
Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341
Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 6 MLJ 15

theory_topics.title: Family Law: Divorce, Custody & Ancillary Reliefs (LRA 1976)
theory_topics.overview: Non-Muslim family law in Malaysia is governed by the Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 (Act 164). It governs marriage, divorce, custody, maintenance and division of matrimonial property. Muslim family matters fall under State Syariah enactments.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: SCOPE OF THE LRA 1976**

The LRA 1976 applies to all non-Muslims in Malaysia (s. 3). Marriage must be registered (s. 22). Polygamy is prohibited for non-Muslims (s. 5 — second marriage during subsistence is void and a criminal offence).

**PART 2: DIVORCE**

(1) **Mutual consent divorce** (s. 52): joint petition by both spouses; reconciliation requirements waived; decree nisi after hearing.

(2) **Divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown** (s. 53): single-ground divorce where the marriage has irretrievably broken down. Must show one of: (i) adultery (s. 54(1)(a)); (ii) unreasonable behaviour (s. 54(1)(b)); (iii) desertion for 2 years (s. 54(1)(c)); (iv) separation for 2 years (s. 54(1)(d)).

**Pre-conditions**: marriage registered for at least 2 years (s. 50 — exception for exceptional hardship/depravity); referral to conciliatory body under s. 106 (the Marriage Tribunal) before petition, unless exempted (e.g. opposite party converted to Islam, imprisoned for 5+ years, certified incurable mental disorder).

**Decree nisi** (s. 61): provisional decree. **Decree absolute** (s. 61(2)): made absolute after 3 months unless cause shown. Marriage dissolved only on decree absolute.

**PART 3: ANCILLARY RELIEFS**

(1) **Custody of children** (s. 88): paramount consideration is the welfare of the child. Children below 7 — rebuttable presumption in favour of mother. Joint custody, sole custody with care and control, and split custody are options.

(2) **Maintenance of spouse** (s. 77): wife may be ordered maintenance; husband only in special cases (incapacitated). Quantum based on means of payor and reasonable needs of payee.

(3) **Maintenance of children** (s. 92): both parents have duty; continues till 18 (or to completion of higher education — s. 95).

(4) **Division of matrimonial assets** (s. 76): court has wide discretion. Distinction between (i) jointly acquired assets and (ii) sole-acquired assets — but s. 76(5) directs equal division of jointly acquired in any case. **Wong Kim Foong v Teau Ah Kau** and **Ching Seng Woah v Lim Shook Lin** are leading FC cases on division.

**PART 4: CONVERSION CASES**

The Federal Court in **Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak [2018] 1 MLJ 545** held that civil courts have jurisdiction in custody disputes following unilateral conversion of children to Islam by one parent — restoring constitutional supremacy.
keyPrinciples: Divorce under LRA 1976 requires irretrievable breakdown evidenced by one of four facts (adultery, unreasonable behaviour, desertion, separation).
Welfare of the child is paramount in custody decisions; mother has rebuttable presumption for children below 7.
Matrimonial assets are divided having regard to contribution; s. 76(5) directs equal division of jointly acquired assets.
Civil courts retain jurisdiction over custody where one parent converts to Islam (Indira Gandhi).
practicalNotes: Always obtain the marriage certificate and confirm the marriage is registered — unregistered marriages may not qualify for divorce relief.
Comply with the Marriage Tribunal (s. 106) referral before filing single petition under s. 53; failure is fatal.
Plead matrimonial assets with full particulars — bank accounts, EPF, properties, shares — and seek a freezing injunction if dissipation is feared.
Custody affidavits must address the welfare checklist with concrete facts: schooling, residence, care arrangements, the child's wishes (if old enough).
relatedCases: Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak [2018] 1 MLJ 545
Wong Kim Foong v Teau Ah Kau [1998] 1 MLJ 359
Ching Seng Woah v Lim Shook Lin [1997] 1 MLJ 109

theory_topics.title: Probate, Letters of Administration & Succession
theory_topics.overview: Succession to a deceased's estate in Malaysia is governed by the Probate and Administration Act 1959, the Wills Act 1959 (for non-Muslims), and the Distribution Act 1958. Muslim estates follow Faraid under State enactments.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: TESTATE AND INTESTATE SUCCESSION**

If the deceased left a valid will, succession is testate — executor applies for **Grant of Probate** (s. 3 PAA 1959). If no will, intestate — beneficiaries apply for **Letters of Administration** (s. 30 PAA 1959).

A will (Wills Act 1959) must be in writing, signed by the testator (or by another in his presence and direction), attested by two or more witnesses. Beneficiary witnesses lose their bequest (s. 9). Marriage revokes a will (s. 12) unless made in contemplation of marriage.

**PART 2: GRANT OF PROBATE**

Application by Originating Summons in the High Court (Originating Summons under O 71 ROC 2012 if non-contentious) or Sessions Court (estates ≤ RM2 million by amendment to PAA 1959). Required documents: original will, death certificate, schedule of assets and liabilities, citation of executors, advertisement.

**Caveat against grant** — any interested person disputing the will may lodge a caveat under O 72; matter then proceeds to contentious probate.

**PART 3: LETTERS OF ADMINISTRATION**

Order of priority for grant under s. 30 PAA 1959 and the Distribution Act 1958:
- Surviving spouse
- Children
- Parents
- Brothers and sisters
- Grandparents, etc.

If estate ≤ RM2 million and no will — the **Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955** applies; jurisdiction lies with the Land Administrator (Pejabat Tanah).

For estates > RM2 million — High Court.

**PART 4: DISTRIBUTION ON INTESTACY**

Section 6 Distribution Act 1958 prescribes shares:
- Spouse only: whole estate
- Spouse + issue: spouse 1/3, issue 2/3
- Spouse + parent (no issue): spouse 1/2, parent 1/2
- Spouse + issue + parent: spouse 1/4, issue 1/2, parent 1/4

**PART 5: CONTENTIOUS PROBATE**

Where a will is challenged on grounds of (i) want of due execution; (ii) lack of testamentary capacity (Banks v Goodfellow test); (iii) want of knowledge and approval; (iv) undue influence or fraud — proceeds as a contentious probate action under O 71/72 ROC 2012. Burden on the propounder of the will.

The Federal Court in **Letchumanan Chettiar Alagappan @ L Allagappan v Secure Plantation Sdn Bhd [2017] 4 MLJ 697** clarified the standards for proving testamentary capacity and suspicious circumstances.
keyPrinciples: Grant of Probate is sought when there is a valid will; Letters of Administration where the deceased died intestate.
Small estates (≤ RM2 million, no will) are administered by the Land Administrator under the Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955.
Distribution on intestacy is governed by s. 6 Distribution Act 1958 with statutory shares.
Contentious probate disputes proceed as a regular action with pleadings; burden on propounder of the will.
practicalNotes: Always check whether the deceased was Muslim — Faraid jurisdiction lies with the Syariah Court, not the civil court.
Lodge a caveat against grant promptly if challenging a will; once Grant is issued, set-aside is more difficult.
Compile a full schedule of assets — banks (s. 17 PAA 1959 freezing of accounts), EPF, shares, land, insurance, vehicles.
For overseas assets (e.g. Singapore property), reseal of Malaysian Grant under the Probate and Administration Act 1959, s. 52 may be necessary.
relatedCases: Letchumanan Chettiar Alagappan v Secure Plantation Sdn Bhd [2017] 4 MLJ 697
Banks v Goodfellow (1870) LR 5 QB 549

theory_topics.title: Judicial Review under Order 53 ROC 2012
theory_topics.overview: Judicial review is the supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court over public bodies under Order 53 of the Rules of Court 2012, paragraph 1 of the Schedule to the Courts of Judicature Act 1964. The court reviews legality, procedural propriety, and rationality — not merits.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: SCOPE AND LEAVE STAGE**

Judicial review under O 53 lies against decisions of public bodies exercising public functions. The applicant must obtain leave of the court before substantive hearing (O 53 r 3). Leave is granted if the applicant has a sufficient interest (locus standi) and an arguable case.

**Time limit**: 3 months from the date when grounds of judicial review first arose (O 53 r 3(6)). Strict — extension only in exceptional circumstances.

**PART 2: GROUNDS**

The classic grounds (Lord Diplock in **Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374** — the GCHQ case) are:

(1) **Illegality** — acting beyond statutory power (ultra vires); failure to comply with statutory pre-conditions; error of law; acting for improper purpose; relevant/irrelevant considerations.

(2) **Procedural Impropriety** — breach of natural justice (audi alteram partem; nemo judex in causa sua); failure to comply with prescribed procedures; legitimate expectation.

(3) **Irrationality / Wednesbury Unreasonableness** — a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable decision-maker could have reached it (**Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223**).

(4) **Proportionality** — emerging in Malaysia for fundamental rights cases (**Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia [2010] 2 MLJ 333**).

**PART 3: REMEDIES (PREROGATIVE WRITS)**

Under para 1 of the Schedule to the CJA 1964 and O 53 r 1:
- **Certiorari**: quashes the impugned decision
- **Prohibition**: prevents further unlawful action
- **Mandamus**: compels performance of a public duty
- **Declaration**: declares the law/rights of parties
- **Injunction**: restrains unlawful action (limited against the federal government — Government Proceedings Act 1956, s. 29)

**PART 4: LOCUS STANDI**

The Federal Court in **Lim Kit Siang v United Engineers (M) Bhd [1988] 2 MLJ 12** narrowed standing — only a person whose private right is infringed or who suffers special damage. The position has loosened post-**Malaysian Trades Union Congress v Menteri Tenaga Air dan Komunikasi [2014] 3 MLJ 145** — public interest standing is recognised in appropriate cases.

**PART 5: REMEDIES — R RAMA CHANDRAN**

The Federal Court in **R Rama Chandran v The Industrial Court of Malaysia [1997] 1 MLJ 145** held that on quashing an unlawful decision, the court has jurisdiction to substitute its own decision in proper cases — not just remit. This expanded the supervisory role significantly.
keyPrinciples: Judicial review reviews legality, procedural propriety, irrationality and (increasingly) proportionality — not merits.
Strict 3-month time limit under O 53 r 3(6); leave stage filters frivolous applications.
Locus standi has loosened post-MTUC — public interest standing is recognised in appropriate cases.
R Rama Chandran allows the court to substitute its own decision, not merely quash and remit.
practicalNotes: Identify the precise impugned decision and date — time runs from when grounds first arose, not when applicant became aware.
Affidavit in support must annex the impugned decision and exhibit all material before the decision-maker (so far as available).
Plead all grounds in the alternative — illegality, procedural impropriety, irrationality — to maximise prospects.
Consider whether internal appeal/statutory remedy exists (alternative remedy doctrine) — failure to exhaust may defeat leave.
legislation: Courts of Judicature Act 1964, Schedule paragraph 1
relatedCases: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374
R Rama Chandran v The Industrial Court of Malaysia [1997] 1 MLJ 145
Lim Kit Siang v United Engineers (M) Bhd [1988] 2 MLJ 12
Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia [2010] 2 MLJ 333
Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223

theory_topics.title: Companies Act 2016: Oppression (s. 346) & Derivative Actions (s. 347)
theory_topics.overview: The Companies Act 2016 (Act 777) provides minority shareholder remedies for oppressive conduct (s. 346) and statutory derivative actions to enforce wrongs against the company (s. 347). These are central to modern shareholder dispute litigation.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: SECTION 346 — OPPRESSION**

Section 346 (formerly s. 181 CA 1965) gives the court wide power to grant relief where the affairs of a company are being conducted in a manner: (a) oppressive to one or more members or holders of debentures; (b) in disregard of their interests; (c) in breach of the rules of fair play; or (d) involving an unfairly prejudicial act or omission of the company or a resolution.

**Standing**: any member, debenture holder, the Minister (in respect of declared companies), or a personal representative of a deceased member.

**Conduct caught**: not limited to majority oppression — can include minority entrenchment. Examples: exclusion from management in a quasi-partnership (Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries); diversion of corporate opportunities; non-payment of dividends despite profits; share dilution; appointment of family members at excessive remuneration.

**Remedies under s. 346(2)** are non-exhaustive and include: (i) directing or prohibiting any act; (ii) cancelling or varying any transaction or resolution; (iii) regulating the conduct of the company's affairs; (iv) **buy-out order** — most common remedy; (v) directing the company to commence proceedings; (vi) winding up.

The Federal Court in **Pang Yong Hock v PKM Industries (M) Sdn Bhd [2004] 3 MLJ 565** confirmed the wide discretion under s. 181 (now s. 346).

**PART 2: SECTION 347 — STATUTORY DERIVATIVE ACTION**

Section 347 enables a 'complainant' (member, former member, director, or any person the court considers proper) to bring an action in the company's name with leave of the court. This is the statutory replacement for the common law rule in **Foss v Harbottle (1843) 2 Hare 461**.

**Pre-conditions for leave** (s. 348):
(i) **30-day notice** of intention to apply for leave served on the directors;
(ii) The complainant is **acting in good faith**;
(iii) It is **prima facie in the best interests of the company** that the action proceed.

**Court's powers on leave**: directions on the conduct of the action; security for costs; staying related proceedings; indemnity for the complainant for costs.

**PART 3: WINDING UP ON JUST AND EQUITABLE GROUND**

Section 465(1)(h) CA 2016 — winding up on the 'just and equitable' ground. The Federal Court has applied **Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries [1973] AC 360** principles — appropriate where (a) quasi-partnership relationship of mutual confidence breaks down; (b) deadlock; (c) loss of substratum.

Court will refuse winding up if a less drastic remedy (e.g. buy-out under s. 346) is available — Re A Company [1986].

**PART 4: PROCEDURAL CONSIDERATIONS**

Section 346 proceedings: by Originating Summons supported by affidavit (or writ if disputed facts demand cross-examination). Filed in the High Court. Joinder of the company and offending parties. Interim relief — Mareva, asset preservation, status quo orders — frequently sought.

Section 347 leave applications: Originating Summons supported by detailed affidavit explaining the wrong, prima facie merits, costs/funding plan.
keyPrinciples: Section 346 oppression remedy is broad — covers oppression, disregard of interests, breach of fair play, and unfair prejudice.
Buy-out order is the most common remedy under s. 346; winding up only as last resort.
Section 347 statutory derivative action requires leave: 30-day notice, good faith, prima facie best interests of the company.
Just and equitable winding up under s. 465(1)(h) follows Ebrahimi principles for quasi-partnerships.
practicalNotes: For s. 346, plead specific oppressive conduct with dates, particulars, and resolutions — generic pleading invites striking out.
For s. 347, comply strictly with the 30-day notice — file proof of service. Plead all three pre-conditions in the supporting affidavit.
Always seek interim freezing orders against directors suspected of asset diversion — Mareva + ancillary asset disclosure.
Buy-out valuation: court may direct independent valuer; parties should prepare expert valuation reports in advance.
relatedCases: Pang Yong Hock v PKM Industries (M) Sdn Bhd [2004] 3 MLJ 565
Foss v Harbottle (1843) 2 Hare 461
Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries Ltd [1973] AC 360

theory_topics.title: Construction Disputes, CIPAA Adjudication & Arbitration
theory_topics.overview: Malaysian construction disputes are resolved through three principal channels: the courts, statutory adjudication under the Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012 (CIPAA), and arbitration under the Arbitration Act 2005.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: CIPAA 2012 — STATUTORY ADJUDICATION**

CIPAA 2012 (Act 746) provides a fast-track payment dispute resolution mechanism for construction contracts (defined under s. 4). Adjudication is a statutory right that cannot be ousted by contract (s. 8).

**Procedure**:
(1) **Payment Claim** under s. 5 — the unpaid party serves a payment claim on the non-paying party.
(2) **Payment Response** under s. 6 — within 10 working days; admit or dispute.
(3) **Notice of Adjudication** under s. 7 — if no response or response disputes payment.
(4) **Adjudicator appointment** by KLRCA (Asian International Arbitration Centre, AIAC) — within 5 working days.
(5) **Adjudication Response** within 10 working days; **Reply** within 5 working days.
(6) **Adjudication Decision** within 45 working days from service of response (s. 12) — extendable by agreement.
(7) **Decision is binding** until set aside or finally determined by court/arbitration (s. 13).

**Setting aside grounds** (s. 15): (a) decision improperly procured through fraud or bribery; (b) denial of natural justice; (c) adjudicator did not act independently/impartially; (d) acted in excess of jurisdiction.

The Federal Court in **View Esteem Sdn Bhd v Bina Puri Holdings Bhd [2018] 2 MLJ 22** clarified the scope of natural justice challenges under s. 15(b).

The Federal Court in **Jack-In Pile (M) Sdn Bhd v Bauer (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd [2020] 1 MLJ 174** held CIPAA does not apply retrospectively to contracts pre-dating commencement.

**PART 2: ARBITRATION ACT 2005**

The Arbitration Act 2005 (Act 646) governs domestic and international arbitration in Malaysia, modelled on the UNCITRAL Model Law. Key features:

- **Section 8** — court interventionism limited; courts shall not intervene except where provided.
- **Section 10** — mandatory stay of court proceedings where there is an arbitration agreement (subject to narrow exceptions).
- **Section 11** — interim measures by court available pre and during arbitration.
- **Section 18** — competence-competence (arbitral tribunal rules on its own jurisdiction).
- **Section 36** — award is final and binding.
- **Section 37** — setting aside grounds (mirroring NYC Article V): (a) party incapacity; (b) invalid arbitration agreement; (c) lack of notice; (d) award beyond scope; (e) tribunal composition irregular; (f) subject not arbitrable; (g) award contrary to public policy.
- **Section 38–39** — recognition and enforcement of foreign awards under the New York Convention (Malaysia is a party).

**PART 3: STAY OF COURT PROCEEDINGS — S. 10**

Where a party commences court proceedings in respect of a matter covered by an arbitration agreement, the court **shall** stay proceedings on application made before substantive defence is filed (s. 10(1)). The Federal Court in **Press Metal Sarawak Sdn Bhd v Etiqa Takaful Bhd [2016] 5 MLJ 417** confirmed the mandatory nature.

**PART 4: ENFORCEMENT OF AWARDS**

Domestic awards — register under s. 38 and enforce as a judgment. Foreign awards — recognition under s. 38/39 by reference to the NYC; setting aside grounds under s. 37.
keyPrinciples: CIPAA adjudication is statutory and cannot be ousted by contract; decision is binding until set aside or finally determined.
CIPAA setting aside under s. 15 is narrow — fraud, denial of natural justice, lack of independence, excess of jurisdiction.
Arbitration Act 2005 mandates stay of court proceedings under s. 10 where arbitration agreement exists.
Section 37 setting aside grounds mirror the New York Convention; public policy is narrowly construed.
practicalNotes: For CIPAA payment claim, ensure all formal requirements of s. 5 are met — invoice number, period, amount — or risk being held bad on adjudication.
Time limits in CIPAA are strict and counted in working days; missed deadlines are usually fatal.
When acting for a defendant in a court action covered by arbitration agreement, file s. 10 stay application BEFORE entering substantive defence — late application may be deemed waiver.
Setting aside an award under s. 37(1)(b)(ii) (public policy) requires clear evidence of conflict with Malaysian public policy — mere error of law/fact is not enough.
legislation: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012 (Act 746)
relatedCases: View Esteem Sdn Bhd v Bina Puri Holdings Bhd [2018] 2 MLJ 22
Press Metal Sarawak Sdn Bhd v Etiqa Takaful Bhd [2016] 5 MLJ 417
Jack-In Pile (M) Sdn Bhd v Bauer (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd [2020] 1 MLJ 174

theory_topics.title: Personal Injury & Motor Vehicle Accident Claims
theory_topics.overview: Personal injury claims, especially from road traffic accidents, form the largest volume of civil litigation in the Sessions and Magistrates' Courts. Governed by the Civil Law Act 1956, the Road Transport Act 1987, and Compendium of Quantum guidelines.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: LIABILITY**

Negligence elements apply (Topic 28). For motor vehicle collisions: standard of care of a reasonable driver (Highway Code as evidence). Common scenarios: rear-end (presumption of fault on rear driver — Tan Chwee Geok v Yeoh Hin Lim); right of way violations; failing to give way; speeding.

**Contributory negligence** under s. 12 Civil Law Act 1956 — common to apportion liability where the plaintiff was also at fault (e.g. failure to wear seatbelt — typically 15-25% reduction).

**PART 2: PROCEDURE**

(1) **Police Report** — file at the nearest police station within 24 hours; obtain abstract.
(2) **Sketch Plan and Investigation Report** — request from JSPT (Bahagian Siasatan Trafik).
(3) **Medical Reports** — from treating hospital and follow-up specialists (cost recoverable).
(4) **Insurance Claim** — under the Road Transport Act 1987, third-party insurance is mandatory (s. 90). MIB (Motor Insurers' Bureau) Agreement covers uninsured/untraced drivers.
(5) **Demand Letter** — to the tortfeasor and insurer; particulars of injuries and special damages.
(6) **Writ of Summons & Statement of Claim** — file in Sessions Court (claims ≤ RM1 million) or High Court (above) within 6 years of accrual (Limitation Act 1953, s. 6(1)) — Malaysia has no separate 3-year personal-injury period. Where the defendant is the Government or a public authority, the much shorter 36-month period under the Public Authorities Protection Act 1948 applies.

**PART 3: QUANTUM**

Damages categories:

(1) **Special Damages** (quantifiable past loss): hospital bills, medical reports, transport costs, loss of earnings to date of trial. Must be specifically pleaded and proved with receipts.

(2) **General Damages** — pain and suffering and loss of amenities (PSLA): assessed by reference to the **Compendium of Personal Injury Awards (Malaysia)** — guideline tariffs for fractures, head injuries, amputations, scarring, etc.

(3) **Loss of Future Earnings**: multiplier × multiplicand approach (s. 28A Civil Law Act 1956 amendments). Multiplier capped by remaining working years.

(4) **Loss of Earning Capacity**: separate award where injury reduces capacity to compete in the labour market.

(5) **Loss of Future Service** (homemaker): under s. 7(3)(iv)(d) CLA 1956.

(6) **Pre-trial Interest**: 4% on special damages; 8% on general damages from date of accident to judgment.

**PART 4: FATAL ACCIDENT CLAIMS**

Two heads under the Civil Law Act 1956:

(1) **Section 7** — dependency claim: dependants (spouse, parents, children, etc.) may claim loss of dependency.

(2) **Section 8** — estate claim: representative may claim loss of expectation of life and pre-death pain and suffering. **Note: 'loss of expectation of life' was abolished by the 1984 amendment** for instant death — only conscious pain and suffering recoverable.

**PART 5: NO-FAULT INSURANCE**

For minor injuries, the insurer may settle on a no-fault basis. The MMIP (Malaysian Motor Insurance Pool) handles high-risk insureds. Recoveries from MIB for untraced/uninsured drivers cap maximum payouts.
keyPrinciples: Negligence elements (duty, breach, causation, damage) govern road traffic accident claims.
Contributory negligence under s. 12 CLA 1956 apportions liability where the plaintiff was also at fault.
Quantum is guided by the Compendium of Personal Injury Awards (Malaysia) — consistency across courts.

Limitation for personal injury is 6 years from accrual under s. 6(1) Limitation Act 1953 — there is no separate 3-year personal-injury period in Malaysia. Only where the defendant is the Government or a public authority does the shorter 36-month period (Public Authorities Protection Act 1948) apply.
practicalNotes: File the police report within 24 hours and preserve evidence — photographs, dashcam, witness statements.
Request the Investigation Paper (IP) from JSPT once police investigation is complete; the IP is critical evidence on liability.
For loss of earnings, produce salary slips, EPF/SOCSO statements, and (for self-employed) tax returns.
Consider direct action against the insurer under s. 96(1) Road Transport Act 1987 — judgment recoverable from insurer regardless of insolvency.
relatedCases: Tan Chwee Geok v Yeoh Hin Lim [1976] 1 MLJ 122
The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] AC 388

theory_topics.title: Employment Law & Industrial Relations
theory_topics.overview: Malaysian employment law is governed by the Employment Act 1955 (terms and conditions for employees within s. 2 definition), the Industrial Relations Act 1967 (collective relations and unfair dismissal), and the Industrial Court (binding awards in trade disputes and dismissal cases).
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: EMPLOYMENT ACT 1955**

The Employment Act 1955 (EA) sets minimum terms and conditions for employees. Following the Employment (Amendment) Act 2022 (in force 1 January 2023), the EA now applies to **all employees** regardless of wages (subject to specific provisions still tied to RM4,000 threshold).

Key entitlements: (i) hours of work (max 45 per week — amended from 48); (ii) annual leave (8-16 days based on service); (iii) sick leave (14-22 days); (iv) maternity (98 days); (v) paternity (7 days for married fathers); (vi) overtime; (vii) termination/lay-off benefits under EA 1955 + Employment (Termination and Lay-Off Benefits) Regulations 1980.

**PART 2: TERMINATION AND DISMISSAL**

(1) **Termination with notice** — by either party as per contract.
(2) **Termination on misconduct** — after due inquiry (audi alteram partem).
(3) **Constructive dismissal** — employer's fundamental breach forces resignation.
(4) **Retrenchment** — for redundancy; LIFO (last in first out) presumption; benefits under the Regulations 1980.

**PART 3: SECTION 20 IRA 1967 — UNFAIR DISMISSAL**

A workman who is dismissed without just cause or excuse may file a representation under s. 20 IRA 1967 to the Director General of Industrial Relations within **60 days** of dismissal (Employment (Amendment) Act 2022 reduced from 90 days for some cases — verify current position). After failed conciliation, the Minister refers to the Industrial Court (no longer required after 2020 amendment — direct reference now).

**Industrial Court hearing**: tests whether the dismissal was for **just cause or excuse**. Burden on the employer (Goon Kwee Phoy v J&P Coats [1981] 2 MLJ 129). Two limbs: (i) proof of misconduct (or other reason); (ii) proportionality of dismissal.

**Remedies**: (i) reinstatement (now cap of 24 months back-wages — Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act 2020 removed back-wages cap for deserving cases); (ii) compensation in lieu (1 month per year of service); (iii) costs orders rare.

The Federal Court in **Ng Hee Thoong v Public Bank [2016] 6 CLJ 1** affirmed the principles for back-wages calculation and post-dismissal earnings deduction.

**PART 4: TRADE UNIONS AND COLLECTIVE BARGAINING**

Trade Unions Act 1959 governs registration. Recognition under s. 9 IRA 1967 — employer must recognise a union representing >50% of employees in scope. Disputes referred for secret ballot. Collective agreements under Part IV IRA 1967 are binding for 3+ years.

**PART 5: JUDICIAL REVIEW OF INDUSTRIAL COURT AWARDS**

Industrial Court awards are amenable to judicial review under O 53 (procedural impropriety, illegality, irrationality) — **R Rama Chandran v The Industrial Court [1997] 1 MLJ 145** confirms High Court can substitute decision in proper cases.
keyPrinciples: Employment Act 1955 (post-2022 amendments) applies to all employees, providing statutory minimum terms.
Section 20 IRA 1967 dismissal claims test 'just cause or excuse' — burden on the employer.
Constructive dismissal arises from employer's fundamental breach forcing employee resignation.
Industrial Court awards are subject to judicial review under O 53 ROC 2012.
practicalNotes: File s. 20 representation within the statutory time limit — late representations are time-barred (60 days from date of dismissal).
For employer clients, conduct due inquiry with proper notice, charge sheet, and right to be heard before any dismissal for misconduct.
Document misconduct contemporaneously — warning letters, performance reviews, attendance records — these are critical at the Industrial Court.
Calculate quantum carefully: 24-month back-wages cap (subject to amendment) plus compensation in lieu of reinstatement (1 month per year).
relatedCases: Goon Kwee Phoy v J&P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 2 MLJ 129
R Rama Chandran v The Industrial Court of Malaysia [1997] 1 MLJ 145
Ng Hee Thoong v Public Bank Bhd [2016] 6 CLJ 1

theory_topics.title: Specific Performance, Equitable Remedies & Specific Relief Act 1950
theory_topics.overview: The Specific Relief Act 1950 (Act 137) codifies equitable remedies in Malaysia: specific performance, rescission, rectification, declarations, and injunctions. These remedies are discretionary and supplement common-law damages.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE (SS. 11–22 SRA 1950)**

Specific performance compels a contracting party to perform contractual obligations. **Section 11 SRA** provides specific performance in any case where (a) damages cannot be ascertained; (b) damages would not afford adequate relief.

**Presumption** under s. 11(2): for contracts to transfer immovable property, damages are presumed inadequate — specific performance is the prima facie remedy.

**Bars to specific performance** (s. 20):
(i) Contract is not enforceable (e.g. lacking certainty, illegal);
(ii) Performance would involve continuous supervision (s. 20(c));
(iii) Damages are an adequate remedy;
(iv) Plaintiff guilty of laches, acquiescence, or unclean hands;
(v) Mutuality lacking — court will not grant SP at suit of A unless court could grant SP at suit of B.

**Personal service contracts** — specific performance generally refused (s. 20(b)) — equity does not enforce slavery.

The Federal Court in **Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v United Malayan Banking Corporation [1993] 3 MLJ 36** affirmed the principles for specific performance of land sale contracts.

**PART 2: RESCISSION (SS. 34–35)**

Rescission terminates the contract ab initio, restoring parties to status quo. Available for: (i) voidable contracts (consent vitiated); (ii) failure of consideration; (iii) breach of condition.

Bars: (i) affirmation; (ii) lapse of time; (iii) inability to make restitution (restitutio in integrum impossible); (iv) third-party rights.

**PART 3: RECTIFICATION (SS. 30–33)**

Where a written instrument fails to express the parties' true intention due to mutual mistake (or unilateral mistake known to the other party), the court may rectify the document. High burden — clear and convincing evidence required.

**PART 4: DECLARATIONS (S. 41)**

Court may make a binding declaration of right whether or not consequential relief is claimed. Requires: (i) real and present dispute; (ii) plaintiff with sufficient interest; (iii) defendant with adverse interest; (iv) court's discretion in favour.

**PART 5: INJUNCTIONS (SS. 50–55)**

(1) **Perpetual injunction** (s. 51): granted at the conclusion of suit; restrains breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff.

(2) **Mandatory injunction** (s. 53): compels performance of an act. Higher threshold than prohibitory — Films Rover principle (high degree of assurance).

(3) **Interim injunction** (s. 54): preserves status quo pending trial — American Cyanamid + serious question + balance of convenience + adequacy of damages.

**Bars to injunction** (s. 54): where damages are adequate; to enforce a continuous obligation requiring constant supervision (subject to limited exceptions); against legislative or judicial functions; where conduct disentitles the plaintiff.

The leading Malaysian case on interim injunctions is **Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah [1995] 1 MLJ 193** (Court of Appeal) — synthesises the American Cyanamid test for Malaysian practice.
keyPrinciples: Specific performance is the prima facie remedy for sale of land contracts (s. 11(2) SRA 1950).
Equitable remedies are discretionary — barred by laches, acquiescence, unclean hands, and where damages are adequate.
Rescission requires restitutio in integrum — affirmation and third-party rights bar rescission.
Mandatory injunctions require a higher threshold than prohibitory injunctions (Films Rover; Keet Gerald Francis).
practicalNotes: For specific performance of sale of land, file the writ promptly and lodge a caveat to protect the equitable interest pending trial.
Plead readiness, willingness, and ability to perform — failure to do so is fatal under s. 24(b) SRA 1950.
For declarations, identify a concrete dispute with adverse interests — courts decline to give 'advisory opinions'.
Always consider whether damages would be adequate — if they would, equitable remedies are barred.
relatedCases: Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v United Malayan Banking Corporation Bhd [1993] 3 MLJ 36
Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah [1995] 1 MLJ 193
Films Rover International Ltd v Cannon Film Sales Ltd [1987] 1 WLR 670

theory_topics.title: Intellectual Property Litigation: Copyright, Trade Marks & Patents
theory_topics.overview: Malaysian IP litigation is governed by three principal statutes: the Copyright Act 1987, the Trade Marks Act 2019, and the Patents Act 1983. The High Court has exclusive jurisdiction; the Intellectual Property Court (KL) hears most IP matters.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: COPYRIGHT ACT 1987**

Copyright subsists automatically in original literary, artistic, musical, dramatic, sound recording, broadcast, film, and derivative works (s. 7). No registration required (Voluntary Notification under s. 26A creates prima facie evidence).

Duration: life + 50 years for individual authorship; 50 years from publication for corporate works.

**Infringement** (s. 36): unauthorised reproduction, distribution, communication to the public, adaptation. **Secondary infringement** (s. 36(2)) — possession or dealing in infringing copies for trade.

**Defences**: (i) fair dealing for research, private study, criticism, review, news reporting (s. 13); (ii) implied licence; (iii) public interest.

**Remedies**: damages, account of profits, injunction, delivery up, statutory damages (s. 37 — up to RM25,000 per work as alternative to actual damages).

**PART 2: TRADE MARKS ACT 2019**

The TMA 2019 (Act 815) repealed and replaced the TMA 1976. Key changes: introduction of multi-class applications; non-traditional marks (sounds, smells, holograms); recognition of well-known marks (Article 6bis Paris Convention); accession to the Madrid Protocol.

**Registration**: application to MyIPO; examination; publication; opposition (2 months); registration. Initial term 10 years, renewable.

**Infringement** (s. 54): use in the course of trade of a mark identical/similar to a registered mark in respect of identical/similar goods or services where likely to confuse.

**Defences**: (i) honest concurrent use; (ii) own name defence; (iii) descriptive use; (iv) prior use.

**Passing off**: parallel common-law remedy — classical trinity (Reckitt & Colman v Borden [1990] 1 WLR 491): goodwill, misrepresentation, damage.

**Remedies**: damages, account of profits, injunction, delivery up, erasure, declaration of invalidity (counterclaim).

**PART 3: PATENTS ACT 1983**

Patent rights are territorial. Application to MyIPO; examination; grant. Term: 20 years from filing date.

**Patentable invention** (s. 11): novelty (s. 14), inventive step (s. 15), industrial application (s. 16). Excluded subject matter (s. 13): discoveries, mathematical methods, business schemes, methods of treatment of human/animal body.

**Infringement**: making, using, selling, importing the patented product or process. Doctrine of equivalents — limited recognition.

**Defences**: invalidity (lack of novelty, obviousness, insufficient disclosure); experimental use; prior use.

**PART 4: PROCEDURAL CONSIDERATIONS**

(1) **Anton Piller orders** (search orders) — ex parte to preserve infringing material. Strict safeguards (independent solicitor supervisor, undertakings, etc.).

(2) **Norwich Pharmacal orders** — to obtain identity of unknown infringers from third parties (e.g. ISPs).

(3) **Border measures** — Customs (Prohibition of Imports) Order; trade mark owner may lodge notice with Customs to seize counterfeit imports under s. 70(I) TMA 2019.

(4) **Criminal sanctions** — copyright (Trade Descriptions Act 2011 + Copyright Act 1987 ss. 41–43); trade marks (Trade Descriptions Act 2011); patents (no criminal sanctions).
keyPrinciples: Copyright subsists automatically; trade marks require registration; patents require grant after examination.
Trade Marks Act 2019 introduced multi-class applications, non-traditional marks, and Madrid Protocol membership.
Passing off (common law) parallels trade mark infringement — three elements: goodwill, misrepresentation, damage.
Patent term is 20 years from filing date; territorial rights only.
practicalNotes: For copyright, secure Statutory Declaration of Authorship and Voluntary Notification with MyIPO — prima facie evidence at trial.
Always conduct trade mark searches before launch; oppositions filed within 2 months from publication.
Anton Piller orders are exceptional — only where evidence is strong, real risk of destruction, and supervising solicitor terms are in place.
Plead infringement specifically (mark-by-mark, work-by-work, claim-by-claim for patents); generic pleadings invite striking out.
relatedCases: Reckitt & Colman Products Ltd v Borden Inc [1990] 1 WLR 491
Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55
Norwich Pharmacal Co v Customs and Excise Commissioners [1974] AC 133

theory_topics.title: Trusts, Equity & Fiduciary Duties
theory_topics.overview: Malaysian trust law inherits from English equity and is supplemented by the Trustee Act 1949 (Act 208) and the Trust Companies Act 1949. Equity supplements statute and provides specific remedies — constructive trusts, tracing, fiduciary accounts.
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: CLASSIFICATION OF TRUSTS**

(1) **Express trust** — created intentionally; requires the three certainties (Knight v Knight): certainty of intention, subject matter, objects.

(2) **Resulting trust** — arises by operation of law where (i) presumed (purchase money cases); (ii) automatic (failed express trust).

(3) **Constructive trust** — imposed by equity to prevent unconscionable conduct (e.g. proceeds of breach of fiduciary duty; secret commissions; bribes — FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital [2014] UKSC 45).

(4) **Statutory trust** — under various statutes (e.g. Trustee Act 1949 default trusts).

**PART 2: TRUSTEE'S DUTIES**

(1) Duty to obey the trust instrument and act gratuitously (unless authorised);
(2) Duty of loyalty — no conflict of interest, no profit (Bray v Ford);
(3) Duty of care under the Trustee Act 1949 — standard of a reasonable prudent trustee;
(4) Duty to invest under the Trustee Act 1949 (authorised investments); broader powers under modern instruments;
(5) Duty to keep accounts and provide information to beneficiaries;
(6) Duty to act unanimously (joint trustees) unless instrument provides otherwise.

**PART 3: BREACH OF TRUST AND REMEDIES**

Personal remedies: equitable compensation; account of profits.
Proprietary remedies: tracing — following the value of misappropriated trust property into substituted assets (Foskett v McKeown [2001] 1 AC 102).

**Knowing receipt** and **dishonest assistance** — third-party liability for participation in breach of trust (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan [1995] 2 AC 378; BCCI v Akindele [2001] Ch 437).

**PART 4: FIDUCIARY DUTIES OUTSIDE TRUSTS**

Fiduciary duties arise in any relationship of trust and confidence — directors of companies (s. 213 CA 2016 codified); partners; agents; solicitors and clients; senior employees.

Two core duties (Bristol & West Building Society v Mothew [1998] Ch 1):
(i) **Duty of loyalty** — single-minded loyalty to the principal; no conflict; no profit.
(ii) **Duty of confidence** — preservation of confidential information.

**Remedies for breach**: account of profits (whether or not the principal suffered loss); equitable compensation; constructive trust over secret profits; injunction.

**PART 5: TRACING**

Tracing follows the value of property into substitutes. Two stages: identification (following) and following (claiming).
**Equitable tracing rules**: (i) Re Hallett's Estate (1880) — fiduciary deemed to draw out his own money first from a mixed account; (ii) Re Oatway (1903) — rule reversed where remaining funds are dissipated; (iii) Re Diplock — pari passu sharing on insolvency of recipient.

The Federal Court has applied these principles in tracing claims in **Tay Choo Foo v Tengku Mohd Saad [2009] 1 MLJ 289** and subsequent cases.
keyPrinciples: Express trusts require the three certainties: intention, subject matter, objects.
Constructive trusts are imposed by equity to prevent unconscionable conduct (e.g. secret commissions, bribes).
Fiduciaries owe duties of loyalty and confidence; remedies include account of profits regardless of loss.
Tracing identifies trust property in substituted assets; equitable rules (Hallett, Oatway, Diplock) govern mixed accounts.
practicalNotes: Plead breach of trust/fiduciary duty with specific particulars: relationship, duty, breach, gain or loss.
For tracing, plead the chain of substitutions clearly with documentary support (bank statements, transaction records).
Seek interim freezing orders (Mareva) and asset disclosure where breach is suspected — preserve assets pending trial.
Equitable defences (laches, acquiescence, change of position) must be pleaded specifically by the defendant.
relatedCases: Foskett v McKeown [2001] 1 AC 102
Royal Brunei Airlines Sdn Bhd v Tan [1995] 2 AC 378
FHR European Ventures LLP v Cedar Capital Partners LLC [2014] UKSC 45
BCCI v Akindele [2001] Ch 437
Re Hallett's Estate (1880) 13 Ch D 696

theory_topics.title: Limitation, Service & Pre-Action Procedure
theory_topics.overview: Pre-action and procedural foundations for civil litigation: limitation under the Limitation Act 1953, service of process under O 10–11 ROC 2012, and pre-action conduct (demand letters, pre-action discovery).
theory_topics.content:
**PART 1: LIMITATION ACT 1953**

The Limitation Act 1953 (Act 254) prescribes the periods within which actions must be commenced. Time runs from accrual of cause of action.

Key periods:
- **Contract and tort** — 6 years (s. 6(1)(a))
- **Personal injury** — 6 years from accrual (s. 6(1)); no separate personal-injury period in Malaysia. Only 36 months where the defendant is the Government or a public authority (Public Authorities Protection Act 1948)
- **Recovery of land** — 12 years (s. 9)
- **Mortgages and charges (recovery of principal)** — 12 years (s. 21)
- **Defamation** — 6 years
- **Specialty (deed)** — 12 years (s. 6(3))
- **Money judgment enforcement** — 12 years (s. 6(3))
- **Trust and fraud** — generally no limitation against express trustees (s. 22) but s. 22(2) imposes 6 years for breach of trust where no fraud.

**Disabilities** under s. 24 — minority and unsound mind suspend time. **Acknowledgement and part payment** under s. 26 reset the clock for debts.

**Postponement** under s. 29 — fraud, concealment, mistake; time runs from discovery.

**Suing public authorities** — Public Authorities Protection Act 1948: 36 months from act/neglect.

**PART 2: SERVICE OF WRIT — ORDER 10**

(1) **Personal service** (O 62 r 4) — handing the document to the recipient; corporate defendants under O 62 r 5 (registered office or principal place of business).
(2) **Substituted service** (O 62 r 5) — where personal service impractical; affidavit + court order; modes include posting at last known address, advertisement in newspaper, AR registered post.
(3) **Service on Government** — Government Proceedings Act 1956, ss. 11, 22, 23 — on AG.
(4) **Service out of jurisdiction** — leave under O 11 + grounds + appropriate forum analysis.

**PART 3: ORDER 11 — SERVICE OUT OF JURISDICTION**

Leave required (subject to limited exceptions like Hague Convention countries). Grounds include:
- Contract made/governed by Malaysian law;
- Contract performed in Malaysia;
- Tort committed in Malaysia;
- Property in Malaysia.

The applicant must show a 'good arguable case' on the merits and that Malaysia is the appropriate forum (forum conveniens — Spiliada).

**PART 4: PRE-ACTION CONDUCT**

(1) **Demand letter** — formal demand for performance/payment; runs interest in many cases; relevant to costs.
(2) **Without prejudice negotiations** — protected by privilege; 'WP save as to costs' offers relevant to costs at trial.
(3) **Pre-action discovery** under O 24 r 7A — for personal injury claims; restricted in scope.
(4) **Pre-action interrogatories** — limited.
(5) **Norwich Pharmacal orders** — to identify wrongdoers from third parties.

**PART 5: RENEWAL OF WRIT**

Writ valid for 6 months from issue (O 6 r 7). Renewal under O 6 r 7(2) — for good reason — application before expiry. Out-of-time renewal possible but exceptional.
keyPrinciples: Limitation periods run from accrual of cause of action; fraud, concealment, mistake postpone under s. 29 LA 1953.
Personal service is the rule; substituted service requires court order on affidavit of attempts.
Service out of jurisdiction under O 11 requires leave + good arguable case + forum conveniens.
Writ is valid 6 months; renewal for good reason before expiry under O 6 r 7.
practicalNotes: Always diary the limitation date; the most common professional negligence claim is statute-barring.
Preserve evidence of demand and acknowledgement — s. 26 LA 1953 acknowledgements reset the limitation clock.
For substituted service, affidavit must show genuine attempts at personal service; mere convenience is not enough.
When suing a foreign defendant, identify O 11 ground precisely in the leave application — wrong ground may be fatal.
relatedCases: Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460

workflows.title: Order for Sale (Foreclosure) — Landed Property
workflows.description: Step-by-step procedure to obtain an Order for Sale in the High Court for a charged landed property under the National Land Code 1965 and Order 83 ROC 2012.
workflows.legalBasis: National Land Code 1965 (ss. 254-259); Rules of Court 2012, Order 83
workflows.applicableTo: Licensed banks and financial institutions holding a registered charge over land

steps.title: Verify Default and Outstanding Balance
steps.description: Confirm the chargor has defaulted and compute total amount outstanding including principal, interest, penalty charges, and legal costs. Obtain a Certificate of Amount Due from the bank's authorized officer.
steps.legalBasis: Loan Agreement; s. 4 Oaths and Affirmations Act 2012
steps.notes: Ensure interest rate applied is as per the agreement — do not overclaim

steps.title: Serve Form 16C (Notice Before Foreclosure)
steps.description: Serve a written notice on the chargor specifying the amount due and demanding payment. The notice must give the chargor at least one month to remedy the default.
steps.notes: Service must be by personal service or registered post — keep proof of delivery

steps.title: Serve Form 16D (Foreclosure Notice)
steps.description: After expiry of Form 16C notice without payment, serve Form 16D — the formal Notice of Application for Order for Sale — at least one month before filing the Originating Summons.

steps.title: Obtain Property Valuation
steps.description: Commission an independent valuation report from a registered valuer for the charged property. The report will form the basis of the reserved price.
steps.legalBasis: Order 83 r 3 ROC 2012; Valuers, Appraisers, Estate Agents and Property Managers Act 1981
documents: Valuation Report (not more than 12 months old)

steps.title: File Originating Summons in High Court
steps.description: Prepare and file an Originating Summons supported by an affidavit in the High Court in the land office district where the land is situated. Exhibit all required documents.
documents: Certified copy of title (Form 5A or Registry Search)
Copy of loan agreement and charge document
Form 16C and 16D with proofs of service

steps.title: Serve Originating Summons on Chargor
steps.description: Serve a sealed copy of the OS and supporting affidavit on the chargor personally or by substituted service if personal service is impracticable.
steps.timeframe: Within 7 days of filing, then 14 days for chargor to respond

steps.title: Attend Hearing of Originating Summons
steps.description: Appear before the judge in chambers on the hearing date. If no appearance by chargor and no defence filed, seek Order for Sale. If chargor appears, argue on the merits.

steps.title: Extract Order for Sale
steps.description: After obtaining the Order for Sale, extract the sealed court order. The order will specify the reserved price and give directions for the sale.

steps.title: Submit to Land Administrator for Auction
steps.description: Forward the sealed Order for Sale to the Land Administrator (Pentadbir Tanah) for the district. The Land Administrator will fix a date for the public auction.
steps.timeframe: 1-3 months for auction to be fixed

steps.title: Public Auction
steps.description: The Land Administrator conducts a public auction. Successful bidder pays 10% deposit on the day. Balance is payable within 90 days (or 120 days for non-citizens).

steps.title: Distribution of Proceeds
steps.description: After auction, proceeds are distributed: (1) Land Administrator's costs and fees; (2) Outstanding sum to chargee (bank); (3) Balance (if any) to chargor. Bank applies remaining balance if proceeds are insufficient.

sampleDocuments: Originating Summons for Order for Sale

workflows.title: Summary Judgment Application under Order 14
workflows.description: Procedure to obtain summary judgment against a defendant where there is no arguable defence, commonly used by banks to recover loan debts without a full trial.
workflows.legalBasis: Rules of Court 2012, Order 14; Order 13
workflows.applicableTo: All civil claims in the High Court, Sessions Court, and Magistrates' Court
workflows.estimatedDuration: 3-6 months from filing writ to judgment

steps.title: File Writ of Summons and Statement of Claim
steps.description: Prepare and file a Writ of Summons with a Statement of Claim setting out the cause of action (breach of loan agreement), amount claimed (principal + interest + costs).

steps.title: Serve Writ on Defendant
steps.description: Serve the Writ personally on the defendant. If personal service fails, apply for substituted service (notice board, advertisement, address of last known residence).
steps.timeframe: 7 days to enter appearance after service

steps.title: File and Serve Summons for Summary Judgment
steps.description: After the defendant enters appearance (or upon expiry of time), file an application for summary judgment supported by an affidavit. The affidavit must verify the cause of action and state the defendant has no defence.
documents: Exhibits: loan agreement, statement of account, notices
steps.timeframe: After appearance, before defence is due

steps.title: Defendant Files Affidavit in Opposition
steps.description: Defendant has 14 days to file an affidavit showing a bona fide triable issue (e.g., fraudulent misrepresentation, non-est factum, payment). Court will reject a sham defence.

steps.title: Hearing of Summary Judgment Application
steps.description: Parties appear before the master or judge. Plaintiff argues there is no triable issue. If court agrees, judgment is granted. If defendant shows a triable issue, matter proceeds to trial or conditional leave is granted.

steps.title: Extract and Enforce Judgment
steps.description: Upon obtaining judgment, extract the sealed judgment. Enforce via Writ of Seizure and Sale, garnishee, charging order, or bankruptcy proceedings.

workflows.title: Winding Up Petition — Company Debtor
workflows.description: Procedure to wind up a company that is unable to pay its debts to the bank under the Companies Act 2016.
workflows.legalBasis: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), ss. 464-475; Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972; Order 87 ROC 2012
workflows.applicableTo: Banks as creditors of insolvent companies
workflows.estimatedDuration: 6-12 months from petition to winding up order

steps.title: Serve Statutory Demand
steps.description: Serve a written statutory demand on the company at its registered address, demanding payment of the outstanding debt (minimum RM10,000) within 21 days. The demand must identify the debt with particularity.
documents: Statutory Demand (Form 69 of Companies Winding Up Rules)

steps.title: Verify Company's Inability to Pay
steps.description: If no payment after 21 days, confirm the company has not applied to set aside the statutory demand. Obtain updated statement of account.
documents: Proof of service of statutory demand

steps.title: File Winding Up Petition in High Court
steps.description: File the petition in the High Court (Company Division/Commercial Division). The petition must comply with Form 3 of Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972.
documents: Statutory demand and proof of service
steps.timeframe: Within 4 months of statutory demand service

steps.title: Serve Petition on Company and Advertise
steps.description: Serve sealed petition on company at registered address. Advertise the hearing date in one Bahasa Malaysia and one English daily newspaper at least 7 clear days before hearing.

steps.title: Attend Hearing — Winding Up Order
steps.description: Appear at the petition hearing. If company does not oppose, court makes a winding up order. If opposed, court hears arguments. Official Receiver appointed as provisional liquidator.

steps.title: Attend Meeting of Creditors
steps.description: Official Receiver calls a creditors' meeting to appoint a licensed insolvency practitioner as liquidator. Bank files Proof of Debt.
steps.timeframe: Within 3 months of winding up order

workflows.title: Bankruptcy Petition — Individual Debtor
workflows.description: Procedure to file a bankruptcy petition against an individual debtor who owes at least RM50,000 under the Insolvency Act 1967.
workflows.legalBasis: Insolvency Act 1967 (Act 360), ss. 4-14; Order 88 ROC 2012
workflows.applicableTo: Banks as creditors of individual debtors
workflows.estimatedDuration: 6-12 months from act of bankruptcy to bankruptcy order

steps.title: Obtain Judgment
steps.description: First obtain a court judgment against the debtor for the outstanding debt. Bankruptcy proceedings require a judgment debt or liquidated demand.

steps.title: Issue Bankruptcy Notice
steps.description: Serve a bankruptcy notice (Form 1 of Insolvency Rules) on the debtor within 6 months of the judgment. The notice demands payment of the judgment debt within 7 days.

steps.title: Non-Compliance — Act of Bankruptcy
steps.description: If the debtor fails to pay or secure the judgment debt within 7 days of the bankruptcy notice, this constitutes an act of bankruptcy — the foundation for the petition.

steps.title: File Bankruptcy Petition
steps.description: File the creditor's petition (Form 7) in the High Court within 6 months of the act of bankruptcy. Pay prescribed filing fees.
documents: Exhibits: judgment, bankruptcy notice, proof of service
steps.timeframe: Within 6 months of act of bankruptcy

steps.title: Serve Petition on Debtor
steps.description: Serve a sealed copy of the petition on the debtor personally at least 7 days before the hearing date.

steps.title: Attend Hearing — Bankruptcy Order
steps.description: Attend the hearing. If no opposition, court makes a bankruptcy order and the Official Assignee (Director General of Insolvency) takes possession of the debtor's property.

steps.title: File Proof of Debt with Official Assignee
steps.description: File a Proof of Debt with the Director General of Insolvency (Jabatan Insolvensi Malaysia). The bank will receive a dividend from the bankrupt estate in due course.

workflows.title: Garnishee Proceedings — Attachment of Bank Account
workflows.description: Procedure to attach a judgment debtor's funds held in a third-party bank account by way of garnishee proceedings under Order 49 ROC 2012.
workflows.legalBasis: Rules of Court 2012, Order 49
workflows.applicableTo: Judgment creditors seeking to attach funds in debtor's bank accounts

steps.title: Obtain Information on Debtor's Bank Accounts
steps.description: Before filing, investigate the debtor's bank accounts by conducting a Judgment Debtor Summons (Order 48 ROC 2012) to compel the debtor to disclose their assets and bank accounts.

steps.title: File Ex Parte Summons for Garnishee Order Nisi
steps.description: File an ex parte application (without notice to debtor) for a garnishee order nisi, specifying the third-party bank (garnishee) and the account details.
steps.timeframe: Filed and heard on the same day or next available date

steps.title: Obtain Garnishee Order Nisi
steps.description: The court grants an order nisi requiring the garnishee (third-party bank) to show cause why it should not pay the judgment debt from the funds it holds for the judgment debtor.

steps.title: Serve Order Nisi on Garnishee and Debtor
steps.description: Serve the order nisi on the garnishee bank and the judgment debtor. The garnishee bank must freeze the identified funds upon service.

steps.title: Show Cause Hearing — Garnishee Order Absolute
steps.description: At the show cause hearing, if the garnishee does not dispute owing money to the debtor and the debtor does not raise a valid objection, the court makes the order absolute — compelling payment to the judgment creditor.
steps.timeframe: On return date (usually 14 days after order nisi)

sampleDocuments: Ex Parte Summons for Garnishee Order Nisi

workflows.title: Mareva Injunction Application
workflows.description: Procedure to obtain a freezing order (Mareva injunction) in the High Court to prevent a defendant from dissipating assets pending judgment.
workflows.legalBasis: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s. 25(2); Schedule; Civil Law Act 1956, s. 24
workflows.applicableTo: Banks and financial institutions seeking to preserve assets pre-judgment
workflows.estimatedDuration: 1-3 days for ex parte order; 2-4 weeks for inter partes hearing

steps.title: Assess Whether Mareva Test is Satisfied
steps.description: Verify the criteria: (1) good arguable case on the merits; (2) real risk that defendant will dissipate or remove assets; (3) balance of convenience favours granting the injunction.
steps.legalBasis: Ninemia Maritime Corp v Trave Schiffahrtsgesellschaft GmbH [1983]; Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA [1975]

steps.title: File Writ of Summons and Statement of Claim
steps.description: Main action must be commenced or ready to be commenced. File Writ and Statement of Claim before or simultaneously with the injunction application.

steps.title: Prepare Ex Parte Application
steps.description: Prepare an ex parte summons and affidavit supporting the Mareva application. The affidavit must make full and frank disclosure of all material facts — failure to do so will result in discharge of the order.
documents: Affidavit with full and frank disclosure
Evidence of assets and risk of dissipation

steps.title: Ex Parte Hearing before Judge
steps.description: Appear before a High Court judge (often the duty judge) for the ex parte application. If satisfied, the judge grants the Mareva injunction until the inter partes hearing.
documents: Undertaking as to damages by plaintiff

steps.title: Serve Injunction Order
steps.description: Immediately serve the sealed injunction order on the defendant and on any banks/institutions holding the defendant's assets. Penal notice on order enables committal for contempt if breached.

steps.title: Inter Partes Hearing
steps.description: Both parties appear for the inter partes hearing. Defendant may argue the injunction should be discharged. Court will continue or vary the order pending trial.

sampleDocuments: Affidavit in Support (with full and frank disclosure)
Sealed Injunction Order with Penal Notice

workflows.title: Interlocutory Application — Notice of Application in Chambers (General Procedure)
workflows.description: Step-by-step procedure for filing and prosecuting an interlocutory application in chambers under Order 32 of the Rules of Court 2012, applicable to the great majority of pre-trial applications (e.g., striking out, summary judgment, discovery, amendment, security for costs).
workflows.legalBasis: Rules of Court 2012, Order 32 (Applications in Chambers); Order 41 (Affidavits); Order 59 (Costs)
workflows.applicableTo: Any party in High Court / Sessions Court / Magistrates Court civil proceedings seeking an interlocutory order between commencement and final judgment
workflows.estimatedDuration: 4–10 weeks from filing to disposal (subject to court's cause list and complexity)

steps.title: Identify the Application and Legal Basis
steps.description: Pinpoint the precise relief sought (e.g., striking out under Order 18 r 19; summary judgment under Order 14; specific discovery under Order 24 r 7) and the rule, statute, or inherent jurisdiction relied upon. Draft the proposed prayers with precision — vague prayers lead to unenforceable orders.
steps.legalBasis: Order 32 r 1 ROC 2012; relevant procedural Order

steps.title: Prepare the Notice of Application (Form 57)
steps.description: Draft the Notice of Application identifying the parties, action number, prayers (numbered), date/time/place of hearing (subject to registry's allocation), and grounds (briefly stated). Reference the supporting affidavit. Sign and date.

steps.title: Prepare and Affirm Supporting Affidavit (Form 65)
steps.description: Draft the affidavit of the party (or their authorised officer/solicitor) deposing to facts within personal knowledge. In interlocutory matters, hearsay is permitted (Order 41 r 5(2)) provided the source is identified. Mark and exhibit all documentary evidence with proper exhibit slips. Affirm before a Commissioner for Oaths.
steps.legalBasis: Order 41 ROC 2012; Oaths and Affirmations Act 2012

steps.title: File at Registry and Pay Filing Fee
steps.description: File the Notice of Application and affidavit at the court registry of the relevant court. Pay the filing fee (typically RM50 per interlocutory summons in the High Court — confirm current scale at the registry). Obtain sealed copies and a hearing date allocated by the registry.
steps.legalBasis: Court fee schedule under Courts of Judicature Act 1964 / Subordinate Courts Act 1948

steps.title: Serve on All Affected Parties
steps.description: Serve the sealed Notice of Application and supporting affidavit on every other party in the action (and any non-party affected). Service must be effected at least 2 clear days before the hearing date (Order 32 r 3). Use personal service or AR Registered post; obtain Affidavit of Service.
steps.timeframe: Within 2–7 days of filing; minimum 2 clear days before hearing

steps.title: Receive and Respond to Affidavit in Reply
steps.description: The respondent will typically file an Affidavit in Reply opposing the application. Review carefully. Decide whether a Rejoinder Affidavit is necessary to address new matters raised. Leave is not required for a single rejoinder, but further affidavits beyond that need leave.

steps.title: Prepare Bundle of Documents and Skeleton Submissions
steps.description: Compile a chambers bundle: index, Notice of Application, all affidavits with exhibits, sealed cause papers, draft order, written submissions, list of authorities (cases marked at relevant passages). File and exchange skeleton submissions at least 2 days before the hearing.

steps.title: Attend the Chambers Hearing
steps.description: Attend before the Judge in Chambers or Senior Assistant Registrar (SAR) at the appointed time. Hearing is in private (not open court). Make oral submissions, respond to questions from the bench, and address opponent's points. Be prepared for the application to be reserved for written ruling, allowed, dismissed or adjourned for further submissions.

steps.title: Draft, Submit and Seal the Order
steps.description: If successful, the winning party's solicitor drafts the Order in compliance with what was ordered (Form 65A or as appropriate), submits to the opposing party for endorsement (or notes any objection), and lodges at the registry for sealing. Insert a penal notice on injunctions and orders requiring positive acts.
documents: Sealed Order with penal notice (where applicable)

steps.title: Consider Appeal Routes
