legal_forms.notes: Unconscionability exception applies in Malaysian courts — fraudulent or unconscionable call may be restrained by injunction

legal_forms.title: Creditor's Bankruptcy Petition
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Insolvency Act 1967, s. 5; Order 88 ROC 2012
legal_forms.purpose: Filed by a creditor to commence bankruptcy proceedings against an individual debtor who owes RM50,000 or more
legal_forms.instructions: Must be filed within 6 months of the act of bankruptcy. Requires a verifying affidavit (Form 8). Must be served personally on the debtor at least 7 clear days before the hearing. Court filing fee: RM600.
legal_forms.filingFee: RM600 court filing fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: File within 6 months of act of bankruptcy; serve at least 7 days before hearing

legal_forms.title: Winding Up Petition
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Companies Act 2016, s. 464; Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972
legal_forms.purpose: Filed by a creditor to commence compulsory winding up proceedings against a company that is unable to pay its debts
legal_forms.instructions: Must comply with Form 3 of Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972. Verified by affidavit. Advertised in newspapers 7 days before hearing. Filed in the High Court (Company Division). Filing fee: RM1,000.
fields: Company Name, Registration Number, and Registered Address
Acts of Insolvency Relied Upon (e.g. statutory demand)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM1,000 court filing fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: File within 4 months of statutory demand service

legal_forms.title: Originating Summons for Order for Sale
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 83 r 3; National Land Code 1965
legal_forms.purpose: Commences judicial foreclosure proceedings in the High Court against a chargor in default of a registered charge
legal_forms.instructions: Filed in the High Court in the district where the land is situated or in the High Court where the defendant resides or has a place of business. Supported by affidavit exhibiting loan documents, charge documents, notices, title search, and valuation report.
fields: Land Title Details (Lot No., Mukim, District, State)
legal_forms.filingFee: Court filing fee (based on amount claimed) + RM3 per page for supporting documents
legal_forms.timeLimit: File at least 1 month after service of Form 16D

legal_forms.title: Summons for Summary Judgment
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 14
legal_forms.purpose: Application for judgment without trial where the defendant has no arguable defence to the plaintiff's claim
legal_forms.instructions: Supported by a supporting affidavit sworn by the plaintiff or an authorized officer. Must state that the plaintiff believes there is no defence to the claim. Defendant has 14 days to file an affidavit in reply showing a bona fide triable issue.
fields: Name of Deponent of Supporting Affidavit
legal_forms.filingFee: Court filing fee: RM50 for summons
legal_forms.timeLimit: File after defendant enters appearance; before defence is due

legal_forms.title: Bankruptcy Notice
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Insolvency Act 1967, s. 3(1)(i); Insolvency Rules
legal_forms.purpose: Formal demand served on a judgment debtor requiring payment of a judgment debt within 7 days, failure of which constitutes an act of bankruptcy
legal_forms.instructions: Must specify the judgment obtained, the court, the date, and the amount outstanding. Issued in the name of the court. Served personally on the debtor. Valid for 6 months from issue date.
legal_forms.filingFee: RM50 fee for issuance
legal_forms.timeLimit: Serve within 6 months of issue; debtor has 7 days to comply

legal_forms.title: Statutory Demand (Winding Up)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Companies Act 2016, s. 466(1)(a); Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972
legal_forms.purpose: Formal demand served on a company requiring payment of a debt of not less than RM10,000 within 21 days, as a precursor to winding up petition
legal_forms.instructions: Served at the company's registered office. Must state the debt with particularity and demand payment within 21 days. The company may apply to court to set aside the demand within the 21-day period.
fields: Basis of Debt (loan agreement, judgment, etc.)
legal_forms.filingFee: No court fee for private demand
legal_forms.timeLimit: Company has 21 days to pay; petition must be filed within 4 months of demand

legal_forms.title: Proof of Debt
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972, r 78; Companies Act 2016
legal_forms.purpose: Filed by a creditor with the liquidator or Official Receiver to prove the amount owed to them in a winding up proceeding
legal_forms.instructions: Must be lodged with the liquidator, supported by documentary evidence of the debt (loan agreement, judgment, statement of account). The liquidator may adjudicate on the proof and admit or reject it.
fields: Security Held (if any) and Value of Security
legal_forms.filingFee: No fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: Lodge within time prescribed by liquidator (usually 6 months of winding up order)

legal_forms.title: Memorandum of Settlement / Consent Judgment
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 42 r 5; Mediation Act 2012
legal_forms.purpose: Records a negotiated settlement between the bank and the borrower/debtor, which may be entered as a consent judgment to be enforceable as a court order
legal_forms.instructions: Must clearly state the terms: repayment schedule, interest rates, waiver of certain amounts, and consequences of default. Signed by both parties and their solicitors. Filed in court to be perfected as a consent order.
legal_forms.filingFee: Court consent order: nominal fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: File within period agreed by parties; court will set aside if not complied with

legal_forms.title: Deed of Assignment (Loan Portfolio)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Contracts Act 1950; Civil Law Act 1956, s. 4(3)
legal_forms.purpose: Transfers a bank's rights in loan agreements and securities to a third-party assignee (e.g., in loan securitisation or portfolio sale)
legal_forms.instructions: An absolute assignment under s. 4(3) of the Civil Law Act 1956 must be: in writing, absolute (not conditional), and notice must be given to the debtor. Stamp duty payable. Legal title passes to assignee upon registration of notice.
legal_forms.filingFee: Stamp duty: ad valorem rate on consideration
legal_forms.timeLimit: Notice to debtor must be given to perfect legal assignment

legal_forms.title: Verifying Affidavit for Bankruptcy Petition
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Insolvency Act 1967; Order 88 ROC 2012
legal_forms.purpose: Affidavit sworn by the petitioning creditor verifying the facts stated in the bankruptcy petition
legal_forms.instructions: Sworn before a Commissioner for Oaths. Must exhibit the judgment, bankruptcy notice, and proof of service. The deponent must have personal knowledge of the facts or state the basis of their belief.
fields: Statement of Facts (debt, judgment, bankruptcy notice, service)
Commissioner for Oaths stamp and signature
legal_forms.filingFee: No separate fee — filed with the petition
legal_forms.timeLimit: Sworn before or simultaneously with filing the petition

legal_forms.title: Statutory Declaration — Proof of Service
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 65; Oaths and Affirmations Act 2012
legal_forms.purpose: Used to prove personal service of court documents (writs, summonses, orders) or statutory notices (Forms 16C, 16D, Bankruptcy Notice) where an affidavit of service is required
legal_forms.instructions: Made by the process server or solicitor's clerk who served the document. Must state: date, time, place, and method of service; description of person served. Declared before a Commissioner for Oaths.
fields: Date, Time, and Place of Service
legal_forms.filingFee: RM5 Commissioner for Oaths fee (standard)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Declare as soon as possible after service — contemporaneous records are essential

legal_forms.title: Banking Facility Letter of Offer
legal_forms.authorizedBy: FSA 2013, Schedule 7 (Disclosure); Consumer Protection Act 1999
legal_forms.purpose: Formal offer by a bank to a borrower setting out the terms and conditions of the approved credit facility
legal_forms.instructions: Must comply with BNM's Guidelines on Product Transparency and Disclosure. For consumer credit: must state: credit limit, interest rate (in APR), all fees and charges, repayment schedule, and early repayment terms. Acceptance by signing and returning to bank.
fields: Interest Rate (and APR for consumer credit)
legal_forms.filingFee: Processing fee (varies by bank)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Acceptance period: usually 14-30 days from date of letter

legal_forms.title: Hire Purchase Agreement (Standard Form)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Hire-Purchase Act 1967, s. 4
legal_forms.purpose: Standard hire purchase agreement setting out the terms under which the owner (bank/finance company) lets goods to the hirer on hire purchase terms
legal_forms.instructions: Must contain all matters prescribed in the Second Schedule of the HPA 1967 including: cash price, hire purchase price, amount of each instalment, total charges, and repayment schedule. Hirer must receive a copy at time of signing.
fields: Description of Goods (make, model, year, registration number)
legal_forms.filingFee: Stamp duty on HP agreement; registration of vehicle with JPJ
legal_forms.timeLimit: Stamp duty within 30 days of execution

legal_forms.title: Debenture (Fixed and Floating Charge)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Companies Act 2016, s. 352; Contracts Act 1950
legal_forms.purpose: Creates a fixed and floating charge over all present and future assets of a company as security for banking facilities
legal_forms.instructions: Must be registered with the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM) within 30 days of creation — failure renders it void against liquidator and creditors (s. 352(3) CA 2016). Stamp duty: 0.5% of secured amount.
fields: Company (Chargor) Name, Co. No., and Address
legal_forms.filingFee: SSM registration fee (scale) + 0.5% stamp duty
legal_forms.timeLimit: Register with SSM within 30 days of creation

legal_forms.title: Memorandum of Transfer (MOT)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: National Land Code 1965, s. 215
legal_forms.purpose: Transfers ownership of land from one person to another. Used in property purchase transactions financed by bank loans, and in enforcement of security after auction
legal_forms.instructions: Must be executed by the transferor before a solicitor. Stamp duty (MOT) payable based on purchase price or market value (whichever is higher). Presented to Land Registry for registration. The Memorandum of Transfer is Form 14A under the NLC.
legal_forms.filingFee: Stamp duty (MOT): 1% first RM100k; 2% next RM400k; 3% excess over RM500k; Registration fee: RM100-500
legal_forms.timeLimit: Present for registration within 3 months of execution

legal_forms.title: Private Caveat
legal_forms.authorizedBy: National Land Code 1965, s. 322
legal_forms.purpose: Lodged by a person claiming an interest in land to give notice of their interest and prevent further dealings with the land without their knowledge
legal_forms.instructions: A bank may lodge a caveat as equitable mortgagee where title deeds are deposited. The caveat is lodged with the Land Registry and prevents registration of any dealing inconsistent with the caveator's interest.
fields: Nature of Caveator's Interest (equitable mortgage, purchaser, etc.)
legal_forms.filingFee: Land Registry fee: RM50-100
legal_forms.timeLimit: Effective for 6 years (renewable); may be removed by caveat-out application

legal_forms.title: Sale and Purchase Agreement (Property)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Housing Development (Control and Licensing) Act 1966 (for developer SPA); Contracts Act 1950
legal_forms.purpose: Agreement for sale and purchase of property, forming the basis for the bank's mortgage/charge documentation in a housing loan transaction
legal_forms.instructions: Solicitors for both vendor and purchaser review and execute the SPA. For housing developers: Housing Development Regulations 1989 prescribes Form H (SPA for sub-sale) and Form G (for strata). Stamp duty on SPA may be adjudicated.
legal_forms.filingFee: Stamp duty on SPA: RM10 or ad valorem (whichever is higher) in addition to MOT stamp duty
legal_forms.timeLimit: Complete within contractual period (typically 3-6 months for sub-sale)

legal_forms.title: Personal Guarantee
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Contracts Act 1950, ss. 79-102
legal_forms.purpose: A personal guarantee executed by an individual (guarantor) to guarantee the repayment of a borrower's debt to the bank
legal_forms.instructions: Must be in writing and signed by the guarantor (s. 82 CA 1950). Must specify the guaranteed amount (or be a continuing guarantee). Independent legal advice is recommended. Stamp duty: RM10 for first RM10,000 guaranteed; RM10 per RM10,000 thereafter.
fields: Joint and Several Liability Clause (if co-guarantors)
Rights of Guarantee (to be given to guarantor)
legal_forms.filingFee: Stamp duty: RM10 per RM1,000 guaranteed (or part thereof)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Enforceable within 6 years of date of default or demand

legal_forms.title: Affidavit in Support — Order for Sale Application
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 83 r 3
legal_forms.purpose: Supporting affidavit for an Originating Summons for Order for Sale, attesting to the bank's right to enforce the charge and the amount outstanding
legal_forms.instructions: Sworn by an authorized officer of the bank. Must exhibit: loan agreement, charge documents, Form 16C and 16D (with proofs of service), land title search, valuation report, and Certificate of Amount Due.
fields: Reference to Loan Agreement and Charge
legal_forms.filingFee: Filed with OS — no separate fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: Contemporaneous with filing of Originating Summons

legal_forms.title: Deed of Variation / Supplemental Agreement
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Contracts Act 1950, s. 62 (accord and satisfaction)
legal_forms.purpose: Formally varies the terms of an existing loan agreement (e.g., to reduce interest rate, extend tenure, or restructure repayment schedule)
legal_forms.instructions: Must be executed by both parties. A deed requires attestation by two witnesses. The variation must be supported by fresh consideration unless executed as a deed. Stamp duty payable if new amount or rate varied.
fields: Borrower Name, NRIC/Co. No., and Address
legal_forms.filingFee: Stamp duty if new money lent; RM10 adjudicated if no new money
legal_forms.timeLimit: Should be executed before expiry of original agreement

legal_forms.title: Solicitors' Letter of Demand
legal_forms.authorizedBy: General practice; Legal Profession Act 1976
legal_forms.purpose: Pre-action letter from the bank's solicitors to the debtor demanding payment of the outstanding amount and threatening legal action if not paid
legal_forms.instructions: Should state: amount claimed, basis of claim (breach of loan agreement), interest claimed, and a clear deadline (usually 7-14 days). Sent by registered post and courier. Keep proof of delivery. A letter of demand is not mandatory but is strongly advisable.
legal_forms.filingFee: No fee — private correspondence
legal_forms.timeLimit: Issue at least 7-14 days before filing court action

legal_forms.title: Judgment Debtor Examination Summons
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 48
legal_forms.purpose: Summons compelling a judgment debtor to attend court and be examined on oath about their assets and means of satisfying the judgment debt
legal_forms.instructions: Filed by the judgment creditor after obtaining a judgment. The judgment debtor is examined before a Senior Assistant Registrar. Failure to attend is contempt of court. The examination assists in tracing assets for enforcement.
fields: Date, Time, and Place of Examination
legal_forms.filingFee: Court filing fee: RM50
legal_forms.timeLimit: File after judgment; serve at least 7 days before examination date

legal_forms.title: Memorandum of Charge — Amendment
legal_forms.authorizedBy: National Land Code 1965, s. 249
legal_forms.purpose: Amends an existing registered charge to reflect changes in the loan terms (e.g., increased credit limit, restructured facility)
legal_forms.instructions: Must be presented to the Land Registry and registered. Stamp duty on any increased secured amount. Both chargor and chargee must execute the amendment.
legal_forms.filingFee: Stamp duty on increment + registration fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: Present within 3 months of execution

legal_forms.title: Discharge of Charge (Form 16N)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: National Land Code 1965, s. 278
legal_forms.purpose: Releases and discharges a registered charge from a land title upon full repayment of the secured debt
legal_forms.instructions: Executed by the chargee (bank) after full repayment. Presented to the Land Registry by the solicitor. Registration cancels the charge endorsed on the title. Solicitor should ensure all redemption monies are received before releasing discharge.
legal_forms.filingFee: Registration fee: RM100 (approximately)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Must be presented within 3 months of execution; usually done at completion of loan

legal_forms.title: Security Bond / Performance Bond
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Contracts Act 1950; Government Contracts Act 1949
legal_forms.purpose: A bond (usually bank-backed) given to guarantee the performance of a contract, particularly in construction, procurement, and government contracts
legal_forms.instructions: Typically issued by a bank on behalf of a contractor/bidder. Performance bonds are usually 5% of contract value; bid bonds are 1-2%. Demand bonds are payable on written demand within the validity period.
legal_forms.filingFee: Bank commission (0.5%-2% p.a.) + RM10 stamp duty
legal_forms.timeLimit: Valid for contract period + warranty period (typically 1-2 years)

legal_forms.title: Trust Receipt Agreement
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Financial Services Act 2013 (trade finance provisions); Contracts Act 1950
legal_forms.purpose: Post-shipment financing document where the bank releases shipping documents to the importer (customer) on trust, allowing the customer to sell the goods and remit proceeds to the bank
legal_forms.instructions: The importer acknowledges holding the goods (or proceeds) as trustee for the bank. The trust receipt must specify the goods, invoice amount, and maturity date for repayment. Standard tenure: 30-120 days.
fields: Customer's Undertaking to Hold Goods on Trust
legal_forms.filingFee: Bank's commission and interest as per facility terms
legal_forms.timeLimit: Repayment on or before maturity date specified

legal_forms.title: Writ of Summons — General Civil Action
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 6; Courts of Judicature Act 1964
legal_forms.purpose: Originating process to commence a civil action in the High Court or Sessions Court for any civil claim — contract, tort, debt, or other civil wrong
legal_forms.instructions: File in the appropriate court based on the amount claimed: High Court (above RM250,000), Sessions Court (RM50,000-RM250,000), Magistrate's Court (up to RM100,000 for contract/tort from 2023). Endorse the nature of claim and, where possible, the Statement of Claim on the reverse. Seal at court registry. Serve on defendant personally within 12 months of issue (extendable).
fields: Plaintiff's Solicitor Name and Address for Service
legal_forms.filingFee: Ad valorem court filing fee based on amount claimed
legal_forms.timeLimit: Valid for 12 months from date of issue; may be renewed

legal_forms.title: Statement of Claim — Breach of Contract
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18
legal_forms.purpose: Formal pleading setting out the plaintiff's case in a breach of contract action, particularising the contract, the breach, and the losses suffered
legal_forms.instructions: Must be concise and contain only material facts — not evidence or law. State: (1) the contract (date, parties, terms); (2) the breach (specific acts/omissions constituting breach); (3) particulars of damage (special damages must be particularised). Served on defendant with or after the Writ. Pleadings must be verified by a Statement of Truth.
fields: Interest Claimed (s.11 Civil Law Act 1956 or contractual)
Relief Sought (judgment for sum + interest + costs)
legal_forms.filingFee: Included in Writ filing fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: Serve within time directed or within 14 days after appearance

legal_forms.title: Statement of Claim — Negligence/Tort
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18; Civil Law Act 1956
legal_forms.purpose: Formal pleading for a tort claim (negligence, nuisance, trespass, defamation) setting out the duty of care, breach, and resulting damage
legal_forms.instructions: For negligence: plead (1) duty of care owed; (2) the specific acts/omissions constituting breach of duty; (3) causation — the breach caused the damage; (4) the heads of damage (personal injury: general and special damages; property damage). For MVA cases, plead the specific act of negligence (speed, failure to keep proper lookout, failure to give way). Attach medical reports for personal injury claims.
fields: Date, Time, and Location of Incident
Heads of Loss (Special Damages: medical expenses, loss of earnings, transport; General Damages: pain and suffering, loss of amenities)
legal_forms.filingFee: Ad valorem court filing fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: Within 6 years of accrual for both personal injury and property damage (Limitation Act 1953, s.6(1)); only 36 months where a public authority is the defendant (Public Authorities Protection Act 1948)

legal_forms.title: Notice of Application for Judicial Review — Form OS (Order 53)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53, r.3
legal_forms.purpose: Originating process to apply for leave to apply for judicial review of a decision, act, or omission by a public authority in Malaysia
legal_forms.instructions: File an Originating Summons (OS) together with: (1) the Statement required by O.53 r.3(2) — stating applicant's name, relief sought, and grounds; (2) Affidavit in Support verifying all material facts. File ex parte in the first instance (the judge may direct the respondent to attend the leave hearing). Must be filed within 3 months of the decision — strict time limit.
legal_forms.filingFee: Court filing fee: RM200-RM400 (Originating Summons)
legal_forms.timeLimit: MUST BE FILED WITHIN 3 MONTHS OF THE DECISION — Strict

legal_forms.title: Petition for Divorce — Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976
legal_forms.authorizedBy: LRA 1976, s.50; Divorce and Matrimonial Proceedings Rules 1980
legal_forms.purpose: To commence divorce proceedings in the High Court (Family Division) or Sessions Court for dissolution of a non-Muslim civil marriage in Malaysia
legal_forms.instructions: File in the High Court Family Division (or Sessions Court if matrimonial assets below RM250,000 and no complex issues). State the ground(s) relied on (unreasonable behaviour, adultery, desertion, separation). Attach marriage certificate. Petitioner must file an affidavit verifying the contents of the petition. Serve personally on the respondent spouse.
fields: Full Names of Petitioner (Plaintiff) and Respondent (Defendant)
Details of Children of the Marriage
Relief Sought: Decree Nisi, Custody, Maintenance, Division of Matrimonial Assets
legal_forms.filingFee: Court filing fee: RM200-RM400
legal_forms.timeLimit: No minimum period before filing (except 2-year rule for joint petition under s.52)

legal_forms.title: Originating Petition — Company Oppression (s.346 CA 2016)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Companies Act 2016, s.346; Rules of Court 2012, Order 88
legal_forms.purpose: To petition the High Court for relief against oppressive or unfairly prejudicial conduct of the affairs of a company, on behalf of a minority or aggrieved shareholder
legal_forms.instructions: File in the High Court (Commercial Division — Company Matters). The Originating Petition must be verified by affidavit. Set out in full: (1) the petitioner's shareholding; (2) the respondents (company + individual controllers); (3) the facts constituting oppressive conduct; (4) the relief sought (share buyout, conduct order, winding up as last resort). The company must be named as the first respondent.
fields: Respondents: (1st) Company Name and Registration Number; (2nd+) Individual Controllers
History of Company and Relationship Between Shareholders
Particulars of Oppressive Conduct (specific acts and dates)
Relief Sought (share buyout at fair value / conduct order / winding up)
legal_forms.filingFee: Court filing fee: RM400-RM500 (Originating Petition)
legal_forms.timeLimit: No strict limitation — act promptly; delay weakens equitable relief claims

legal_forms.title: Notice of Adjudication — CIPAA 2012
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012 (Act 746), s.8
legal_forms.purpose: To formally initiate the statutory adjudication process under CIPAA 2012 for recovery of unpaid amounts under a construction contract
legal_forms.instructions: Serve on the respondent (the party who has failed to pay or disputed the payment). Must contain: (1) identification of the construction contract; (2) description of the dispute; (3) the relief sought (specific sum + interest); (4) proposal for appointment of adjudicator (if any). After serving the Notice, the parties have 10 working days to agree on an adjudicator — failing which apply to AIAC for appointment.
fields: Identification of Construction Contract (date, project name)
Description of Dispute (summary of payment claim and non-payment)
Relief Sought (payment of claimed amount + interest + costs of adjudication)
legal_forms.filingFee: No court fee — private notice. AIAC appointment fee applies if adjudicator appointed by AIAC.
legal_forms.timeLimit: No statutory time limit for Notice — but serve as soon as dispute crystallises

legal_forms.title: Form A — Representation under s.20 Industrial Relations Act 1967
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Industrial Relations Act 1967 (Act 177), s.20(1)
legal_forms.purpose: Formal complaint by a dismissed employee to the Director General of Industrial Relations to challenge dismissal without just cause and excuse
legal_forms.instructions: File at the nearest Industrial Relations Department (Jabatan Perhubungan Perusahaan) office. MUST BE FILED WITHIN 60 DAYS OF DISMISSAL — time limit is jurisdictional, no extension. Attach the termination letter and any domestic inquiry records. State the relief sought: reinstatement with back wages, or compensation in lieu of reinstatement.
fields: Employee Full Name, NRIC, Address, and Contact
Nature of Employment (job title, nature of work)
Reasons Given by Employer for Dismissal
Grounds of Complaint (dismissal without just cause and excuse)
legal_forms.filingFee: No fee — free service by the Industrial Relations Department
legal_forms.timeLimit: MANDATORY: Within 60 days of dismissal. Strictly enforced.

legal_forms.title: Originating Summons for Grant of Probate
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Probate and Administration Act 1959 (Act 97), s.5; Rules of Court 2012, Order 71
legal_forms.purpose: Application to the High Court Probate Registry by an executor named in a will to obtain the court's official authority (Grant of Probate) to administer the deceased's estate
legal_forms.instructions: File in the High Court Probate Registry of the state where the deceased was domiciled at death. Submit the ORIGINAL will (not a copy). The affidavit of executor must confirm: the will is the last and final will, it was duly executed, testator had testamentary capacity, and the deponent is the executor named in the will. The Schedule of Assets must list all estate assets with estimated values.
fields: Deceased's Full Name, NRIC, Last Address, and Date of Death
Executor's Full Name, NRIC, and Address
Date and Execution Details of the Will
Statement that the Will is the Last Will of the Deceased
Schedule of Assets: Immovable Property (land), Movable Property (bank accounts, shares, vehicles, EPF, insurance), Total Gross Estate Value
legal_forms.filingFee: Ad valorem filing fee based on estate value (approximately 0.1%-0.5% of gross estate)
legal_forms.timeLimit: No strict time limit but delays may cause administrative difficulties — apply promptly after death

legal_forms.title: Notice of Appeal — Court of Appeal
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.68; Rules of the Court of Appeal 1994, r.6
legal_forms.purpose: To formally notify all parties and the court that the appellant is appealing against the whole or part of the decision of the High Court to the Court of Appeal
legal_forms.instructions: File at the High Court Registry (not the Court of Appeal directly) within 30 days of the decision for an appeal against a final judgment, or within 10 days for an interlocutory order. Failure to file within time is fatal unless leave to extend time is obtained. Attach a copy of the sealed order/judgment being appealed. Pay the RM200 filing fee. The Notice must specify whether the whole or part of the decision is being appealed and must state the general grounds of appeal.
fields: Date and Nature of Decision Appealed
Whether appealing whole or part of decision
legal_forms.filingFee: RM200 (Court of Appeal filing fee)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Final judgment: within 30 days; Interlocutory order: within 10 days; Extensions require formal application with strong grounds
legal_forms.notes: A notice of appeal does not automatically stay execution of the High Court order — a separate application for stay must be made

legal_forms.title: Memorandum of Appeal — Court of Appeal
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of the Court of Appeal 1994, r.7
legal_forms.purpose: A document filed alongside or shortly after the Notice of Appeal setting out in specific detail the grounds on which the High Court decision is challenged and the orders sought from the Court of Appeal
legal_forms.instructions: The Memorandum must contain numbered, specific grounds of appeal — not vague general grounds. Each ground must identify: (1) the specific finding or ruling being challenged; (2) why it is wrong in law or fact; (3) the applicable legal principle. Grounds not in the Memorandum cannot be argued without leave. File simultaneously with the Notice of Appeal or within the time directed by the Court of Appeal.
fields: Numbered Grounds of Appeal (specific legal and factual errors)
Orders Sought from Court of Appeal
Reference to Relevant Findings, Pages, and Records Below
legal_forms.filingFee: Filed together with Notice of Appeal — no separate fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: Same as Notice of Appeal or as directed by the Court
legal_forms.notes: Grounds of law (errors of law) are reviewed de novo; findings of fact are disturbed only where they are plainly wrong or against the weight of evidence

legal_forms.title: Originating Summons — Application for Judicial Review (Order 53)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.25(2)
legal_forms.purpose: To commence proceedings for judicial review of a decision, act, or omission of a public authority or inferior court/tribunal, and to obtain prerogative orders (certiorari, mandamus, prohibition) or declarations and injunctions
legal_forms.instructions: File in the Administrative Law Division of the High Court (Kuala Lumpur) or the relevant state High Court. Leave must first be obtained — file an ex parte application supported by an affidavit and a Statement (Form as per Order 53 r 3). If leave is granted, the OS is served on the respondent. The Statement must set out the decision being challenged, the grounds, and the relief sought. Strict time limits apply: generally, apply within 3 months of the decision unless there is good reason for delay.
fields: Respondent(s): Public Authority / Inferior Court / Tribunal
Nature of Decision / Act / Omission Challenged
Grounds for Review (ultra vires, breach of natural justice, illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety)
Relief Sought (Certiorari / Mandamus / Prohibition / Declaration / Injunction)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM400 (Originating Summons — Administrative Law Division)
legal_forms.timeLimit: 3 months from the date of the decision or such other period as the court directs

legal_forms.title: Statement — Grounds for Judicial Review (Order 53 r 3(2))
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53 r 3(2)
legal_forms.purpose: A mandatory document filed with every judicial review application setting out the name and description of the applicant, the relief sought, and the grounds for seeking the relief, with a concise statement of the facts relied upon
legal_forms.instructions: This Statement is read by the judge at the leave stage and at the full hearing. It must be precise and well-organised: (1) identify the decision-maker and the decision; (2) set out the relevant statutory framework; (3) articulate each ground of review (illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety) with reference to specific facts and authorities. Lengthy narrative should be in the affidavit — the Statement should be crisp. Cross-reference exhibits in the affidavit.
fields: Nature and Date of Decision / Act / Omission Challenged
Relief Sought (specify each prerogative order / declaration / injunction)
Grounds of Review (numbered): illegality / irrationality / procedural impropriety / breach of natural justice / legitimate expectation
Statutory provisions and key authorities relied upon
legal_forms.filingFee: No separate fee — filed with the Originating Summons
legal_forms.timeLimit: Filed simultaneously with the Originating Summons for Judicial Review

legal_forms.title: Petition for Divorce — Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 (Act 164), s.52–53; Rules of Court 2012, Order 99
legal_forms.purpose: To formally commence divorce proceedings in the High Court (Family Division) by a petitioner seeking dissolution of marriage under the civil law. Applicable to non-Muslim marriages registered under the LRA 1976 or the Civil Marriage Ordinance 1952.
legal_forms.instructions: File in the High Court Family Division at the place where either party resides or where the marriage was registered. The petition must state the ground for divorce: irretrievable breakdown evidenced by (a) adultery; (b) unreasonable behaviour; (c) desertion for 2 years; (d) separation for 2 years (consensual); (e) separation for 5 years (non-consensual). A marriage must have subsisted for at least 2 years before a petition may be filed. Attach: Marriage Certificate (original), Birth Certificates of children, Affidavit of Means, and Draft Minutes of Order for ancillary matters.
fields: Petitioner Full Name, NRIC, Address, Occupation
Respondent Full Name, NRIC, Address, Occupation
Details of Children (name, NRIC, age, custodian)
Ancillary Relief Sought (custody, maintenance, division of matrimonial assets)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM400 (Petition for Divorce) + affidavit fees
legal_forms.timeLimit: Marriage must be at least 2 years old unless exceptional circumstances (s.52 LRA 1976)

legal_forms.title: Affidavit of Means — Matrimonial Proceedings
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s.76–79; Rules of Court 2012, Order 99; Matrimonial Causes Rules 1980
legal_forms.purpose: Compulsory disclosure document in matrimonial proceedings requiring each party to fully and frankly disclose their financial position — income, assets, liabilities, and expenses — to enable the court to make a fair order on maintenance, division of matrimonial assets, and children's support
legal_forms.instructions: Each party must file their own Affidavit of Means. Full and frank disclosure is mandatory — failure to disclose may result in the court drawing adverse inferences or setting aside an order. Include ALL assets: real property (with valuations), bank accounts (with balances), vehicles, EPF, shares, insurance policies, businesses, and any other assets. State ALL liabilities and monthly expenses.
fields: Deponent's Full Name, NRIC, Date of Birth, Occupation, Employer
Monthly Income (salary, allowances, bonuses, dividends, rental income)
Immovable Property (address, title, estimated value, encumbrances)
Movable Property (vehicles, bank accounts, shares, EPF, insurance)
legal_forms.filingFee: Affidavit filing fee: RM40 per affidavit
legal_forms.timeLimit: To be filed and served on the opposite party at the directions stage of matrimonial proceedings

legal_forms.title: Summons in Chambers — Application for Interlocutory Injunction (Order 29)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Specific Relief Act 1950, s.52; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.25
legal_forms.purpose: Application for a temporary injunction (restraining order or mandatory injunction) to preserve the status quo or prevent irreparable harm pending the determination of the main suit
legal_forms.instructions: The applicant must satisfy the American Cyanamid three-part test: (1) there is a serious question to be tried; (2) the balance of convenience favours granting the injunction; (3) damages would not be an adequate remedy. Where an ex parte injunction is sought, full and frank disclosure of ALL material facts is mandatory. The applicant must give an undertaking as to damages. The application must be supported by an affidavit deposing to the facts urgently. Inter partes hearing must follow promptly.
fields: Acts to be Restrained or Compelled
Grounds: Serious Question, Balance of Convenience, Adequacy of Damages
Return Date for Inter Partes Hearing
legal_forms.filingFee: RM100 (Summons in Chambers) + affidavit filing fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: Apply as urgently as the circumstances require — delay may disentitle applicant to ex parte relief

legal_forms.title: Originating Summons — Specific Performance of Contract
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Specific Relief Act 1950 (Act 137), ss.11–21; Contract Act 1950, s.40
legal_forms.purpose: Application for a court order compelling the defendant to specifically perform their obligations under a valid and enforceable contract — typically used in land sale and purchase agreements, share sale agreements, or unique goods contracts where damages are inadequate
legal_forms.instructions: File in the High Court Civil Division. Specific performance will not be granted where: (1) the contract is not valid and binding; (2) the plaintiff has not performed their own obligations (or is not ready and willing to perform); (3) a third party has acquired an interest for value without notice; (4) the contract involves personal services. The Originating Summons must state the specific term(s) to be performed and be supported by an affidavit exhibiting the contract and all correspondence. Caveat may be necessary to protect land interest.
fields: Description of Contract (date, parties, subject matter)
Facts showing Plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform
Facts showing Defendant's breach / refusal to perform
Relief Sought (specific performance + damages in lieu or in addition)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM400 (Originating Summons — Civil Division)
legal_forms.timeLimit: 6 years from breach (Limitation Act 1953, s.6) — but equitable remedy, so act promptly; laches may bar relief

legal_forms.title: Statement of Claim — Personal Injury (Negligence)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18; Civil Law Act 1956, s.7–8; Limitation Act 1953, s.6
legal_forms.purpose: Pleading setting out the plaintiff's cause of action in tort for personal injury caused by the defendant's negligence — most commonly arising from road accidents, workplace accidents, or occupier's liability
legal_forms.instructions: The Statement of Claim must plead: (1) the duty of care owed by the defendant; (2) breach of that duty by specific negligent acts or omissions; (3) causation — the breach directly caused the injury; (4) damage — itemised by special damages (quantified losses) and general damages (pain, suffering, future loss). The Schedule of Special Damages must be attached and specifically pleaded. Obtain medical reports before filing. Note: for fatal accidents, also plead under Civil Law Act 1956, s.7 (dependency claim) and s.8 (loss of estate).
fields: Date, Time, and Location of Accident
Description of Accident and How It Occurred
Injuries Sustained (with reference to medical reports)
Schedule of Special Damages (medical expenses, transport, loss of income)
General Damages Claimed (pain and suffering, loss of amenities, future medical, future loss of earnings)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM300-RM1,000 depending on quantum (Subordinate Court / High Court)
legal_forms.timeLimit: 6 years from date of accrual — Limitation Act 1953, s.6(1)(a); Malaysia has no separate 3-year personal-injury period. Only 36 months where the defendant is the Government or a public authority (Public Authorities Protection Act 1948)

legal_forms.title: Schedule of Special and General Damages — Personal Injury
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18 r 15; Judicial appointments Commission Guidelines
legal_forms.purpose: A detailed itemised schedule served by the plaintiff computing all heads of damages in a personal injury claim, categorised as special damages (quantified pre-trial losses) and general damages (prospective and non-pecuniary losses)
legal_forms.instructions: The Schedule must be precise — each item must be supported by invoices, receipts, payslips, or medical evidence. Special damages are strictly proved; general damages are assessed using judicial scales (Malaysian Bar scale / Guidelines on Quantum) and reference to decided cases. Always reference the Judicial Commission's Guidelines on Quantum of Damages for heads such as pain and suffering, loss of limb, and loss of faculty. In fatal accident claims, also compute: bereavement award, dependency, and funeral expenses.
fields: SPECIAL DAMAGES: Medical expenses (hospital bills, medication, physiotherapy)
Loss of income during hospitalization / recovery (multiply daily rate x days off work)
Cost of future care (if permanent disability)
GENERAL DAMAGES: Pain and suffering (based on injury type — use Guidelines on Quantum)
Future loss of earnings (multiplier x multiplicand)
Bereavement award (RM30,000 per CJA 1964 s.8A, fatal accidents only)
legal_forms.filingFee: No separate fee — filed with Statement of Claim or at directions
legal_forms.timeLimit: Updated and re-served before trial if special damages change

legal_forms.title: Payment Claim — CIPAA 2012 (s.5)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012 (Act 746), s.5
legal_forms.purpose: A formal claim by a contractor, subcontractor, or supplier for payment of an unpaid amount under a construction contract, which initiates the right to adjudication under CIPAA 2012 if the respondent fails to respond or disputes the claim
legal_forms.instructions: Serve the Payment Claim on the non-paying party. It must: (1) be in writing; (2) identify the construction contract; (3) describe the work / goods / services to which the claim relates; (4) state the amount claimed and due date for payment; (5) include a supporting statement detailing how the amount is calculated. If the Respondent fails to serve a Payment Response within 10 working days, the entire claimed amount is deemed admitted. A Payment Claim starts the CIPAA timeline.
fields: Reference to Construction Contract (date, project name, contract value)
Amount Claimed (breakdown: contract work, variations, retention monies, other)
Payment Due Date under the Contract
legal_forms.filingFee: No court fee — served privately. AIAC registration fee if adjudication is later initiated.
legal_forms.timeLimit: No strict time limit, but serve promptly after the payment due date

legal_forms.title: Adjudication Response — CIPAA 2012 (s.10)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012 (Act 746), s.10
legal_forms.purpose: The respondent's formal written response to the Adjudication Claim filed by the claimant in CIPAA adjudication proceedings, in which the respondent sets out its defence and, if applicable, a cross-claim against the claimant
legal_forms.instructions: File the Adjudication Response within 10 working days of receiving the Adjudication Claim. This is a strict deadline — failure to file is equivalent to admitting the Adjudication Claim. The Response must address every item in the Adjudication Claim with particularity. Raise all defences here — you cannot raise new defences at the hearing without leave of the adjudicator. Include all supporting documents (payment certificates, inspection reports, correspondence, relevant contract clauses).
fields: Reference to CIPAA Adjudication No. / AIAC File No.
Date of Adjudication Claim being responded to
Disputed Amount and Detailed Grounds of Dispute (item by item)
Cross-Claim (if any) — set out particulars and amount claimed by respondent against claimant
legal_forms.filingFee: No court fee — filed directly with the adjudicator and served on claimant
legal_forms.timeLimit: STRICTLY within 10 working days of receiving Adjudication Claim — fatal if missed

legal_forms.title: Writ of Seizure and Sale — Enforcement of Judgment (Form 83)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Orders 45–47; Subordinate Courts Rules 1980 (for Sessions Court)
legal_forms.purpose: A court order directed to the Bailiff / Registrar authorising seizure and sale of the judgment debtor's movable property (and in some cases, land) in satisfaction of an unsatisfied money judgment
legal_forms.instructions: File an ex parte application for leave to issue WSS if more than 6 years have elapsed since judgment, or if there has been a change of parties. For standard enforcement within 6 years, file the prescribed form with the sealed judgment and an affidavit confirming the amount outstanding (including accrued post-judgment interest at 5% p.a.). The Bailiff will attend the judgment debtor's premises to seize property. Exempt property (clothing, basic household goods up to RM200, tools of trade up to RM200) cannot be seized.
fields: Court Name and Civil Suit Number
Judgment Debtor (Defendant) Name and Last Known Address
Post-Judgment Interest Rate (5% per annum under CJA 1964, s.11(2))
legal_forms.filingFee: RM100–RM200 (WSS application fee) + Bailiff fees (% of amount levied)
legal_forms.timeLimit: 6 years from date of judgment without leave; beyond 6 years requires court leave (Order 46 r 2)

legal_forms.title: Summons in Chambers — Application for Substituted Service (Order 62 r 5)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 62 r 5
legal_forms.purpose: Application for court leave to serve legal process on a defendant or respondent by a method other than personal service (e.g. by post, by advertisement, by pasting on the door) when personal service has proved impracticable
legal_forms.instructions: File a Summons in Chambers supported by an affidavit detailing all genuine attempts at personal service, the responses received (if any), and why personal service is impracticable. Propose a specific method of substituted service. The court will specify the method and deem service effected after a specified time. Common methods: registered post to last known address, advertisement in a national daily newspaper, pasting on the front door of last known address.
fields: Party to be Served and Relationship to Case
Date(s) and Details of Attempted Personal Service (diary of attempts)
Enquiries Made to Locate the Party
Proposed Method of Substituted Service (post / advertisement / pasting)
Proposed Period After Which Service Deemed Effected
legal_forms.filingFee: RM50–RM100 (Summons in Chambers)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Apply as soon as personal service is shown to be impracticable — courts are strict about genuine attempts

legal_forms.title: Consent Judgment / Consent Order — By Agreement of Parties
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 42 r 5A; Order 45
legal_forms.purpose: A judgment or order made with the consent of all parties to record the terms of settlement of a dispute. Has the same legal effect as a judgment obtained after contested litigation and can be enforced accordingly
legal_forms.instructions: Draft the terms of settlement with precision — all figures, deadlines, and obligations must be clear and unambiguous. Both parties' solicitors must sign the Consent Judgment / Order. Present it to the court for endorsement by the Registrar or Judge in Chambers. Obtain a sealed copy. For consent judgments involving land or title documents, additional steps (e.g. discharge of charge, transfer) may be needed.
fields: Terms of Consent Judgment (payment schedule, acts to be done, restraining orders, costs)
Both Parties' Solicitors' Signatures and Dates
Space for Court Seal and Registration Date
legal_forms.filingFee: RM50–RM100 (for recording consent judgment)
legal_forms.timeLimit: File and present to court as soon as settlement is reached — before any trial or continued hearing

legal_forms.title: Notice of Change of Solicitor (Order 64 r 1)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 64 r 1
legal_forms.purpose: Formal notification to the court and all other parties that a party has changed its legal representation — the new solicitor replacing the previous firm acting for the party in the proceedings
legal_forms.instructions: File the Notice of Change of Solicitor at the court registry. Serve it on all other parties and on the outgoing solicitors. The new solicitor must sign the Notice. The outgoing solicitor must be formally discharged — if they are disputing their discharge (e.g. due to unpaid fees or a lien), the party must apply to court. After the Notice is filed, all future correspondences and documents in the suit must be served on the new solicitor.
fields: Outgoing Solicitor Firm Name and Address
Incoming (New) Solicitor Firm Name, Address, Contact, and Email
Certificate of Service on Outgoing Solicitor
legal_forms.filingFee: Minimal — RM10–RM20 registry fee
legal_forms.timeLimit: File as soon as change of solicitor is effective

legal_forms.title: Bill of Costs — Contentious Business (Taxation by Registrar)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 59; Legal Profession Act 1976 (Act 166), Part VI
legal_forms.purpose: A detailed itemised account of legal costs claimed by a solicitor for work done in litigious matters, presented for taxation (assessment) by the court Registrar to determine the reasonable amount payable by the paying party
legal_forms.instructions: A Bill of Costs must be filed and served on the paying party. It must be divided into: (1) Section 1: Getting up the case; (2) Section 2: Attendance at court; (3) Section 3: Disbursements. All items must specify date, nature of work, time spent (if Solicitor-Client), and amount claimed. The Registrar will tax the bill at a taxation hearing. Both parties may appear. Items may be 'taxed off' (disallowed) or reduced. The Certificate of Taxation is issued after taxation and forms the basis for enforcement of the costs award.
fields: Receiving Party (the party to whom costs were awarded)
Section 1 — Getting Up: instructions received, advices given, attendances, letters, documents prepared
Section 2 — Court Attendance: each hearing date, duration, preparation time
Section 3 — Disbursements: court fees, process server fees, stenographer, expert fees, miscellaneous
legal_forms.filingFee: Filing fee for Bill of Costs: RM100–RM150; taxation fee: percentage of bill amount
legal_forms.timeLimit: Present for taxation within 12 months of completing the work or of the costs order

legal_forms.title: Summons in Chambers — Application to Set Aside Judgment in Default
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 13 r 8; Order 19 r 9
legal_forms.purpose: Application by a defendant to set aside a judgment in default of appearance or defence, which was entered against the defendant without a hearing on the merits. The court has discretion to set aside to allow the defendant to defend the claim.
legal_forms.instructions: The applicant must show (1) a regular judgment (entered within the Rules): there is a prima facie defence on the merits; OR (2) an irregular judgment (not entered within the Rules): set aside as of right. A defence on the merits must be disclosed in the supporting affidavit — vague denials will not suffice. Apply promptly — unexplained delay is a factor the court considers. The usual order is: set aside on terms (defendant pays costs thrown away and files defence within a prescribed time).
fields: Date Judgment in Default was Entered
Grounds for Setting Aside (meritorious defence / irregularity)
Draft Defence (annexed as exhibit to affidavit)
Explanation for Failure to Enter Appearance / File Defence in Time
Explanation for Any Delay in Making This Application
legal_forms.filingFee: RM100 (Summons in Chambers)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Apply as soon as the defendant becomes aware of the judgment — delay is prejudicial

legal_forms.title: Private Caveat — Form 19B (National Land Code 1965)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: National Land Code 1965, ss.319–328
legal_forms.purpose: A statutory entry on the register of a piece of land lodged by a person claiming an interest in that land to prevent any dealings with or dispositions of the land without the caveator's knowledge. The caveat gives public notice of the caveator's claim.
legal_forms.instructions: Lodge the caveat at the Land Registry in the state where the land is situated. Only a person with a registrable interest or a claim to a trust in the land may lodge a private caveat. False or frivolous caveats may result in liability to the registered proprietor for damages. The caveat remains in force for 6 years (unless sooner removed or withdrawn). If a challenge is made (application to remove), the caveator has 14 days to respond or the caveat is removed. Do NOT lodge a caveat as a delaying tactic — it must be supported by a genuine and bona fide claim.
fields: Land Title Number (Geran / H.S.(D) No., Lot/P.T. No., Mukim, District, State)
Caveator's Full Name, NRIC, and Address
Nature of Interest or Claim Caveated (e.g., purchaser under SPA, trust beneficiary, mortgagee)
Reference to Document Creating the Interest (date, parties)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM100 per title lodgement (Land Office fees vary by state)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Caveat remains for 6 years or until removed — lodge promptly upon arising of interest

legal_forms.title: Statement of Claim — Defamation (Libel / Slander)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18; Defamation Act 1957 (Act 286); Civil Law Act 1956; Penal Code, ss.499–502
legal_forms.purpose: Pleading establishing the plaintiff's cause of action in civil defamation — proving publication of a false statement of fact that was defamatory of the plaintiff, and claiming general and special damages
legal_forms.instructions: The Statement of Claim must: (1) set out the exact words complained of (verbatim) — for libel, exhibit a copy of the defamatory publication; (2) plead the natural and ordinary meaning or, if innuendo, the special meaning relied upon; (3) identify the publishees (who read/heard the defamatory statement); (4) plead that the statement was false (if the defendant may raise justification); (5) plead special damage if any — but for libel, damage is presumed. Time bar: 2 years from publication under Limitation Act 1953.
fields: Plaintiff Name, Address, Occupation / Status (relevant to reputation)
Date, Place, and Medium of Publication (newspaper / social media / speech / broadcast)
Verbatim Reproduction of the Defamatory Words
Natural and Ordinary Meaning / Innuendo Meaning alleged
General Damages Claimed (injury to reputation, mental distress, business loss)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM300–RM1,000 depending on court (Subordinate Court / High Court); High Court if general damages exceed RM250,000
legal_forms.timeLimit: 2 years from date of publication (Limitation Act 1953, s.6(1)(a))

legal_forms.title: Defence and Counterclaim
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18 rr 2–3, 13–14
legal_forms.purpose: A combined pleading in which the defendant denies or admits (in whole or part) the plaintiff's claim in the Defence, and in the same document asserts a separate cause of action against the plaintiff (the Counterclaim) arising from the same facts or related matters
legal_forms.instructions: File the Defence and Counterclaim within 14 days of service of the Statement of Claim (or 28 days if service was out of jurisdiction). The Defence must plead specifically to each material allegation — bare denials are insufficient for assertions of fact. The Counterclaim is treated as a separate claim and the plaintiff must file a Defence to Counterclaim within 14 days. If the counterclaim exceeds the plaintiff's claim in value, the defendant may be awarded a net judgment.
fields: DEFENCE PART: Admit / Deny each paragraph of Statement of Claim specifically
Positive Defences Raised (limitation, estoppel, illegality, frustration, payment, contributory negligence)
COUNTERCLAIM PART: Identification of Counterclaim Defendant(s)
Facts constituting the Counterclaim cause of action
Particulars of Damage / Loss claimed in Counterclaim
legal_forms.filingFee: No additional fee beyond the defence — filed as one document
legal_forms.timeLimit: 14 days from service of Statement of Claim (extendable by consent or court order)

legal_forms.title: Summons in Chambers — Application for Security for Costs (Order 23)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 23; Companies Act 2016, s.580
legal_forms.purpose: Application by a defendant for a court order requiring the plaintiff to pay a sum of money into court as security for the defendant's costs of the proceedings, before the action is allowed to proceed — most commonly sought where the plaintiff is ordinarily resident outside Malaysia or is a company in financial difficulty
legal_forms.instructions: The court has a discretion — it must be shown that: (1) the plaintiff is ordinarily resident outside Malaysia; OR (2) the plaintiff is a company and there is reason to believe it cannot pay the defendant's costs if the defendant succeeds; OR (3) the plaintiff has changed its address to avoid service. The amount of security is assessed on the likely costs of the action. The order stays the action until security is paid into court. Note: impecuniosity alone (for individual plaintiffs) is NOT a ground.
fields: Ground for Application (residence abroad / corporate impecuniosity / changed address)
Evidence in Support (e.g., company search, CTOS report, evidence of overseas residence)
Proposed Amount of Security and Basis of Calculation
Mode of Security Proposed (payment into court / banker's guarantee)
legal_forms.filingFee: RM100 (Summons in Chambers)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Apply early in the proceedings — after close of pleadings; unduly late applications may be refused

legal_forms.title: Claimant's Statement of Case — Industrial Court
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.30; Industrial Court Rules 1967
legal_forms.purpose: The formal document filed by the claimant (employee) in Industrial Court proceedings setting out in full the facts of the dismissal, the grounds for challenging it, all evidence relied upon, and the relief sought
legal_forms.instructions: File the Claimant's Statement of Case within the time directed by the Industrial Court after the reference is made by the Minister of Human Resources. The statement must: (1) state the date of appointment, job title, last salary; (2) narrate the events leading to dismissal; (3) specifically identify what the claimant says was unjust; (4) address any domestic inquiry and its fairness or lack thereof; (5) set out the relief claimed (reinstatement / back wages / compensation). Attach all relevant documents as exhibits.
fields: Claimant Name, NRIC, Address, and Contact
Narrative of Events Leading to Dismissal
Grounds for Challenging Dismissal (no just cause, procedural breach, victimisation)
Domestic Inquiry Details (if held): date, panel, charges, finding
Relief Sought: reinstatement with back wages / compensation in lieu of reinstatement
legal_forms.filingFee: No fee — Industrial Court proceedings are free to workers
legal_forms.timeLimit: Filed within the time specified by the Industrial Court in the directions order

legal_forms.title: Originating Summons — Letters of Administration (Intestacy)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Probate and Administration Act 1959, s.30; Rules of Court 2012, Order 71; Distribution Act 1958
legal_forms.purpose: Application by the next-of-kin (usually spouse, children, or parents) to be appointed administrator of the estate of a person who died intestate (without a valid Will), to manage and distribute the estate under the Distribution Act 1958
legal_forms.instructions: File in the High Court Probate Registry. The applicant must be entitled to administer the estate under the established order of priority. Two sureties (guarantors) are usually required unless the estate is small. Attach a death certificate, identity documents of the deceased and applicant, and a full Schedule of Assets. If there are multiple persons entitled to apply, all must join or renounce their right. The Letters of Administration grants the administrator authority to collect and distribute the estate.
fields: Deceased's Full Name, NRIC, Last Address, Date and Place of Death
Applicant (Administrator) Full Name, NRIC, Address, and Relationship to Deceased
Names of All Beneficiaries and Their Relationships to Deceased
Declaration that Deceased Died Intestate (no Will)
Schedule of Assets: property, bank accounts, EPF, shares, vehicles, insurance, total gross estate
Names and Details of Sureties (Guarantors) if required
legal_forms.filingFee: Ad valorem filing fee based on estate value; surety bond (percentage of estate value)
legal_forms.timeLimit: Apply promptly after death to avoid complications with financial institutions and estate preservation

legal_forms.title: Originating Summons — Rectification of Land Register (s.421 NLC 1965)
legal_forms.authorizedBy: National Land Code 1965, s.421; Rules of Court 2012
legal_forms.purpose: Application to the High Court to rectify an error or omission in the Register of Titles where the applicant's title or interest has been wrongly registered, omitted, or incorrectly recorded
legal_forms.instructions: Must show that: (1) there is an error or omission in the register; (2) the applicant has a genuine legal interest affected by the error; (3) no innocent third party purchaser for value has acquired an interest relying on the register. The court may order rectification of the register and may make consequential orders. Common scenarios: wrong party registered as proprietor, fraudulent transfer, clerical error in title description.
fields: Land Title Number (Geran / H.S.(D) No., Lot/P.T., Mukim, District, State)
Applicant Name, NRIC, and Interest in Land
Respondent (Current Registered Proprietor if different from applicant)
Nature of Error or Omission in Register
Facts and Documents showing the Error
legal_forms.filingFee: RM400 (Originating Summons) + Land Office fees for rectification
legal_forms.timeLimit: No strict limitation but apply promptly — delay may give rise to third party rights

legal_forms.title: Affidavit of Service — Proof of Personal Service
legal_forms.authorizedBy: Rules of Court 2012, Order 62 r 9; Evidence Act 1950, s.3
legal_forms.purpose: A sworn affidavit by the person who personally served court process (Writ, Originating Summons, Summons, Injunction Order, etc.) on a party, constituting formal proof to the court that service was properly effected
legal_forms.instructions: The deponent (process server or solicitor's clerk who served) must affirm the affidavit before a Commissioner for Oaths or a Solicitor. Include: (1) date, time, and place of service; (2) description of the person served (name, NRIC if known, physical description); (3) what document was served and its date; (4) how service was effected (personal service into their hand / left at residence with adult); (5) the person's response (if any). Exhibit a photo of service (if available). File as soon as possible after service.
fields: Deponent's Full Name, NRIC, Occupation, and Address
Document(s) Served (title and date of document)
Date, Time, and Place of Service
Description of Manner of Service (handed personally / left with adult at residence)
Physical Description of Person Served or Identification Given
Any Acknowledgment or Response from Person Served
legal_forms.filingFee: Affidavit filing: RM40 per affidavit
legal_forms.timeLimit: File promptly — required before any default judgment application or injunction enforcement

legal_cases.caseName: Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Kobchai Sosothikul
legal_cases.facts: Kobchai Sosothikul obtained a transfer of land through a forged document. The Federal Court was asked whether the registered owner acquired indefeasible title upon registration, even if the transfer was obtained by forgery.
issues: Whether title obtained through forgery is indefeasible under s. 340 NLC
Whether an immediate registered proprietor who is a bona fide purchaser for value is protected under s. 340(3) NLC
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that a bona fide purchaser for value who registered title, even if that title was obtained by forgery, acquires an indefeasible title under s. 340(3) NLC — the proviso protecting subsequent purchasers. Indefeasibility is immediate, not deferred.
legal_cases.significance: This landmark decision affirmed immediate indefeasibility of title in Malaysia, protecting bona fide purchasers for value who deal with registered proprietors. It departed from the deferred indefeasibility view and had significant implications for land financing transactions.

legal_cases.caseName: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San & Ors
legal_cases.facts: The Federal Court revisited the indefeasibility of title issue and the scope of exceptions in s. 340 NLC, including fraud, misrepresentation, and insufficient consideration.
issues: Scope of exceptions to indefeasibility under s. 340(2) NLC
Whether deferred or immediate indefeasibility applies in Malaysia
Effect of forgery on title of subsequent purchasers
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court upheld the Adorna Properties decision that immediate indefeasibility applies. The exceptions in s. 340(2) NLC are personal — they attach to the immediate registered proprietor who committed fraud/misrepresentation, not to a subsequent bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
legal_cases.significance: Confirmed immediate indefeasibility in Malaysian land law. Critical for banks as chargees — a bank acquiring a charge from a bona fide registered proprietor is protected even if earlier in the chain there was fraud.

legal_cases.caseName: Arab-Malaysian Finance Bhd v Taman Ihsan Jaya Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Taman Ihsan Jaya Sdn Bhd sought to set aside a BBA (Bai' Bithaman Ajil) financing facility and sought ibra' (rebate) arguing that the BBA was tantamount to a conventional loan and was structured to avoid giving the proper ibra' upon early settlement.
issues: Whether a BBA contract is Shariah-compliant or a conventional loan in disguise
Whether a customer is entitled to ibra' (rebate) upon early termination of BBA
Appropriate relief for non-Shariah-compliant Islamic banking contracts
legal_cases.held: Justice Abdul Wahab Patail controversially held that in some BBA structures the customer was only entitled to pay the original cost price (not the inflated selling price) upon early settlement. The judge held BBA as structured was akin to a conventional loan. He granted the rebate (ibra').
legal_cases.significance: This case sparked a major debate on BBA structuring in Malaysia and led to BNM issuing the Shariah Standard on Ibra' in 2011, requiring all Islamic banks to provide ibra' upon early settlement. It fundamentally changed Islamic home financing practice.

legal_cases.caseName: Bank Islam Malaysia Bhd v Lim Kok Hoe
legal_cases.facts: Lim Kok Hoe entered into a BBA facility with Bank Islam to finance property purchase. Upon default, Bank Islam demanded the full selling price (including profit element) rather than just the cost price. Lim argued he was entitled to ibra'.
issues: Whether a customer under BBA facility is entitled to ibra' upon early settlement
Quantum of ibra' — whether it must cover the unearned profit
Nature of civil courts' jurisdiction over Islamic banking disputes
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that the civil courts had jurisdiction to hear the dispute. It held that whilst there is no strict legal right to ibra', equity and conscience compelled the bank to provide ibra'. The court called for BNM to issue guidelines on ibra'.
legal_cases.significance: Contributed to BNM's issuance of the Shariah Standard on Ibra', making it mandatory for Islamic banks to provide rebate on early settlement. Confirmed civil courts' (not Syariah courts') jurisdiction over Islamic banking disputes.
legislation: Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009, s. 57

legal_cases.caseName: Affin Bank Bhd v Zulkifli bin Abdullah
legal_cases.facts: Zulkifli entered into a home loan agreement with Affin Bank. The bank applied for an Order for Sale under Order 83 ROC upon his default. Zulkifli argued the bank's interest rate computation was wrong and that the reserved price was too low.
issues: Procedure for obtaining Order for Sale under Order 83 ROC
Whether the court has discretion to refuse Order for Sale
Adequacy of reserved price in foreclosure proceedings
legal_cases.held: The High Court granted the Order for Sale but directed the bank to review the interest computation. The court held it has a discretionary jurisdiction — not a mechanical process — and must consider whether the chargor has a genuine defence or equitable grounds. Reserved price must reflect market value.
legal_cases.significance: Confirmed that foreclosure is not automatic — courts exercise genuine discretion. A chargor may challenge the amount claimed, the validity of the charge, or the adequacy of the reserved price. Critical for understanding the equity jurisdiction of courts in foreclosure.

legal_cases.caseName: RHB Bank Bhd v Travellers (M) Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: RHB Bank presented a winding up petition against Travellers (M) Sdn Bhd for an outstanding term loan debt. The company challenged the petition arguing there was a genuine dispute as to the debt and that the company was solvent.
issues: Whether a winding up petition should be restrained where there is a genuine dispute on the debt
Proper procedure for challenging a winding up petition
Threshold for staying a winding up petition
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that where a company can demonstrate a genuine and substantial dispute as to the debt, the winding up petition will be dismissed or stayed. A creditor must first obtain judgment on a disputed debt before presenting a winding up petition.
legal_cases.significance: Established the 'genuine dispute' principle in Malaysian winding up law. Companies with genuine defences to the debt are protected from winding up petitions being used as a debt collection tool. Banks must resolve disputed debts in ordinary civil proceedings first.

legal_cases.caseName: Public Bank Bhd v Narayanan Nair
legal_cases.facts: Public Bank obtained a judgment in default against Narayanan Nair for a credit card debt. The bank sought summary judgment on the credit card debt and interest. The court examined the applicable interest rate and whether the bank's unilateral right to vary interest rates was enforceable.
issues: Unilateral right of bank to vary interest rates on credit card debt
Enforceability of terms permitting unilateral variation
Computation of interest on credit card debt
legal_cases.held: The High Court held that the bank's right to unilaterally vary interest rates without notice was oppressive and unenforceable as it offended the principle of mutual consent. The bank was limited to the rate agreed at the time of the agreement.
legal_cases.significance: Established important consumer protections against unilateral interest rate variation by banks. Banks must obtain the customer's consent to interest rate changes. BNM's guidelines on product transparency subsequently addressed this concern.

legal_cases.caseName: Eon Finance Bhd v Moh Bak Seng
legal_cases.facts: Eon Finance repossessed a vehicle on hire purchase after the hirer defaulted on more than one-third of the hire purchase price, without first obtaining a court order. The hirer sued for wrongful repossession.
issues: Mandatory requirement for court order before repossession where one-third of HP price has been paid
Effect of wrongful repossession on the owner's right to deficiency claim
Quantum of damages for wrongful repossession
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that where a hirer has paid one-third or more of the hire purchase price, the owner must obtain a court order before repossessing. Repossession without a court order is wrongful, entitling the hirer to damages. The owner forfeits the deficiency claim.
legal_cases.significance: Established the strict one-third rule in Malaysian hire purchase law. Banks and finance companies must rigorously check the amount paid before exercising self-help repossession. Non-compliance is costly in terms of losing the deficiency claim and facing damages.

legal_cases.caseName: Ayer Molek Rubber Co v Insas Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Insas Bhd sought a Mareva injunction (freezing order) against Ayer Molek Rubber Co to prevent dissipation of assets pending its claim for payment under a share subscription agreement. The court examined the applicable test for Mareva injunctions in Malaysia.
issues: Applicable test for granting a Mareva injunction in Malaysia
Whether risk of dissipation must be proven
Balance of convenience in Mareva applications
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that for a Mareva injunction: (1) good arguable case on the merits; (2) real risk that assets will be dissipated or removed; (3) balance of convenience favours granting the order. The court must also consider the undertaking as to damages by the applicant.
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on Mareva injunctions. Sets the tripartite test applied in all subsequent Mareva applications in Malaysian courts. Essential reference for banking litigation involving asset preservation.

legal_cases.caseName: OCBC Bank (Malaysia) Bhd v Tay Kian Aik
legal_cases.facts: OCBC Bank obtained a summary judgment against Tay Kian Aik for an outstanding overdraft facility. Tay resisted summary judgment arguing there were triable issues regarding the bank's computation of interest and the alleged oral agreement to freeze the account.
issues: What constitutes a 'bona fide triable issue' to resist summary judgment under Order 14
Whether an alleged oral agreement to vary written contract can resist summary judgment
Bank's burden of proof in summary judgment application
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal upheld the summary judgment, holding that Tay's defence was a bare assertion without evidence and did not disclose a bona fide triable issue. An alleged oral agreement that contradicts a written contract faces significant hurdles due to the parol evidence rule.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the low threshold for banks to obtain summary judgment on loan claims. A defendant must adduce cogent evidence of a genuine defence — bare assertions are insufficient. Confirmed the parol evidence rule's application to banking contracts.

legal_cases.caseName: Hong Leong Finance Bhd v Staghorn Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Hong Leong Finance held a fixed and floating charge over Staghorn's assets. Upon default, Hong Leong appointed a receiver and manager. The central issue was whether the appointment of the receiver crystallised the floating charge and the priority of competing secured creditors.
issues: When does a floating charge crystallise upon appointment of Receiver and Manager
Priority between fixed charge holder and floating charge holder over same assets
Effect of crystallisation on preferential creditors
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that a floating charge crystallises automatically upon the appointment of a receiver and manager, becoming a fixed charge attaching to all assets then owned by the company. Fixed charge holders rank ahead of floating charge holders. Preferential creditors rank ahead of floating charges.
legal_cases.significance: Leading authority on crystallisation of floating charges in Malaysia. Critical for understanding priorities in corporate insolvency and receivership. Banks holding debentures must ensure fixed charges are properly drafted to secure specific assets.

legal_cases.caseName: Malayan Banking Bhd v Hwang Kim Soon
legal_cases.facts: Maybank applied for an Order for Sale against Hwang Kim Soon, who was in default on a housing loan. Hwang argued his financial difficulties were temporary and sought more time to sell the property privately at a better price than the reserved price.
issues: Court's discretion to adjourn foreclosure proceedings to allow chargor to sell privately
Factors relevant to adjournment of Order for Sale applications
Balance between chargee's rights and chargor's equity of redemption
legal_cases.held: The High Court adjourned the Order for Sale application for a reasonable period to allow the chargor to attempt a private sale at market value. The court held that the equity of redemption is a fundamental right that courts should protect by allowing the chargor a final opportunity to redeem.
legal_cases.significance: Demonstrated the courts' equity jurisdiction to protect chargors from precipitous foreclosure. Banks must demonstrate they have followed proper procedures and that the chargor has had a genuine opportunity to regularize the account or sell the property.

legal_cases.caseName: Tenaga Nasional Bhd v Duta Expressway Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: This case involving a financing dispute raised the important question of whether Malaysian courts would recognize and enforce a demand guarantee (first demand bond) without proof of actual default by the principal debtor, and the unconscionability exception thereto.
issues: Whether a demand guarantee is payable on demand without proof of actual default
Unconscionability exception to demand guarantees in Malaysia
Fraud vs. unconscionability as grounds to restrain a demand on a bank guarantee
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal confirmed that a demand guarantee (performance bond / first demand bond) is payable on first demand without proof of underlying default. However, Malaysian courts (unlike English courts) also recognize unconscionability as a ground to restrain a call, in addition to fraud.
legal_cases.significance: Established the Malaysian unconscionability exception to demand guarantees. Malaysian courts will grant an injunction to restrain a beneficiary from calling on a bank guarantee if the call would be unconscionable, even without fraud. This is broader than the English position.

legal_cases.caseName: Development & Commercial Bank Bhd v Bajaj Auto Ltd
