legal_cases.caseName: Megat Najmuddin Dato' Seri (Dr) Megat Khas v Bank Bumiputra (M) Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Bank Bumiputra obtained a summary judgment against Megat Najmuddin on a guarantee. The debtor sought a stay of execution pending appeal under Order 45 rule 11. The question arose whether a stay should be granted as of right or whether the applicant must show 'special circumstances'.
issues: Test for stay of execution pending appeal
Whether a stay of execution is granted as of right
Meaning of 'special circumstances' in the context of a stay application
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that a stay of execution pending appeal is not granted as of right. The applicant must show 'special circumstances' which include: the appeal will be rendered nugatory if no stay is granted, the appellant will suffer irreparable injury, and the balance of convenience favours granting the stay.
legal_cases.significance: The leading authority on stay of execution pending appeal in Malaysia. Established the 'special circumstances' test that governs all stay applications.

legal_cases.caseName: Badiaddin bin Mohd Mahidin v Arab Malaysian Finance Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Arab Malaysian Finance obtained an Order for Sale of charged property. The chargor challenged the validity of the charge itself, arguing it was obtained through fraud and misrepresentation by a third party. The question was whether the chargor could raise this defence in the Order 83 proceedings.
issues: Whether fraud in obtaining the charge is a defence to Order for Sale proceedings
The scope of defences available in Order 83 proceedings
Whether the chargor must bring a separate suit to challenge the charge
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that a chargor may raise the defence of fraud, illegality, or invalidity of the charge in Order for Sale proceedings under Order 83. The court must consider such defences before granting the Order for Sale. The chargor is not required to first bring a separate suit to challenge the charge.
legal_cases.significance: Expanded the scope of defences available to chargors in foreclosure proceedings. Essential authority confirming that equity and fraud defences can be raised in Order 83 applications.

legal_cases.caseName: United Overseas Bank (M) Bhd v Ng Aik Chuan
legal_cases.facts: United Overseas Bank filed a Bankruptcy Notice against Ng Aik Chuan. The debtor applied to set aside the Bankruptcy Notice arguing it was irregular and that the judgment debt was disputed.
issues: Requirements for a valid Bankruptcy Notice
Grounds for setting aside a Bankruptcy Notice
Whether a cross-claim or counterclaim against the petitioner is a valid ground
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that a Bankruptcy Notice may be set aside if: (1) there is a defect in form rendering it a nullity; (2) the debtor has a counterclaim, set-off, or cross-demand that exceeds the judgment debt; (3) the court is satisfied it is unjust to make a receiving order. A genuine counterclaim exceeding the judgment debt is a complete defence.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the grounds for challenging Bankruptcy Notices and the availability of the counterclaim defence. Essential for practitioners handling bankruptcy proceedings.

legal_cases.caseName: Lee Ah Chor v Southern Bank Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Southern Bank served interrogatories on Lee Ah Chor under Order 26 of the Rules of the High Court. Lee objected to answering several of the interrogatories, arguing they were oppressive, irrelevant, and amounted to a fishing expedition.
issues: Test for ordering answers to interrogatories under Order 26
When interrogatories are oppressive or constitute fishing
The relevance test for interrogatories
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that interrogatories must relate to matters in question in the cause or matter. They should not be oppressive or constitute a fishing expedition. However, the test is liberal — interrogatories are permissible if they may lead to a train of inquiry that could be relevant to the issues.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the scope and limits of interrogatories in Malaysian civil procedure. Applied the liberal 'train of inquiry' test while confirming the court's discretion to refuse oppressive interrogatories.

legal_cases.caseName: Sime Darby Bhd v Syed Zubir Syed Othman
legal_cases.facts: Syed Zubir commenced an action by Originating Summons against Sime Darby. Sime Darby objected, arguing the matter should have been commenced by Writ of Summons as there were substantial disputes of fact.
issues: When is an Originating Summons the appropriate mode of commencement
When must proceedings be commenced by Writ of Summons instead
The court's power to convert an Originating Summons to a Writ
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that an Originating Summons is appropriate where the principal question is one of construction of a statute, deed, or document, or where there is unlikely to be a substantial dispute of fact. Where there are substantial factual disputes, the matter must be commenced by Writ of Summons. The court has power to order conversion.
legal_cases.significance: The leading authority on the choice between Originating Summons and Writ of Summons as modes of commencement. Essential for understanding originating process in Malaysian civil litigation.

legal_cases.caseName: Abdul Rahim bin Aki v Burhanuddin bin Harun
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff applied for a mandatory injunction at the interlocutory stage, requiring the defendant to restore the plaintiff's possession of property. The issue was whether mandatory injunctions could be granted at the interlocutory stage.
issues: Whether mandatory injunctions are available at the interlocutory stage
The higher test for mandatory injunctions compared to prohibitory injunctions
What constitutes a 'high degree of assurance' for mandatory interlocutory relief
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that mandatory injunctions may be granted at the interlocutory stage but a higher threshold applies. The applicant must show a 'high degree of assurance' that he will succeed at trial, not merely a 'serious question to be tried'. The court must also consider whether the injunction is needed to prevent irreparable harm.
legal_cases.significance: Established the higher test for mandatory interlocutory injunctions in Malaysia. Distinguishes between prohibitory (American Cyanamid test) and mandatory (high degree of assurance test) interlocutory injunctions.

legal_cases.caseName: Kerajaan Malaysia v Perbadanan Niaga Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: The Government of Malaysia applied for certiorari to quash the decision of an arbitral tribunal. The case raised the fundamental question of the scope of judicial review in relation to arbitral awards and public law decisions.
issues: Scope of judicial review under Order 53 in Malaysia
Distinction between private law and public law remedies
When certiorari is available to quash an administrative decision
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that judicial review under Order 53 is available against decisions of public authorities exercising public functions. The three traditional remedies are certiorari, mandamus, and prohibition. The applicant must show that the decision-maker exceeded its jurisdiction, acted in breach of natural justice, or made an error of law on the face of the record.
legal_cases.significance: Comprehensive statement of the scope and limits of judicial review in Malaysia. Confirmed the traditional grounds and the requirement for a public law element in the decision under challenge.

legal_cases.caseName: Majlis Perbandaran Pulau Pinang v Syarikat Bekerjasama-Sama Serbaguna Sungai Gelugor
legal_cases.facts: MPPP made a decision to acquire land for a public purpose. The landowner challenged the decision by judicial review, arguing the acquisition was not for a genuine public purpose and was Wednesbury unreasonable.
issues: Application of the Wednesbury test of unreasonableness in Malaysian judicial review
When is a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it
The proportionality test as an alternative to Wednesbury
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court applied the Wednesbury test: a decision may be set aside if it is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority would ever consider imposing it. The court does not substitute its view for that of the decision-maker but reviews whether the decision falls within the range of reasonable outcomes.
legal_cases.significance: Confirmed the application of the Wednesbury unreasonableness test in Malaysian judicial review. The Federal Court discussed but did not adopt the proportionality test as a general standard of review.

legal_cases.caseName: Damansara Realty Bhd v Malaysia National Insurance Bhd
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff applied for further and better particulars of the defendant's defence. The defendant resisted, arguing the request was oppressive and amounted to a demand for evidence rather than particulars of pleadings.
issues: Test for ordering further and better particulars
Distinction between particulars of pleadings and evidence
When a request for particulars is oppressive
legal_cases.held: The High Court held that further and better particulars serve to inform the opposing party of the case it has to meet and to prevent surprise at trial. They must relate to facts, not evidence. A request is oppressive if it goes beyond what is necessary to define the issues and seeks to obtain the other party's evidence before trial.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the law on further and better particulars in Malaysian civil procedure. Important for the pre-trial process and the distinction between pleading facts and disclosing evidence.

legal_cases.caseName: Asean Security Paper Mills Sdn Bhd v Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance (Malaysia) Bhd
legal_cases.facts: The Federal Court considered whether there was a duty of parties to litigation to give discovery of documents in their possession, custody, or power, and the proper scope of automatic discovery under Order 24.
issues: Scope of automatic discovery under Order 24 rule 1
The Peruvian Guano test for relevance in discovery
Whether electronic documents are discoverable
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court confirmed that under Order 24 rule 1, each party must disclose all documents in their possession, custody, or power that are relevant to the matters in issue. The Peruvian Guano test applies: a document is relevant if it is one that may, directly or indirectly, enable a party to advance its own case or damage the case of the adversary, or may lead to a train of inquiry.
legal_cases.significance: Comprehensive restatement of the law of discovery in Malaysia. Confirmed the Peruvian Guano test and extended the scope of discovery to electronic documents. Essential for modern litigation practice.

legal_cases.caseName: Yong Tim v Hoo Kok Chong
legal_cases.facts: The appellant brought an appeal out of time. The question arose whether the court had discretion to extend the time for filing a notice of appeal and what factors should be considered.
issues: The court's power to extend time for filing notice of appeal
Factors considered in an application for extension of time to appeal
Whether delay alone is sufficient to refuse an extension
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that in considering whether to extend time for filing a notice of appeal, the court considers: (1) length of delay; (2) reasons for the delay; (3) chances of the appeal succeeding if time is extended; (4) the degree of prejudice to the other party. All four factors are weighed together — no single factor is determinative.
legal_cases.significance: Established the four-factor test for extension of time to appeal in Malaysia. Applied consistently in subsequent cases. Essential for appellate practice.

legal_cases.caseName: Hock Hua Bank Bhd v Sahari bin Murid
legal_cases.facts: Hock Hua Bank applied for summary judgment under Order 14 against the guarantor. The guarantor resisted, raising various technical defences about the guarantee's validity and claiming the bank varied the underlying loan without consent.
issues: Whether variation of the underlying loan without guarantor's consent discharges the guarantee
Application of summary judgment procedure to guarantee claims
Scope of the guarantor's defences under Order 14
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that any material variation of the terms of the underlying loan agreement without the guarantor's consent discharges the guarantor's liability under the guarantee. The bank cannot unilaterally change the terms of the facility and then enforce the guarantee. This is a triable issue defeating summary judgment.
legal_cases.significance: Landmark case on the law of guarantees and the guarantor's discharge by material variation. Widely cited in banking litigation involving guarantee claims.

legal_cases.caseName: Sim Kie Chon v Superintendent of Pudu Prison
legal_cases.facts: Sim Kie Chon applied for habeas corpus and judicial review challenging the legality of his detention. The case raised the question of the relationship between habeas corpus and judicial review and when each remedy is appropriate.
issues: The relationship between habeas corpus and judicial review
When habeas corpus is the appropriate remedy
Scope of certiorari in challenging detention orders
legal_cases.held: The Supreme Court held that habeas corpus and judicial review are distinct remedies. Habeas corpus tests the legality of the detention itself — whether the detaining authority has lawful power. Judicial review (certiorari) reviews the decision-making process — whether the authority exercised its power properly. Both may be invoked simultaneously where appropriate.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the distinction between habeas corpus and judicial review in Malaysia. Important for constitutional and administrative law practitioners.

legal_cases.caseName: Sivalingam Periasamy v Periasamy & Ors
legal_cases.facts: The defendant applied for stay of proceedings under s. 6 of the Limitation Act 1953, arguing the plaintiff's claim was time-barred. The plaintiff argued the limitation period had been extended by acknowledgment of the debt.
issues: Application of the Limitation Act 1953 to civil claims
Whether acknowledgment of debt extends the limitation period
The effect of part payment on limitation
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that under the Limitation Act 1953, an action founded on simple contract must be brought within 6 years. An acknowledgment in writing or part payment restarts the limitation period. The acknowledgment must be clear and unambiguous, and made to the person entitled to receive it.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the law on limitation periods and their extension through acknowledgment or part payment. Essential for any civil litigation practitioner assessing the viability of claims.

legal_cases.caseName: Tenaga Nasional Bhd v Tekali Prospecting Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Tekali Prospecting brought a claim against Tenaga Nasional that was alleged to be time-barred. The issue was whether the cause of action accrued when the damage occurred or when the damage was discovered.
issues: When does a cause of action accrue for limitation purposes
Application of the discoverability principle in Malaysia
Distinction between accrual in contract and tort for limitation
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal considered the principles of accrual of cause of action. In contract, time runs from the date of breach. In tort, time runs from the date damage occurs, which may be later than the tortious act. The court acknowledged that in some cases the discoverability principle may apply where damage is latent.
legal_cases.significance: Important for understanding when limitation periods begin to run in different types of civil claims. Particularly relevant for professional negligence and latent damage cases.

legal_cases.caseName: Wong Bark Chwan David v Professional Assessment Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff applied for summary judgment under Order 14 against the defendant for a debt. The defendant sought to rely on a counterclaim as a defence. The question was whether a counterclaim could operate as a defence to defeat a summary judgment application.
issues: Whether a counterclaim is a defence to a summary judgment application
When a counterclaim should be treated as a set-off operating as a defence
The court's approach to connected cross-claims in summary judgment
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that a counterclaim per se is not a defence to a summary judgment application unless it also operates as a set-off arising from the same transaction. An equitable set-off arising from the same transaction may defeat summary judgment if it would be manifestly unjust to enforce the claim without considering the cross-claim.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified when a counterclaim can defeat summary judgment. Important distinction between mere counterclaims and equitable set-offs from the same transaction.

legal_cases.caseName: Protasco Bhd v Tey Por Yee
legal_cases.facts: Protasco Bhd applied to strike out the counterclaim filed by Tey Por Yee on the grounds that it was scandalous, frivolous, and vexatious. The counterclaim alleged oppression and misconduct by the company's directors.
issues: Principles governing striking out of counterclaims
Whether the same principles apply to striking out counterclaims as to statements of claim
The threshold for 'scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious'
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that the same principles governing striking out of statements of claim under O.18 r.19 apply to counterclaims. A counterclaim should only be struck out if it is plain and obvious that it discloses no reasonable cause of action, or is scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious. The test is stringent as the court does not conduct a mini-trial at the striking out stage.
legal_cases.significance: Confirmed that the O.18 r.19 principles apply equally to counterclaims and statements of claim. Important for interlocutory practice.

legal_cases.caseName: Takako Sakao v Ng Pek Yuan
legal_cases.facts: Takako Sakao, a Japanese national, commenced proceedings in Malaysia by Writ of Summons. The question arose as to whether a foreign plaintiff had locus standi and whether she needed to provide security for costs.
issues: Locus standi of foreign plaintiffs in Malaysian courts
When security for costs will be ordered against a foreign plaintiff
The court's discretion in ordering security for costs
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court confirmed that foreign plaintiffs have locus standi to bring proceedings in Malaysian courts. However, the court has discretion under Order 23 to order a foreign plaintiff to provide security for the defendant's costs. The court considers the merits of the claim, the plaintiff's means, and whether ordering security would stifle a genuine claim.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the position of foreign plaintiffs in Malaysian litigation and the principles governing security for costs. Important for cross-border banking and commercial disputes.

legal_cases.caseName: Master Strike Sdn Bhd v Sterling Heights Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Master Strike applied for a stay of proceedings under s. 10 of the Arbitration Act 2005, arguing the dispute was subject to an arbitration clause. Sterling Heights resisted, arguing the arbitration clause was not wide enough to cover the claim.
issues: When will the court stay proceedings in favour of arbitration under s. 10 Arbitration Act
Construction of arbitration clauses — narrow vs wide
The court's discretion in granting a stay
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that where there is a valid arbitration clause covering the dispute, the court must stay the proceedings and refer the parties to arbitration. The court should give effect to the parties' agreement to arbitrate. A widely-worded arbitration clause covering 'any dispute arising out of or in connection with' the contract would encompass all related claims.
legal_cases.significance: Important for understanding stay of proceedings in favour of arbitration. Applied widely in commercial disputes where parties have agreed to arbitrate.

legal_cases.caseName: Public Finance Bhd v Phuah Cheng Hock
legal_cases.facts: Public Finance applied for an order for committal for contempt of court against Phuah Cheng Hock for breach of a Mareva injunction. The respondent had dealt with frozen assets in breach of the freezing order.
issues: The procedure for committal for contempt for breach of a court order
Standard of proof in contempt proceedings
What constitutes breach of a Mareva injunction
legal_cases.held: The High Court held that contempt for breach of a court order (civil contempt) requires proof beyond reasonable doubt. The applicant must show: (1) a clear and unambiguous order existed; (2) the order was properly served on the respondent; (3) the respondent had knowledge of the order; (4) the respondent deliberately breached the order. The respondent's breach of the Mareva injunction was established.
legal_cases.significance: Established the procedure and standard of proof for contempt proceedings arising from breach of Mareva injunctions. Essential for enforcement of court orders in civil litigation.

legal_cases.caseName: Insun Development Sdn Bhd v Azali bin Bakar
legal_cases.facts: The appellant sought to adduce fresh evidence on appeal. The question was whether the Court of Appeal had jurisdiction to receive further evidence and under what conditions.
issues: Conditions for adducing fresh evidence on appeal
Application of the Ladd v Marshall conditions in Malaysia
The court's discretion in receiving further evidence
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal applied the Ladd v Marshall conditions: fresh evidence will only be admitted on appeal if (1) it could not have been obtained with reasonable diligence for use at the trial; (2) it is such that if given it would probably have an important influence on the result of the case; (3) it is apparently credible. All three conditions must be satisfied.
legal_cases.significance: Confirmed the application of the Ladd v Marshall conditions for fresh evidence on appeal in Malaysia. The three conditions are applied strictly and all must be met.

legal_cases.caseName: Harun bin Mahmud v Shahruddin bin Tahir
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff applied for default judgment under Order 13 after the defendant failed to enter appearance within the prescribed time. The defendant subsequently applied to set aside the default judgment.
issues: Requirements for entering default judgment under Order 13
Grounds for setting aside default judgment
Whether the defendant must show a meritorious defence to set aside default judgment
legal_cases.held: The High Court held that a default judgment entered regularly may be set aside under Order 13 rule 8 if the defendant can show: (1) a defence on the merits; (2) a satisfactory explanation for the failure to enter appearance; (3) that the application to set aside was made promptly. Where the judgment was entered irregularly (not in compliance with the Rules), it may be set aside as of right.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the distinction between setting aside regular and irregular default judgments. Essential for understanding default judgment practice in Malaysian litigation.

legal_cases.caseName: Ho Hup Construction Co Bhd v Bukit Rajah Rubber Co Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Ho Hup Construction commenced proceedings against Bukit Rajah Rubber for damages arising from a construction contract. The plaintiff raised the question of res judicata, arguing the same issue had been decided in earlier proceedings between the parties.
issues: Application of res judicata in Malaysian civil litigation
Distinction between cause of action estoppel and issue estoppel
Requirements for res judicata to apply
legal_cases.held: The Supreme Court held that res judicata applies where (1) the earlier judgment was final and on the merits; (2) the same parties or their privies are involved; (3) the same cause of action or issue was decided. Issue estoppel prevents re-litigation of specific issues already decided, while cause of action estoppel prevents re-litigation of the entire cause of action.
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on res judicata and issue estoppel. Fundamental to understanding the finality of litigation in Malaysia.

legal_cases.caseName: Tan Geok Lan v La Kah Chun
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff sought to join additional parties to the proceedings under Order 15. The question was whether the proposed parties were necessary or proper parties, and whether the joinder would prejudice the existing defendant.
issues: Test for joinder of parties under Order 15 ROC
Distinction between necessary and proper parties
The court's discretion to refuse joinder
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal held that a person may be joined as a party if (1) their presence is necessary to ensure all matters in dispute can be effectually and completely determined (necessary party), or (2) any question or issue relating to the matter in dispute may exist between them and any existing party (proper party). The court retains discretion to refuse joinder if it would cause prejudice or delay.
legal_cases.significance: Clarified the principles governing joinder of parties in Malaysian civil litigation. Important for multi-party disputes and representative actions.
legislation: Rules of Court 2012, Order 15, rules 4 and 6

legal_cases.caseName: CIMB Bank Bhd v Maybank Trustees Bhd
legal_cases.facts: CIMB Bank applied for an Order for Sale under Order 83 against property charged as security for a loan facility. The chargor opposed the application, raising issues about the validity of the charge and the computation of the amount due.
issues: Current procedural requirements for Order for Sale under Order 83
The interplay between National Land Code remedies and Rules of Court remedies
Whether a chargor can raise equitable defences in Order 83 proceedings
legal_cases.held: The High Court set out the modern procedural requirements for Order for Sale applications: (1) proof of a valid charge; (2) proof of default; (3) proof that the statutory notice (Form 16D/16E) was served; (4) proof of the amount due. The court has jurisdiction to consider equitable defences including unconscionability and fraud.
legal_cases.significance: A comprehensive modern guide to Order for Sale procedure. Updated the procedural requirements in light of the 2012 Rules of Court and recent NLC amendments. Essential reference for foreclosure practitioners.

legal_cases.caseName: AmBank (M) Bhd v Kamariyah bte Hamid
legal_cases.facts: AmBank applied for a bankruptcy order against Kamariyah for failure to pay a judgment debt. Kamariyah opposed, arguing the bankruptcy notice was defective and that the debt should have been pursued through other enforcement mechanisms first.
issues: Whether a creditor must exhaust other enforcement mechanisms before resorting to bankruptcy
Requirements for a valid bankruptcy notice
The court's discretion in making bankruptcy orders
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that a judgment creditor is not required to exhaust other enforcement mechanisms (garnishee, charging order, WSS) before filing a bankruptcy petition. The choice of enforcement mechanism is the creditor's. However, the court retains discretion and should consider all relevant circumstances, including whether bankruptcy is a proportionate response.
legal_cases.significance: Confirmed that bankruptcy is available as a direct enforcement mechanism without first exhausting other remedies. Important for banking institutions choosing enforcement strategies.

legal_cases.caseName: Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah & Ors
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff sought an interim injunction to restrain the defendants from acting on a purported notice of expulsion from a political party. The Court of Appeal had to consider the proper test for the grant of interim injunctions in Malaysia following American Cyanamid.
issues: What is the proper test for granting an interim injunction in Malaysia
Whether the American Cyanamid principles are to be applied in Malaysian practice
The role of the balance of convenience and adequacy of damages
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal authoritatively endorsed the American Cyanamid test as applied in Malaysia. Per Gopal Sri Ram JCA, the court must consider: (1) whether there is a serious question to be tried (a low threshold — not frivolous or vexatious); (2) whether damages would be an adequate remedy; (3) where the balance of convenience lies, including the desirability of preserving the status quo. The judge re-stated the principles in clear, structured form which has been universally followed since.
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on the test for an interim injunction. Cited in virtually every interim injunction application heard in Malaysian courts. The 'Keet Gerald approach' is the backbone of interlocutory injunction practice.
legislation: Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s. 25(2) & Schedule

legal_cases.caseName: Asia Commercial Finance (M) Bhd v Kawal Teliti Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: A dispute arose as to whether a particular order made by the High Court was 'interlocutory' or 'final' for the purposes of determining the appeal route under s.68 of the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 — which restricts appeals to the Court of Appeal in respect of certain interlocutory matters.
issues: The proper test for distinguishing an interlocutory order from a final order
Whether to apply the 'order test' or the 'application test'
Implications for the right of appeal under s.68 CJA 1964
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court adopted the 'order test' (also called the Salaman test): one looks at the order actually made and asks whether it finally disposes of the rights of the parties. If yes, the order is final; if no, it is interlocutory — irrespective of the nature of the application that was made. Thus a refusal of a striking out application is interlocutory; a successful striking out which dismisses the suit is final.
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on classifying orders as final or interlocutory. Determines whether leave to appeal is required under s.68 CJA 1964. Practitioners must apply this test before drafting a Notice of Appeal — getting it wrong can be fatal to the appeal.
legislation: Rules of the Court of Appeal 1994

legal_cases.caseName: Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v United Malayan Banking Corporation Bhd
legal_cases.facts: An application was made under Order 18 r 19 of the Rules of the High Court 1980 (now ROC 2012) to strike out the Statement of Claim on grounds that it disclosed no reasonable cause of action and was an abuse of process. The Supreme Court reviewed the principles governing the summary striking out jurisdiction.
issues: The threshold for striking out under Order 18 r 19
Whether the court should hear lengthy argument on points of law on a striking out application
The interplay between Order 18 r 19 and inherent jurisdiction (Order 92 r 4)
legal_cases.held: The Supreme Court held that the summary procedure under Order 18 r 19 should be used only in plain and obvious cases. The court will not embark on a minute examination of the case to decide whether a claim is bound to succeed or fail; it is sufficient if the claim is sustainable on a reasonable view of the facts and law. Striking out should be granted only where the claim is 'obviously unsustainable'. The inherent jurisdiction under Order 92 r 4 supplements but does not displace the rule.
legal_cases.significance: The foundational Malaysian authority on striking out applications. Sets a high threshold — courts will not strike out merely because the claim is weak, only where it is obviously unsustainable. Routinely cited in interlocutory chamber applications.
legislation: Rules of Court 2012, Order 92 r 4 (inherent jurisdiction)

legal_cases.caseName: National Company for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff applied for summary judgment under Order 14 of the Rules of the High Court 1980 (now ROC 2012). The defendant resisted on the basis that there were triable issues of fact. The Federal Court restated the principles for summary judgment in Malaysia.
issues: The proper approach to a summary judgment application under Order 14
What constitutes a 'triable issue' or 'arguable defence'
The plaintiff's burden and the defendant's burden on an Order 14 application
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that the plaintiff must first show a prima facie case for summary judgment. The burden then shifts to the defendant to show cause — to demonstrate by affidavit a bona fide triable issue or some other reason why the case should go to trial. The defence raised must be more than a mere assertion; the defendant must condescend upon particulars. A 'shadowy' defence may be allowed in only on terms (e.g., payment into court).
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on Order 14 summary judgment. Practitioners must be intimately familiar with its formulation when bringing or resisting summary judgment applications. The 'show cause' burden shift remains the analytical framework today.

legal_cases.caseName: Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Bank Bumiputra obtained ex parte Mareva injunctions freezing the assets of Aspatra and related parties in connection with the BMF scandal. The defendants applied to discharge the injunctions on grounds including want of full and frank disclosure on the ex parte application.
issues: The principles governing the grant of Mareva injunctions in Malaysia
The duty of full and frank disclosure on ex parte applications
The court's response to material non-disclosure
legal_cases.held: The Supreme Court affirmed the availability of the Mareva injunction in Malaysia, founded on s.25(2) and the Schedule to the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 read with Order 29 RHC 1980. The court emphasised the absolute duty of full and frank disclosure on any ex parte application; material non-disclosure (whether deliberate or innocent) is normally fatal and leads to discharge of the order with costs on the indemnity basis. The Mareva remedy is exceptional and to be granted only on strong evidence.
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on Mareva injunctions and the duty of full and frank disclosure. Required reading for any practitioner contemplating an ex parte injunction. The case is regularly cited and applied in current practice.
legislation: Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.25(2) and Schedule

legal_cases.caseName: Lian Keow Sdn Bhd (in liquidation) v Paramjothy
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff applied ex parte for an Anton Piller order permitting entry into the defendants' premises to search for and preserve documents and items alleged to be evidence of fraud. The Federal Court considered the conditions under which such an order should be granted in Malaysia.
issues: Whether the Anton Piller jurisdiction is part of Malaysian law
The conditions for the grant of an Anton Piller order
The need for stringent safeguards given the draconian nature of the order
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court accepted the Anton Piller order as part of Malaysian law and adopted the three conditions in Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976]: (a) an extremely strong prima facie case; (b) very serious actual or potential damage to the applicant; (c) clear evidence that the defendant has incriminating documents/items and a real possibility they will be destroyed before any inter partes application. The court emphasised that this is an exceptional remedy granted only in the rarest cases with stringent safeguards.
legal_cases.significance: The seminal Malaysian decision recognising the Anton Piller (search) order. Today, the order is rare but vital in IP infringement, fraud, and serious breach of confidence cases. The three-condition test remains the law.
legislation: Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.25(2) and Schedule

legal_cases.caseName: Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA
legal_cases.facts: Shipowners sought to freeze the time-charterers' bank account in London to secure a claim for unpaid hire. There was evidence the charterers, a Liberian company, were about to dissipate the funds.
issues: Whether the court has jurisdiction to grant an injunction restraining a defendant from disposing of assets pending judgment
The conditions for the grant of such relief
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal granted the injunction, holding that where a plaintiff has a good arguable case and there is evidence of risk of dissipation of assets, the court has jurisdiction to grant a pre-judgment freezing injunction. This decision created what is now universally known as the Mareva injunction or freezing order.
legal_cases.significance: The originating decision on freezing orders, applied throughout the common-law world including Malaysia (received via Aspatra v Bank Bumiputra [1988] 1 MLJ 97). The remedy has been refined and codified but the essential rationale remains.

legal_cases.caseName: Ninemia Maritime Corp v Trave Schiffahrtsgesellschaft GmbH (The Niedersachsen)
legal_cases.judge: Mustill J (at first instance, approved by CA)
legal_cases.facts: Charterers sought a Mareva against shipowners pending arbitration. Disputed whether the 'good arguable case' threshold was met.
issues: The proper formulation of the 'good arguable case' threshold for Mareva relief
How it differs from 'serious question to be tried' and 'balance of probabilities'
legal_cases.held: Mustill J formulated the test as 'a case which is more than barely capable of serious argument and yet not necessarily one which the judge believes to have a better than 50 per cent chance of success'. This is the formulation now universally adopted, including in Malaysia.
legal_cases.significance: The leading authority on the merits threshold for Mareva relief. Cited and applied in Malaysian Mareva practice. Distinguishes the higher Mareva threshold from the lower Cyanamid threshold for ordinary interim injunctions.

legal_cases.caseName: Bank Mellat v Nikpour
legal_cases.facts: Bank Mellat obtained an ex parte Mareva but failed to disclose certain material facts. The defendant applied to discharge.
issues: The duty of full and frank disclosure on ex parte applications
The consequences of breach of that duty
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal discharged the Mareva and reaffirmed that on any ex parte application the applicant owes an absolute duty to make full and frank disclosure of all material matters, including those adverse to the application. Material non-disclosure (whether deliberate or innocent) will normally lead to discharge with indemnity costs. A renewed application may be refused.
legal_cases.significance: The leading authority on the full and frank disclosure duty in ex parte applications. Adopted in Malaysian law via Aspatra v Bank Bumiputra [1988] 1 MLJ 97. Essential reading for any practitioner contemplating ex parte relief.

legal_cases.caseName: Universal Thermosensors Ltd v Hibben
legal_cases.facts: Following execution of an Anton Piller order, the defendants complained the search had been conducted oppressively and beyond the order's scope.
issues: Proper conduct of execution of an Anton Piller order
Required safeguards
legal_cases.held: The Vice-Chancellor laid down detailed guidelines for the proper execution of Anton Piller orders, including: independent supervising solicitor; execution during business hours on a working day; right of respondent to take legal advice before search; restraint on items removable; female respondent and female searcher; lists and receipts. These guidelines were adopted in subsequent CPR practice and are widely followed in Malaysia.
legal_cases.significance: The execution-conduct manual for Anton Piller orders. Universally cited and applied in Malaysian practice on Anton Piller execution.

legal_cases.caseName: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd
legal_cases.facts: Patent infringement action. Cyanamid sought interim injunction to restrain Ethicon's marketing of an allegedly infringing surgical suture pending trial.
issues: The principles for the grant of interim injunctions
legal_cases.held: Lord Diplock laid down the now-standard test: (1) is there a serious question to be tried? (2) are damages an adequate remedy for either party? (3) where does the balance of convenience lie? (4) special factors. The court should not attempt to resolve disputed questions of fact or law on an interlocutory application.
legal_cases.significance: The foundational test for interim injunctions, adopted throughout the common-law world. In Malaysia, refined and operationalised in Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor [1995] 1 MLJ 193 (CA).

legal_cases.caseName: Norwich Pharmacal Co v Customs and Excise Commissioners
legal_cases.facts: Norwich Pharmacal, holders of a patent on a chemical, sought an order against Customs to disclose the names of importers of the patented chemical so as to identify infringers.
issues: Whether and when an innocent third party who has become 'mixed up' in wrongdoing can be compelled to disclose information identifying the wrongdoer
legal_cases.held: The House of Lords held that where a person, through no fault of their own, has become involved in the wrongful acts of others so as to facilitate that wrongdoing, the person comes under a duty to assist the person wronged by giving full information and disclosing the identity of the wrongdoers. This is now known as a 'Norwich Pharmacal order'.
legal_cases.significance: The originating authority for third-party disclosure orders. Routinely applied in Malaysia, particularly against banks to identify recipients of misappropriated funds (e.g., in fraud and asset-tracing cases). Combined with Mareva relief in many cases.

legal_cases.caseName: Yamaha Motor Co Ltd v Yamaha Malaysia Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Application for amendment of pleadings to introduce additional matters in an IP/contractual dispute.
issues: The principles governing amendment of pleadings under Order 20 RHC 1980 (now ROC 2012)
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that amendment is a matter of discretion. It should generally be allowed at any stage of proceedings unless it would cause real prejudice to the other party that cannot be compensated by costs or adjournment. The overriding objective is to enable the real controversy between the parties to be determined.
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on amendment of pleadings under Order 20. Routinely cited at amendment applications.

legal_cases.caseName: Tractors Malaysia Bhd v Tio Chee Hing
legal_cases.facts: Application to strike out the defendant's pleading on the basis that it disclosed no reasonable defence.
issues: The proper approach to applications under limb (a) of Order 18 r 19 (no reasonable cause of action/defence)
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that, on a striking-out application under limb (a), the court considers only the pleading itself. No evidence may be admitted. The court must be satisfied that the case is 'plain and obvious' — only obviously unsustainable claims/defences should be struck out. If there is any prospect of a triable issue, the matter must go to trial.
legal_cases.significance: Foundational Malaysian authority on Order 18 r 19(a). Together with Bandar Builder v UMBC [1993] 3 MLJ 36, governs striking out practice.

legal_cases.caseName: Evans v Bartlam
legal_cases.facts: Defendant sought to set aside default judgment entered against him for failure to enter appearance.
issues: The principles governing setting aside of default judgments
legal_cases.held: The House of Lords held that the discretion to set aside a default judgment is unfettered. The defendant must show: (1) a defence on the merits (i.e., a triable issue); (2) reasonable explanation for the default; (3) promptness in applying. The court may impose terms (e.g., payment into court, costs).
legal_cases.significance: The leading authority on setting aside default judgments. Adopted in Malaysia in Mageswari v United Asian Bank [1985] 1 MLJ 145 and applied across all subsequent cases under Order 13 r 8 / Order 19 r 9 ROC 2012.

legal_cases.caseName: Henderson v Henderson
legal_cases.facts: Subsequent action raising matters that could have been raised in earlier litigation between the same parties.
issues: Whether subsequent litigation raising matters that should have been raised in an earlier suit constitutes abuse of process
legal_cases.held: Wigram V-C laid down the principle that, where a given matter becomes the subject of litigation in a court of competent jurisdiction, the court requires the parties to bring forward their whole case and will not (except in special circumstances) permit the same parties to open the same subject of litigation in respect of matters which might have been brought forward as part of the subject in contest.
legal_cases.significance: The foundational doctrine of 'extended res judicata' or abuse of process. Routinely applied in Malaysian striking-out applications under Order 18 r 19(d) (abuse of process). Particularly important in banking litigation where a borrower may attempt to raise matters that should have been litigated in earlier proceedings.

legal_cases.caseName: Films Rover International Ltd v Cannon Film Sales Ltd
legal_cases.facts: Application for interim mandatory injunction in a film distribution dispute.
issues: The threshold for interim mandatory injunctions (as distinct from prohibitory injunctions)
legal_cases.held: Hoffmann J held that the principles in American Cyanamid apply but with an enhanced threshold for mandatory injunctions: the court should be reluctant to grant a mandatory injunction unless it has a 'high degree of assurance' that at trial it would appear the order was rightly made. The court should consider which course carries the lower risk of injustice if the decision turns out to be wrong.
legal_cases.significance: Leading authority on interim mandatory injunctions. Applied in Malaysian practice when mandatory orders (positive obligations) are sought as interim relief.

legal_cases.caseName: Compagnie Financière du Pacifique v Peruvian Guano Co
legal_cases.facts: Discovery dispute on the scope of relevant documents in a commercial action.
issues: The test for relevance of documents on discovery
legal_cases.held: Brett LJ formulated the test: a document is relevant for discovery if it 'may, either directly or indirectly, enable the party requiring [discovery] either to advance his own case or to damage the case of his adversary, or which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry which may have either of these consequences'. This is a deliberately broad test.
legal_cases.significance: The foundational discovery test, applied in Malaysia under Order 24 ROC 2012. Establishes that discovery is broad — even 'train of inquiry' documents must be disclosed. Subject only to relevance, possession/custody/power, and privilege.

legal_cases.caseName: Donoghue v Stevenson
legal_cases.facts: Mrs Donoghue drank ginger beer from an opaque bottle bought for her by a friend; on pouring the remainder she discovered the decomposed remains of a snail. She sued the manufacturer for negligence.
issues: Whether a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer in the absence of contract
legal_cases.held: Lord Atkin formulated the neighbour principle: 'You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour.' A manufacturer of products owes a duty to the ultimate consumer.
legal_cases.significance: The foundation of the modern law of negligence. Adopted throughout the Commonwealth and applied in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956. Origin of the 'neighbour principle' which underlies all duty of care analysis.

legal_cases.caseName: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman
legal_cases.facts: Caparo bought shares in Fidelity plc relying on audited accounts prepared by Dickman, the auditors. The accounts were inaccurate and Caparo sued for negligence.
issues: The test for the existence of a duty of care in novel situations
legal_cases.held: The House of Lords formulated a three-stage test: (i) reasonable foreseeability of harm; (ii) sufficient proximity between the parties; and (iii) whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.
legal_cases.significance: The modern test for duty of care in novel situations, applied throughout the Commonwealth. Adopted by the Federal Court in Majlis Perbandaran Ampang Jaya v Steven Phoa Cheng Loon (Highland Towers). Replaced the broad Anns v Merton two-stage test.

legal_cases.caseName: Foo Fio Na v Dr Soo Fook Mun & Anor
legal_cases.facts: The plaintiff suffered paralysis after spinal surgery. She alleged the surgeon failed to disclose material risks and obtain informed consent.
issues: Whether the Bolam test applies to medical advice and disclosure of risks
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court adopted the Rogers v Whitaker (Australian High Court) approach for medical advice: the standard of disclosure is set by the court, not the medical profession. The Bolam test continues to apply only for diagnosis and treatment.
legal_cases.significance: Landmark Malaysian case modifying the Bolam test for medical negligence. Aligned Malaysia with Australia and (subsequently) the UK (Montgomery). Patients have a right to be informed of material risks.

legal_cases.caseName: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San & Ors
legal_cases.facts: A registered owner had his title forged; the property was charged to a bank and then transferred. The original owner sought rectification of the register.
issues: The proper construction of s. 340(3) NLC 1965 and indefeasibility of title
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court overruled Adorna Properties v Boonsom Boonyanit. The proviso to s. 340(3) only protects a subsequent purchaser in good faith for value, not the immediate transferee from a forger. Indefeasibility under the NLC 1965 is deferred, not immediate.
legal_cases.significance: Landmark Federal Court decision restoring the proper construction of indefeasibility under the Torrens system. Original owners are protected against forgery — their title is restored against the forger and the immediate transferee.

legal_cases.caseName: Sim v Stretch
legal_cases.facts: Defamation claim arising from a telegram sent by the defendant.
issues: The test for what constitutes defamatory matter
legal_cases.held: Lord Atkin proposed the test: words are defamatory if they tend 'to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally'.
legal_cases.significance: The classic test for defamatory matter, universally applied including in Malaysian defamation cases under the Defamation Act 1957. Sets the objective standard against which words are judged.

legal_cases.caseName: Reynolds v Times Newspapers Ltd
legal_cases.facts: The Sunday Times published an article about Albert Reynolds, the former Irish Taoiseach. The newspaper sought to defend on grounds of qualified privilege.
issues: Whether qualified privilege extends to political information published to the public at large
legal_cases.held: Lord Nicholls formulated the 'Reynolds test' (responsible journalism) — qualified privilege available for publication of matters of public concern subject to ten non-exhaustive factors including seriousness of allegation, source verification, urgency, comment sought from claimant, etc.
legal_cases.significance: Adopted in Malaysia in defamation cases involving the press. Provides the 'responsible journalism' defence. Has since been substantially codified in UK by the Defamation Act 2013 (public interest defence).

legal_cases.caseName: R Rama Chandran v The Industrial Court of Malaysia & Anor
legal_cases.facts: Judicial review of an Industrial Court award which dismissed an unfair dismissal claim. Question whether the High Court could substitute its own decision on quashing the award.
issues: The scope of remedies in judicial review under O 53 ROC 2012
legal_cases.held: On quashing an unlawful decision of an inferior tribunal, the High Court has jurisdiction in proper cases to substitute its own decision rather than merely remit. The court is not confined to a 'choice between two evils' (quash without more, or remit).
legal_cases.significance: Landmark case expanding judicial review remedies in Malaysia. Allows the supervisory court to give substantive relief, not just quash. Frequently invoked in Industrial Court judicial review and other administrative law cases.
legislation: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, Schedule

legal_cases.caseName: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (GCHQ)
legal_cases.facts: Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) staff were prevented from joining trade unions by Order in Council. The unions challenged the decision by judicial review.
issues: The grounds of judicial review
legal_cases.held: Lord Diplock classified the grounds of judicial review into three: (i) illegality (acting beyond power, error of law); (ii) procedural impropriety (breach of natural justice or prescribed procedures); (iii) irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness). A fourth — proportionality — was foreseen.
legal_cases.significance: The classic taxonomy of judicial review grounds, applied throughout the Commonwealth including Malaysia. The framework for all administrative law analysis. Proportionality has since become an established fourth ground in fundamental rights cases.
legislation: Common Law; Rules of Court 2012, Order 53

legal_cases.caseName: Pang Yong Hock v PKM Industries (M) Sdn Bhd & Ors
legal_cases.facts: Minority shareholder petition under s. 181 CA 1965 (now s. 346 CA 2016) alleging oppression and unfair prejudice in family-controlled company.
issues: The scope of relief under s. 181 (oppression remedy)
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court confirmed the wide discretion of the court under s. 181 to grant any relief considered just to bring an end to the oppression. Buy-out at fair value is the most common remedy. The court will look at the substance of the conduct, not its form.
legal_cases.significance: Leading Malaysian case on oppression remedy under s. 181 CA 1965 (now s. 346 CA 2016). Confirms the broad discretion available and the centrality of buy-out orders.

legal_cases.caseName: View Esteem Sdn Bhd v Bina Puri Holdings Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Application to set aside a CIPAA adjudication decision on grounds of denial of natural justice — the adjudicator allegedly failed to consider material defences.
issues: The scope of the natural justice ground for setting aside CIPAA decisions under s. 15(b)
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that natural justice under s. 15(b) requires the adjudicator to consider material defences raised. Failure to consider a substantial defence amounts to denial of natural justice. However, the court will not engage in a merits review.
legal_cases.significance: Key Federal Court decision clarifying the s. 15(b) natural justice ground for setting aside CIPAA decisions. Adjudicators must engage with material defences but courts will not micromanage their reasoning.

legal_cases.caseName: Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Dispute over enforceability of a liquidated damages clause in a commercial contract; the defendant argued actual loss must be proved.
issues: Whether s. 75 Contracts Act 1950 requires proof of actual loss to recover liquidated damages
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that s. 75 Contracts Act 1950 does not require proof of actual loss. Once a breach is proved, the innocent party is entitled to reasonable compensation up to the stipulated sum. The burden is on the defendant to show the stipulated sum is extravagant or unconscionable.
legal_cases.significance: Resolves the long-running debate on s. 75 — clarifies that Malaysian law diverges from English law on liquidated damages. Significantly strengthens enforceability of LD clauses in contracts.

legal_cases.caseName: Press Metal Sarawak Sdn Bhd v Etiqa Takaful Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Dispute over whether the court should stay proceedings under s. 10 Arbitration Act 2005 in favour of arbitration.
issues: The mandatory nature of stay under s. 10 AA 2005
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court confirmed that stay under s. 10 AA 2005 is mandatory where (i) there is an arbitration agreement; (ii) the matter falls within scope; and (iii) the application is made before substantive defence. The court has no discretion to refuse stay on grounds such as multiplicity of proceedings.
legal_cases.significance: Establishes mandatory nature of stay under the Arbitration Act 2005. Aligns Malaysian arbitration law with the UNCITRAL Model Law and the New York Convention's pro-arbitration policy.

legal_cases.caseName: Foss v Harbottle
legal_cases.facts: Two minority shareholders sued the directors alleging fraud against the company. The directors objected that only the company could sue.
issues: Whether minority shareholders can sue for wrongs done to the company
legal_cases.held: The proper plaintiff in respect of a wrong done to the company is the company itself (proper plaintiff rule). The court will not interfere in matters of internal management which can be ratified by ordinary majority (majority rule).
legal_cases.significance: The foundational rule of company law on standing. Now significantly modified in Malaysia by the statutory derivative action under s. 347 Companies Act 2016, which provides a procedure for shareholders to sue in the company's name with leave of the court.

legal_cases.caseName: Goon Kwee Phoy v J&P Coats (M) Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Industrial dispute on whether the dismissal of a workman was for just cause or excuse.
issues: The burden of proof in s. 20 Industrial Relations Act 1967 dismissal cases
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that in a s. 20 IRA 1967 case, the burden lies on the employer to prove (a) the misconduct or other ground of dismissal; and (b) that the dismissal was proportionate. The Industrial Court is not bound by strict rules of evidence and considers equity and good conscience.
legal_cases.significance: Landmark Federal Court case on the burden of proof and standard in Industrial Court dismissal cases. The cornerstone of Malaysian unfair dismissal jurisprudence.

legal_cases.caseName: Lim Kit Siang v United Engineers (M) Bhd
legal_cases.facts: An opposition Member of Parliament sought judicial review of the award of a major public works contract by the Government to UEM.
issues: Whether the applicant had locus standi to bring judicial review
legal_cases.held: The Supreme Court held the applicant lacked locus standi — only persons whose private rights are infringed or who suffer special damage may bring judicial review. Public interest standing was rejected on the facts.
legal_cases.significance: Restrictive standing decision. Significantly criticised; subsequent cases (notably Malaysian Trades Union Congress v Menteri Tenaga [2014]) have loosened standing for public interest cases. Often cited as the high-water mark of restrictive standing.

legal_cases.caseName: Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak & Ors
legal_cases.facts: A Hindu mother's three children were unilaterally converted to Islam by her former husband without her consent. She sought judicial review and orders for return of her children.
issues: Whether civil courts have jurisdiction over custody disputes following unilateral conversion of children to Islam
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that civil courts retain jurisdiction. Unilateral conversion without the consent of both parents is unconstitutional. Article 12(4) Federal Constitution requires the consent of 'parent' (in plural sense). Constitutional supremacy applies.
legal_cases.significance: Landmark constitutional and family law case. Restored civil court jurisdiction in conversion cases. Reinforced constitutional supremacy and the rights of non-converting parents.

legal_cases.caseName: Letchumanan Chettiar Alagappan @ L Allagappan v Secure Plantation Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Contentious probate dispute on the validity of a will alleged to have been executed under suspicious circumstances by a testator with declining capacity.
issues: The standards for proving testamentary capacity and suspicious circumstances
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court reaffirmed the Banks v Goodfellow test for testamentary capacity and held that where suspicious circumstances surround the execution of a will, the propounder bears the burden of removing the suspicion before the will can be admitted to probate.
legal_cases.significance: Key Federal Court decision on contentious probate. Reinforces the high standard of proof for wills executed in suspicious circumstances. Frequently cited in elder care/inheritance disputes.
legislation: Wills Act 1959; Probate and Administration Act 1959

legal_cases.caseName: Photo Production Ltd v Securicor Transport Ltd
legal_cases.facts: A security guard employed by Securicor deliberately set fire to a factory it was contracted to protect. The contract contained a wide exclusion clause.
issues: Whether exclusion clauses can cover fundamental breach
legal_cases.held: The House of Lords held that the doctrine of fundamental breach is one of construction, not law. Whether a wide exclusion clause covers a particular breach (including fundamental breach) is a question of construction of the clause itself.
legal_cases.significance: Restored party autonomy in commercial contracts. Adopted in Malaysia. Significant in commercial drafting — well-drafted exclusion clauses are enforceable even for serious breaches.

legal_cases.caseName: Hadley v Baxendale
legal_cases.facts: Hadley's mill shaft broke. He engaged Baxendale to deliver it for repair. The carrier was late, causing extended mill closure. Hadley sued for lost profits.
issues: The principle for assessment of damages for breach of contract
legal_cases.held: Damages recoverable for breach of contract are: (i) such as may fairly and reasonably be considered to arise naturally from the breach (first limb); or (ii) such as may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contract (second limb).
legal_cases.significance: The foundational rule on remoteness of damages in contract. Codified in s. 74 Contracts Act 1950 ('loss arising naturally...or which the parties knew when they made the contract'). Universally applied in commercial litigation.

legal_cases.caseName: Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah
legal_cases.facts: Application for interim injunction in a property dispute. The Court of Appeal restated the test for interim injunctions in Malaysia.
issues: The test for grant of interim injunctions
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal synthesised the American Cyanamid principles for Malaysian practice. The court must consider: (i) whether there is a serious question to be tried; (ii) whether damages would be an adequate remedy; (iii) the balance of convenience; and (iv) preservation of the status quo.
legal_cases.significance: The leading Malaysian authority on interim injunctions. Provides the working framework for all interim relief applications in Malaysia. Frequently cited at all court levels.

legal_cases.caseName: Foskett v McKeown
legal_cases.facts: A trustee misappropriated trust money to pay premiums on a life insurance policy. On the trustee's death, the question was whether the beneficiaries could trace into the policy proceeds.
issues: The principles of equitable tracing into substituted assets
legal_cases.held: Equitable tracing follows the value of misappropriated trust property into substituted assets. Beneficiaries are entitled to a proportionate share of the substituted asset (the policy proceeds), not merely a charge for the amount misappropriated. Tracing is a process, not a remedy.
legal_cases.significance: Leading modern authority on equitable tracing. Applied in Malaysia in trust and fiduciary cases. Establishes the proprietary remedy of beneficiaries against substituted assets.

legal_cases.caseName: Royal Brunei Airlines Sdn Bhd v Tan
legal_cases.facts: Travel agency held airline funds on trust. The agent's director (Tan) misappropriated the funds. The airline sued the director for dishonest assistance.
issues: The standard for accessory liability for dishonest assistance in breach of trust
legal_cases.held: Lord Nicholls held that the touchstone of accessory liability is dishonesty (not knowledge per se). Dishonesty is assessed objectively: did the defendant act in a way that an honest person would not have acted in the circumstances?
legal_cases.significance: Leading Commonwealth authority on dishonest assistance. Applied in Malaysian trust litigation. Establishes the objective dishonesty test for accessory liability.

legal_cases.caseName: FHR European Ventures LLP v Cedar Capital Partners LLC
legal_cases.facts: An agent received a secret commission from the seller in a property transaction. The principal sued for the commission as held on constructive trust.
issues: Whether secret commissions/bribes received by a fiduciary are held on constructive trust for the principal
legal_cases.held: The UK Supreme Court unanimously held that all benefits received by a fiduciary in breach of duty (including secret commissions and bribes) are held on constructive trust for the principal. The proprietary remedy is available; the principal is not confined to a personal claim.
legal_cases.significance: Leading modern Commonwealth authority on the proprietary nature of secret commissions. Applied in Malaysia. Significant in fraud and corruption litigation — the principal can trace into substituted assets and rank ahead of unsecured creditors on insolvency.

legal_cases.caseName: Majlis Perbandaran Ampang Jaya v Steven Phoa Cheng Loon (Highland Towers)
legal_cases.facts: Following the collapse of Block 1 of the Highland Towers condominium in 1993 (which killed 48 people), residents of Blocks 2 and 3 sued the local authority for negligence in approving and supervising development around the site.
issues: Whether a local authority owes a duty of care to property owners affected by its statutory functions
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court applied the Caparo three-stage test and held the local authority owed a duty of care, breached it, and was liable in negligence to the residents whose property was damaged.
legal_cases.significance: Leading Malaysian authority applying the Caparo test. Establishes that statutory bodies can owe a duty of care in tort in respect of negligent exercise of statutory functions. Significant for public authority liability cases.

legal_cases.caseName: Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v United Malayan Banking Corporation Bhd
legal_cases.facts: Dispute on the principles for striking out under O 18 r 19 ROC and specific performance of land sale contracts.
issues: The threshold for striking out and the availability of specific performance for sale of land
legal_cases.held: Striking out is reserved for plain and obvious cases — where the pleading is unarguable. For specific performance of land sale, damages are presumed inadequate and the equitable remedy is the prima facie relief.
legal_cases.significance: Twin propositions: foundational on striking out (still cited) and on specific performance for land sales. The Bandar Builder principle on striking out is the touchstone applied in every striking out application in Malaysia.
legislation: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18 r 19; Specific Relief Act 1950

legal_cases.caseName: Semenyih Jaya Sdn Bhd v Pentadbir Tanah Daerah Hulu Langat
legal_cases.facts: A land acquisition reference in which the role of assessors and the constitutional position of the judicial power of the courts were challenged, the developer contending that vesting decision-making in non-judicial members undermined the court's adjudicative function.
issues: Whether the judicial power of the Federation is vested exclusively in the courts under Article 121 of the Federal Constitution
Whether the doctrine of the basic structure of the Constitution applies in Malaysia
Validity of decision-making by assessors in land acquisition references
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that judicial power is an inherent feature of the basic structure of the Constitution and cannot be removed or diluted even by constitutional amendment. The 1988 amendment to Article 121(1) did not divest the courts of their inherent judicial power.
legal_cases.significance: Landmark constitutional decision reviving the basic structure doctrine in Malaysia and reaffirming the separation of powers and the supremacy of judicial power. It is the cornerstone authority for constitutional and administrative law challenges.
legislation: Federal Constitution, Article 121; Land Acquisition Act 1960

legal_cases.caseName: Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak
legal_cases.facts: A mother challenged the unilateral conversion of her three children to Islam by her husband. The question arose whether the civil High Court had jurisdiction to review the conversion certificates issued by the religious authority.
issues: Whether the civil courts retain the power of judicial review over administrative action by religious authorities
Whether judicial review and the inherent judicial power form part of the basic structure
Requirement of consent of both parents for the conversion of a minor
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that the power of judicial review is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution that cannot be ousted. The civil courts have jurisdiction to review the legality of administrative action, including conversion certificates. Both parents' consent is required to convert a minor.
legal_cases.significance: Reaffirmed Semenyih Jaya. Confirmed that judicial review of administrative action is constitutionally entrenched and beyond the reach of ouster clauses — central authority for administrative law and constitutional litigation.
legislation: Federal Constitution, Articles 4, 121; Courts of Judicature Act 1964

legal_cases.caseName: Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia
legal_cases.facts: A member of the Bar challenged the constitutionality of a provision restricting members of the Bar Council from holding office while being a member of certain political/legislative bodies, alleging breach of fundamental liberties.
issues: The proper approach to interpreting fundamental liberties in Part II of the Constitution
Whether the right to associate under Article 10 can be subject to reasonable restriction
Application of proportionality in constitutional review
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that fundamental rights must be read generously and purposively, that Article 8 embodies a guarantee against arbitrariness, and that any restriction on a fundamental right must be proportionate. The phrase 'in accordance with law' imports a requirement that the law be fair and not arbitrary.
legal_cases.significance: A leading authority on the liberal and purposive interpretation of fundamental liberties and the introduction of proportionality into Malaysian constitutional review.

legal_cases.caseName: Government of Malaysia v Lim Kit Siang
legal_cases.facts: Lim Kit Siang sought a declaration and injunction to restrain the award of the North-South Highway contract, claiming the award was unlawful. The Government challenged his locus standi to bring the action.
issues: The test for locus standi in public law challenges
Whether a member of the public or legislator has standing to challenge a government contract
legal_cases.held: The Supreme Court (by majority) held that to have standing a plaintiff must show that some private right of his has been infringed or that he has suffered special damage peculiar to himself beyond that suffered by the public generally. On that test the plaintiff lacked standing.
legal_cases.significance: The long-standing benchmark on locus standi in Malaysian public law. Though later decisions have liberalised standing, it remains the starting point for any discussion of standing in public interest litigation.
legislation: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Government Contracts Act 1949

legal_cases.caseName: Maria Chin Abdullah v Ketua Pengarah Imigresen
legal_cases.facts: A travel ban was imposed on the applicant. She challenged the decision and the validity of an ouster clause purporting to exclude judicial review of immigration decisions.
issues: Whether an ouster clause can validly exclude judicial review
The reach of the basic structure doctrine over ouster clauses
Scope of judicial review of immigration decisions
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court (by majority) addressed the effect of ouster clauses against the entrenched power of judicial review, reaffirming that judicial review for jurisdictional error and illegality cannot be wholly ousted, consistent with the basic structure cases.
legal_cases.significance: Continues the Semenyih Jaya / Indira Gandhi line on the constitutional entrenchment of judicial review and the limited effect of ouster clauses — important for administrative law practitioners.

legal_cases.caseName: Berjaya Times Square Sdn Bhd v M Concept Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: A dispute over a contract for the sale/licensing of retail lots in which one party alleged repudiation and frustration. The court examined the doctrines of repudiatory breach and frustration under the Contracts Act 1950.
issues: When a breach amounts to a repudiation entitling the innocent party to terminate
The distinction between frustration and breach under ss 40 and 57 of the Contracts Act 1950
Election to affirm or terminate
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court clarified the principles of repudiatory breach and frustration, holding that termination requires a breach going to the root of the contract or a clear refusal to perform, and that frustration operates only where performance becomes radically different through no fault of the parties.
legal_cases.significance: A leading modern restatement of repudiation, termination and frustration under Malaysian contract law, frequently cited in commercial disputes.

legal_cases.caseName: CIMB Bank Bhd v Anthony Lawrence Bourke & Anor
legal_cases.judge: David Wong Dak Wah CJ (Sabah & Sarawak)
legal_cases.facts: Borrowers suffered loss when the bank failed to disburse a loan despite an approved facility. The bank relied on an exclusion clause in the letter of offer purporting to exclude all liability for loss arising from any delay or failure to disburse.
issues: Whether an exclusion clause that wholly excludes liability for the bank's own breach is enforceable
Whether such a clause offends s 29 of the Contracts Act 1950 (restraint of legal proceedings)
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that an exclusion clause which has the effect of entirely depriving the innocent party of any remedy for breach offends s 29 of the Contracts Act 1950 and is void, as it restrains the party from enforcing their rights through legal proceedings.
legal_cases.significance: Important consumer- and borrower-protective decision limiting the use of sweeping exclusion clauses in standard-form banking and commercial contracts under s 29 of the Contracts Act 1950.

legal_cases.caseName: Jack-In Pile (M) Sdn Bhd v Bauer (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd
legal_cases.facts: A construction contract contained a 'pay-when-paid' (conditional payment) clause. The question was whether s 35 of CIPAA, which renders conditional payment provisions void, applied to a contract entered into before CIPAA came into force.
issues: Whether s 35 of CIPAA (voiding conditional payment terms) applies retrospectively or prospectively
Validity of pay-when-paid clauses under CIPAA
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that CIPAA, including s 35, operates prospectively and applies to construction contracts made after CIPAA came into force on 15 April 2014. Conditional/'pay-when-paid' payment terms in contracts within CIPAA's reach are void under s 35.
legal_cases.significance: Settled the temporal application of CIPAA and confirmed that pay-when-paid clauses are void under s 35 — a frequently cited authority on the operation of the Act and cash-flow protection in construction.
legislation: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012, s 35

legal_cases.caseName: Pioneer Haven Sdn Bhd v Ho Hup Construction Co Bhd
legal_cases.facts: A dispute among shareholders/directors of a company involving allegations that the affairs of the company were being conducted in a manner oppressive to, and in disregard of, the interests of certain members.
issues: The principles governing the statutory oppression remedy
What conduct amounts to oppression or disregard of members' interests
The range of remedies available to the court
legal_cases.held: The Court of Appeal restated the principles of the oppression remedy, holding that the court looks at commercial unfairness and the legitimate expectations of members, and has a wide discretion to grant remedies to bring the oppressive conduct to an end.
legal_cases.significance: A leading exposition of the statutory oppression remedy (now s 346 of the Companies Act 2016), widely cited in shareholder and minority-protection disputes.
legislation: Companies Act 2016, s 346 (formerly s 181 Companies Act 1965)

legal_cases.caseName: Pacific Forest Industries Sdn Bhd v Lin Wen-Chih
legal_cases.facts: A claim for damages for breach of contract in which the basis on which damages are to be assessed under the Contracts Act 1950 was in issue.
issues: The proper measure of damages for breach of contract
Whether a plaintiff must prove actual loss to recover substantial damages
Application of ss 74 and 75 of the Contracts Act 1950
legal_cases.held: The Federal Court held that damages for breach of contract are compensatory — designed to put the innocent party in the position they would have been in had the contract been performed — and a plaintiff must prove the loss actually suffered; damages are not awarded for loss not proved.
legal_cases.significance: A leading authority on the assessment of contractual damages and the compensatory principle under Malaysian law, regularly applied in commercial damages claims.

cost_schedules.title: Party-Party Costs in Civil Litigation (Order 59 ROC 2012)
cost_schedules.description: Scale of party-party costs awarded by the court in civil litigation. The governing principle is that costs follow the event — the unsuccessful party ordinarily pays the successful party's costs, subject to the court's discretion under Order 59 of the Rules of Court 2012.

items.amount: Losing party pays winning party's party-party costs
items.notes: Order 59 r 2 ROC 2012; court retains full discretion
