items.notes: Order 59 r 16(2) ROC 2012

items.amount: All costs unless unreasonably incurred; doubt resolved in favour of receiving party
items.notes: Granted where losing party's conduct is reprehensible or agreement provides for it

items.amount: All costs reasonably incurred on a full indemnity basis
items.notes: Applicable where contractually agreed (e.g., loan agreement clause)

cost_schedules.title: Solicitor-Client Costs for Contentious Business (Litigation)
cost_schedules.description: Costs charged by a solicitor to their own client for conducting litigation (contentious business). Unlike conveyancing, there is no fixed statutory scale for contentious work. Fees are agreed by Warrant to Act or Letter of Engagement, subject to the Legal Profession Act 1976.

items.description: Basis of charging: Time-based or brief fee
items.amount: By agreement in Warrant to Act / Letter of Engagement

cost_schedules.title: Industrial Court: Employment Dispute Costs & Awards
cost_schedules.description: Cost framework for unfair dismissal and industrial relations disputes referred to the Industrial Court under the Industrial Relations Act 1967. The Industrial Court is a tribunal of limited jurisdiction — it does not award party-party costs as a general rule.

items.notes: AIAC Fee Schedule; parties may agree alternative fee arrangement

items.notes: CIPAA 2012, s. 18; adjudicator has discretion to award costs

items.notes: CIPAA 2012, s. 28; enforcement via ROC 2012 enforcement proceedings

items.notes: CIPAA 2012, s. 15; grounds: breach of natural justice, fraud, adjudicator acted beyond jurisdiction

items.notes: CIPAA 2012, s. 3 exclusions

cost_schedules.title: Post-Judgment Enforcement Costs (Writs of Execution)
cost_schedules.description: Costs and fees associated with enforcing a civil judgment in Malaysia. Enforcement is governed by Orders 46–50 of the Rules of Court 2012. The judgment creditor may use one or more enforcement methods, each attracting separate court fees and costs.

items.description: Writ of Seizure and Sale (WSS) — movable property (Order 46)
items.amount: RM50 filing fee + RM25 per item seized; bailiff levy applies
items.notes: Bailiff entitled to charge for transport, storage; sheriff may require deposit before execution

items.description: Writ of Seizure and Sale — immovable property
items.amount: RM50 filing fee; sale conducted by court-appointed auctioneer
items.notes: Auctioneer's commission on immovable property: approximately 1–2% of sale price

items.amount: RM50 (Garnishee Order Nisi); RM50 (Garnishee Order Absolute); served on garnishee (e.g., bank)
items.notes: Debtor's bank account or debts due from third parties attached

items.amount: RM50 per order; Charging Order Nisi then Absolute
items.notes: Charges debtor's beneficial interest in securities, funds, or property

items.amount: RM50 per summons; debtor examined on assets and means
items.notes: Failure to attend: contempt of court; basis for Committal Order

items.amount: RM50 filing fee; application by OS and supporting affidavit
items.notes: Applies where judgment debtor disobeys court order (e.g., injunction breach); up to 3 years imprisonment

items.amount: RM50; enforces court order for delivery of possession of land/premises
items.notes: Used in OS Order for Sale proceedings after auction; sheriff effects possession

items.description: Bankruptcy Proceedings (as enforcement): Statutory Demand + Petition
items.amount: Statutory Demand: RM50 issue fee; Bankruptcy Petition: RM600
items.notes: Insolvency Act 1967; requires judgment debt exceeding RM50,000 (threshold as of 2017 amendment)

glossary_terms.definition: The voluntary relinquishment by a creditor of its right to enforce a security interest, whether expressly or by conduct inconsistent with the intention to enforce the security.
glossary_terms.source: Common law; Contracts Act 1950
glossary_terms.example: A bank that writes off a loan and returns the title documents to the chargor without formally discharging the charge may be found to have abandoned its security.

glossary_terms.definition: A term in a loan agreement providing that upon the occurrence of a specified event (e.g., default, bankruptcy, material adverse change), the entire outstanding principal and accrued interest becomes immediately due and payable.
glossary_terms.source: Loan Agreement standard terms; Contracts Act 1950
glossary_terms.example: Upon the borrower failing to make two consecutive monthly repayments, the acceleration clause in the facility letter causes the entire RM500,000 term loan to become immediately due.

glossary_terms.definition: Any of the acts specified in Section 3(1) of the Insolvency Act 1967 which, if committed by a debtor, entitles a creditor to present a bankruptcy petition. The most common act of bankruptcy used in practice is non-compliance with a bankruptcy notice.
glossary_terms.source: Insolvency Act 1967 (Act 360), s. 3(1)
glossary_terms.example: The debtor's failure to comply with a bankruptcy notice within 7 days constitutes an act of bankruptcy under s. 3(1)(i) of the Insolvency Act 1967.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin for 'according to value'. A tax, duty, or fee that is calculated as a percentage of the value of the transaction or property.
glossary_terms.source: Stamp Act 1949 (Act 378); taxation principles
glossary_terms.example: The stamp duty on a memorandum of transfer is ad valorem — 1% on the first RM100,000 of the property value, 2% on the next RM400,000, and 3% on the balance.

glossary_terms.definition: A written statement of facts sworn or affirmed before a person authorized to administer oaths, such as a Commissioner for Oaths or a Magistrate. Used as evidence in civil and criminal proceedings.
glossary_terms.source: Oaths and Affirmations Act 2012 (Act 728); Rules of Court 2012
glossary_terms.example: The bank filed an affidavit sworn by its Credit Recovery Officer exhibiting the loan agreement, statement of account, and pre-action notices to support its Order for Sale application.

glossary_terms.definition: A charge over property that secures all present and future indebtedness of the chargor to the chargee, not limited to a specific loan amount. Common in banking facility structures.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965; Banking practice
glossary_terms.example: The Form 16A charge executed by the borrower was expressed to secure 'all monies owed to the bank from time to time', covering both the term loan and the overdraft facility.

glossary_terms.definition: Now called a 'search order', this is an ex parte court order granted without notice to the respondent, allowing the applicant to enter the respondent's premises and search for, inspect, and seize evidence that might otherwise be destroyed.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29A; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s. 25
glossary_terms.example: The bank obtained an Anton Piller order against a fraudulent borrower to seize forged banking documents before they could be destroyed.

glossary_terms.definition: The act of witnessing the execution of a document and signing it to confirm that it was properly executed. For certain instruments (e.g., Form 16A charges, deeds), attestation by a solicitor is required.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965; Legal requirements for deeds
glossary_terms.example: The solicitor attested the charge (Form 16A) by certifying that the chargor appeared before them, was identified, and executed the document as their free and voluntary act.

glossary_terms.definition: An Islamic financing concept involving the bank purchasing an asset and reselling it to the customer at a higher deferred price, payable in instalments. The difference between the purchase price and the sale price constitutes the bank's profit (not interest).
glossary_terms.source: Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 (Act 759); BNM Shariah Standards
glossary_terms.example: Under the BBA facility, the bank purchased the customer's property at RM300,000 and sold it back to the customer at RM500,000, payable over 20 years at RM2,083 per month.

glossary_terms.definition: A common law right of a bank to retain property of a customer that is lawfully in the bank's possession until the customer's indebtedness is satisfied. The bank need not take formal possession — the lien arises by operation of law.
glossary_terms.source: Common law; Chitty on Contracts; Contracts Act 1950
glossary_terms.example: When the customer deposited share certificates at the bank to secure a loan, the bank acquired a lien over the certificates which it could exercise if the customer defaulted on any facility.

glossary_terms.definition: A purchaser who acquires property in good faith, for adequate consideration, and without notice of any prior adverse claim or defect in title. Such a purchaser is protected by law against prior unregistered interests.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 340; Common law equity
glossary_terms.example: The bank as chargee was a bona fide purchaser for value — it lent money, took a charge in good faith, and had no notice of the earlier unregistered agreement to sell. The bank's registered charge prevailed.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin for 'the effective cause'. In causation, the causa causans is the proximate (direct) cause of the loss or injury, as distinguished from a more remote cause.
glossary_terms.source: Common law tort principles; Evidence Act 1950
glossary_terms.example: In a negligence claim against the bank for a negligent valuation, the causa causans of the loss was the negligent valuation report, not the broader property market decline.

glossary_terms.definition: A legal notice registered against a land title (under s. 322 of the NLC 1965) that prevents any further dealing with the land without the caveator's knowledge and consent. A private caveat lapses after 6 years unless renewed.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, ss. 319-344
glossary_terms.example: The bank lodged a private caveat against the title as equitable mortgagee, preventing the registered owner from registering any transfer or charge without the bank's consent.

glossary_terms.definition: A certificate issued under Section 4 of the Oaths and Affirmations Act 2012 by an officer of the lending institution, certifying the exact amount outstanding under the loan facility. This certificate is prima facie evidence of the amount owed and is required in Order for Sale applications.
glossary_terms.source: Oaths and Affirmations Act 2012 (Act 728), s. 4; Order 83 ROC 2012
glossary_terms.example: The bank's Senior Credit Officer signed a Certificate of Amount Due certifying that as of 30 June 2024, the outstanding sum under the term loan was RM187,456.00 (principal RM150,000, interest RM35,000, charges RM2,456).

glossary_terms.definition: The primary instrument by which security over registered land is created under the National Land Code 1965. A charge is the equivalent of a mortgage in peninsular Malaysia. Upon registration, the chargee (bank) obtains a security interest in the land.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965 (Act 56 of 1965), s. 243; Form 16A
glossary_terms.example: The bank's solicitors prepared and presented Form 16A (the Charge) for registration at the Kuala Lumpur Land Registry, creating a registered first charge over the borrower's property in Damansara.

glossary_terms.definition: The party (typically a bank) in whose favour a charge over property is created. The chargee holds a security interest in the charged property and may enforce it upon the chargor's default.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 243
glossary_terms.example: CIMB Bank Berhad was the chargee under the registered charge over the borrower's Petaling Jaya condominium unit.

glossary_terms.definition: The owner of property who creates a charge over it in favour of a lender as security for a debt. The chargor retains ownership and possession of the property subject to the chargee's security interest.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 243
glossary_terms.example: Ahmad bin Ali was the chargor — as property owner, he charged his land to the bank as security for his RM300,000 term loan.

glossary_terms.definition: Asset or property pledged by a borrower as security for a loan. If the borrower defaults, the lender may seize and sell the collateral to recover the outstanding debt.
glossary_terms.source: Banking and financial practice; Contracts Act 1950
glossary_terms.example: The borrower provided the following collateral for the RM2 million term loan: a registered first charge over the factory land and a debenture over all company assets.

glossary_terms.definition: A judgment entered by the court based on the agreement of both parties to settle the dispute on agreed terms. A consent judgment is enforceable as a court order.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 42 r 5A
glossary_terms.example: The parties entered into a settlement agreement whereby the bank agreed to restructure the loan and the borrower consented to judgment being entered for the outstanding amount, to be paid by agreed instalments.

glossary_terms.definition: A rule of contractual interpretation whereby ambiguous terms in a contract are construed against the party who drafted or proposed them. Banks, as drafters of standard form agreements, bear the risk of ambiguity in their loan agreements.
glossary_terms.source: Common law; Contracts Act 1950; Asia Pacific Higher Learning v Majlis Perubatan Malaysia [2020] 2 MLJ 1
glossary_terms.example: The loan agreement was silent on whether the bank's right to vary the interest rate applied to fixed rate loans. Applying the contra proferentem rule, the ambiguous clause was construed against the bank — the right to vary did not apply to fixed rate loans.
glossary_terms.latinOrigin: Contra proferentem (Latin: against the one who put forward)

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which a floating charge becomes fixed, attaching to specific assets owned by the company at the moment of crystallisation. This occurs upon events prescribed in the debenture (appointment of receiver, winding up, cessation of business) or by operation of law.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777); Hong Leong Finance Bhd v Staghorn Sdn Bhd [2005] 2 MLJ 620
glossary_terms.example: Upon the bank's appointment of a Receiver and Manager over the company's assets under the debenture, the floating charge crystallised and became a fixed charge over all assets then owned by the company.

glossary_terms.definition: A document issued by a company evidencing its indebtedness and granting security over its assets by way of a fixed and floating charge. Under the Companies Act 2016, a debenture must be registered with the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM) within 30 days of creation.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), s. 352; Financial Services Act 2013
glossary_terms.example: The bank required the borrowing company to execute a debenture creating a fixed charge over the company's factory machinery and a floating charge over its current assets, as security for a RM5 million term loan.

glossary_terms.definition: A higher rate of interest charged on outstanding amounts that have not been paid by the due date. The default rate is usually specified in the loan agreement and applies from the date of default until full payment.
glossary_terms.source: Loan agreement standard terms; Consumer Protection Act 1999; BNM Guidelines
glossary_terms.example: Under the term loan agreement, the normal interest rate was 6% p.a. The default interest rate was 8% p.a. on the overdue amount from the date of default.

glossary_terms.definition: A claim by a hire purchase owner or mortgage lender against the debtor for the shortfall between the outstanding debt and the net proceeds of sale of the repossessed or foreclosed asset.
glossary_terms.source: Hire-Purchase Act 1967, s. 20; National Land Code 1965, s. 259
glossary_terms.example: After selling the repossessed vehicle for RM25,000, the outstanding hire purchase balance was RM35,000. The finance company filed a deficiency claim for RM10,000 plus costs.

glossary_terms.definition: The official designated under the Insolvency Act 1967 who administers the estates of bankrupt individuals and wound-up companies. Also known as the Official Assignee in bankruptcy contexts.
glossary_terms.source: Insolvency Act 1967 (Act 360), s. 2 and Part XI; MDTCC Act
glossary_terms.example: Upon the bankruptcy order, the DGI (Jabatan Insolvensi Malaysia) took possession of the bankrupt's assets, including his share in a jointly-owned property, and administered the distribution to creditors.

glossary_terms.definition: The formal instrument by which a chargee (bank) releases its charge over property upon full repayment of the secured debt. The Form 16N must be registered at the Land Registry to remove the charge from the title.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 278; Form 16N
glossary_terms.example: After the borrower repaid the full loan amount of RM200,000, the bank's solicitors prepared Form 16N (Discharge of Charge) which was presented to the Land Registry. The charge notation was removed from the title, and the borrower obtained a clean title.

glossary_terms.definition: Illegitimate pressure applied to a party to a contract, amounting to more than ordinary commercial pressure, which coerces the party into entering a contract or performing an act against their will. Economic duress may vitiate a contract.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, s. 15; Cheah Theam Swee v Equiticorp Finance [1992] 2 MLJ 241
glossary_terms.example: The guarantor argued he signed the personal guarantee under economic duress — the bank had threatened to immediately recall the company's entire banking facilities unless he signed the guarantee within 24 hours.

glossary_terms.definition: The fundamental right of a mortgagor or chargor to redeem (pay off) the mortgage or charge and recover the property free from the lender's security interest, at any time before the security is sold or enforced. Courts protect this right against 'clogs'.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965; Equity principles; Common law
glossary_terms.example: The chargor exercised his equity of redemption by paying the full outstanding sum of RM456,789 to the bank on the day before the auction. The bank's Order for Sale became academic.

glossary_terms.definition: A defined event or circumstance in a loan or security agreement, the occurrence of which entitles the lender to accelerate the loan, enforce security, and/or take other remedial action. Common events of default include payment default, breach of covenant, insolvency, cross-default, and material adverse change.
glossary_terms.source: Standard banking facility terms; Contracts Act 1950; Boustead Holdings v Arab Malaysian Merchant Bank [1995]
glossary_terms.example: The following constituted Events of Default under the facility agreement: failure to pay any instalment within 7 days of the due date; the borrower being wound up or declaring insolvency; breach of any financial covenant.

glossary_terms.definition: Proceedings conducted with only one party present, without notice to the other party. Ex parte orders are typically interlocutory (e.g., Mareva injunction, Anton Piller order) and are subject to a duty of full and frank disclosure by the applicant.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012; Common law
glossary_terms.example: The bank applied ex parte for a Mareva injunction to freeze the defendant's bank accounts before the defendant could dissipate his assets. The judge granted the order without hearing the defendant.

glossary_terms.definition: The primary Malaysian legislation (Act 758) governing conventional banks, insurance companies, investment banks, operators of payment systems, and money brokers. It replaced the Banking and Financial Institutions Act 1989 and several other statutes. Administered by Bank Negara Malaysia.
glossary_terms.source: Financial Services Act 2013 (Act 758)
glossary_terms.example: Under Section 11 of the FSA 2013, no person may carry on a banking business, investment banking business, or any other regulated financial business without a valid licence from BNM.

glossary_terms.definition: A security interest over specific, identified assets of a company that prevents the company from disposing of those assets without the chargee's consent. A fixed charge gives the holder priority over the proceeds of sale of the charged assets.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777); Debenture terms
glossary_terms.example: The debenture created a fixed charge over the company's factory land, buildings, and plant and machinery — the company could not sell or dispose of these assets without the bank's prior written consent.

glossary_terms.definition: A security interest that 'floats' over a class of assets of a company (e.g., current assets, book debts) and does not attach to specific assets until it crystallises. The company is free to deal with the assets in the ordinary course of business until crystallisation.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), s. 352; Debenture terms
glossary_terms.example: The floating charge in the debenture covered the company's stock-in-trade, book debts, and cash at bank — assets that change daily in the ordinary course of business.

glossary_terms.definition: The legal process by which a mortgagee/chargee enforces its security over charged property by obtaining a court order for sale and selling the property to recover the outstanding debt. In Malaysia, conducted under Order 83 ROC 2012 and ss. 254-259 NLC 1965.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, ss. 254-259; Rules of Court 2012, Order 83
glossary_terms.example: After the borrower defaulted on 12 consecutive monthly instalments, the bank commenced foreclosure proceedings by serving Form 16C and Form 16D and subsequently filing an Originating Summons for Order for Sale in the High Court.

glossary_terms.definition: The obligation of an applicant in an ex parte application to disclose to the court all material facts, including those that may be adverse to the applicant's case. Failure to make full and frank disclosure may result in discharge of any order obtained.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Common law; Standard Chartered Bank v City Properties [1997] 3 MLJ 488
glossary_terms.example: When applying ex parte for a Mareva injunction, the bank's solicitors disclosed to the court that the defendant had offered to pay part of the debt, even though this weakened the case for an injunction — this was a requirement of full and frank disclosure.

glossary_terms.definition: A third party (usually a bank) who is indebted to the judgment debtor and against whom a garnishee order is made, requiring payment of the judgment debtor's funds to the judgment creditor.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 49
glossary_terms.example: Upon obtaining a judgment against the debtor, the bank applied for a garnishee order nisi against the debtor's other bank (Maybank), which held RM50,000 in the debtor's savings account. Maybank was the garnishee.

glossary_terms.definition: A court order requiring a third party (garnishee) who owes money to the judgment debtor to pay that money directly to the judgment creditor in satisfaction of a judgment debt. It proceeds in two stages: order nisi (interim) and order absolute (final).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 49
glossary_terms.example: The bank obtained a garnishee order absolute against the judgment debtor's insurance company, requiring it to pay the debtor's matured insurance policy proceeds of RM80,000 directly to the bank in partial satisfaction of the RM200,000 judgment debt.

glossary_terms.definition: A person who agrees to be secondarily liable for another person's debt — i.e., to pay the debt if the principal debtor defaults. A guarantee must be in writing and signed by the guarantor under s. 82 of the Contracts Act 1950.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), ss. 79-102
glossary_terms.example: Ah Kow signed as guarantor for his company's RM1 million term loan from the bank. When the company defaulted, the bank demanded payment from Ah Kow under the guarantee.

glossary_terms.definition: An Arabic/Shariah term meaning 'rebate' or 'acquittance'. In Islamic banking, ibra' refers to the bank's waiver of its right to collect the outstanding unearned profit upon early settlement of a financing facility. Since 2011, BNM's Shariah Standard makes ibra' mandatory for Islamic banks.
glossary_terms.source: BNM Shariah Standard on Ibra' (2011); Islamic Financial Services Act 2013; Arab-Malaysian Finance v Taman Ihsan Jaya [2008]
glossary_terms.example: When Ahmad settled his BBA home financing 5 years early, the bank granted ibra' by waiving RM45,000 of the remaining profit element. Ahmad only paid the cost price portion remaining.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin for 'in equal fault'. A legal principle that a court will not assist either party to an illegal contract — both parties are equally at fault and neither may recover from the other.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, s. 24; Common law
glossary_terms.example: Both the borrower and the bank knowingly structured the loan to evade a regulatory restriction. When the loan went bad and the borrower refused to repay, the court applied in pari delicto and refused to enforce the illegal loan agreement.
glossary_terms.latinOrigin: In pari delicto (Latin: in equal fault)

glossary_terms.definition: The principle under Section 340 of the National Land Code 1965 that once a dealing with registered land is registered, the title of the registered proprietor is indefeasible (cannot be challenged) except in specified circumstances (fraud by the registered proprietor, insufficient consideration, etc.).
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 340; Adorna Properties v Kobchai [2005] 1 MLJ 586; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010]
glossary_terms.example: The bank registered its charge over the property in good faith and for valuable consideration (the loan advanced). Its registered charge was indefeasible under s. 340 NLC even if the chargor later claimed the charge was obtained by a fraudulent third party.

glossary_terms.definition: Legal proceedings conducted with all parties present and heard, as opposed to ex parte proceedings. An inter partes hearing gives the respondent/defendant an opportunity to be heard before an order is made.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012; Principles of natural justice
glossary_terms.example: After an ex parte Mareva injunction was granted, the parties appeared at the inter partes hearing where the defendant challenged the injunction and sought its discharge.

glossary_terms.definition: The Malaysian legislation (Act 759) governing Islamic banks, Islamic insurance (takaful) companies, international Islamic banks, and international takaful operators. IFSA 2013 requires compliance with Shariah principles in all products and activities. Administered by Bank Negara Malaysia.
glossary_terms.source: Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 (Act 759)
glossary_terms.example: Under the IFSA 2013, Islamic banks must establish a Shariah Committee to ensure all their products, services, and operations comply with Shariah principles as determined by the SAC.

glossary_terms.definition: A judgment entered by the court against a defendant who fails to enter an appearance or file a defence within the prescribed time. No hearing on the merits is required. Common in banking recovery cases where the debtor ignores court proceedings.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Orders 13 and 19
glossary_terms.example: The bank obtained judgment in default of appearance against the borrower after he failed to enter appearance within 7 days of service of the writ. Judgment was entered for RM150,000 plus interest and costs.

glossary_terms.definition: The government officer appointed under the National Land Code 1965 to administer land matters in a district. In foreclosure proceedings, the Land Administrator conducts the public auction of charged land under Section 256 of the NLC.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, ss. 5 and 256; Land (Group Settlement Areas) Act 1960
glossary_terms.example: The Land Administrator for Kuala Lumpur fixed the auction date for the charged property as 15 October 2024 at the Land Office. The Proclamation of Sale was published in two newspapers.

glossary_terms.definition: A right of a creditor to retain possession of the debtor's property as security for a debt, until the debt is satisfied. Unlike a pledge, the lienholder need not have physical possession at all times. A banker's lien arises by operation of law.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, ss. 170-172; Common law
glossary_terms.example: The bank exercised its lien over the customer's fixed deposit account as set-off against the customer's overdue loan, retaining the FD proceeds until the loan was settled.

glossary_terms.definition: A pre-agreed, fixed sum payable upon breach of contract, specified in the contract itself. Unlike unliquidated damages (assessed by the court), liquidated damages are recoverable without proof of actual loss, provided they are a genuine pre-estimate of loss (not a penalty).
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, s. 75; Common law
glossary_terms.example: The loan agreement included a liquidated damages clause providing that on default, the borrower would pay a sum equivalent to 2 months' interest as liquidated damages for the cost of early termination.

glossary_terms.definition: A freezing order granted by the court restraining a defendant from dealing with or disposing of their assets before judgment is obtained, to prevent dissipation. The applicant must show a good arguable case and a real risk of asset dissipation.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s. 25; Ayer Molek Rubber Co v Insas [1995] 2 MLJ 11
glossary_terms.example: The bank obtained a Mareva injunction freezing the defendant-borrower's bank accounts and real property, after discovering that the borrower was in the process of transferring assets overseas.

glossary_terms.definition: The prescribed instrument (Form 14A under NLC 1965) used to transfer ownership of registered land from one person to another. Stamp duty and registration fees are payable. A MOT obtained pursuant to a foreclosure auction is prepared by the Land Administrator.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 215; Form 14A
glossary_terms.example: After the successful bidder paid the full auction price for the foreclosed property, the Land Administrator issued a Memorandum of Transfer in favour of the bidder. Stamp duty on the MOT was based on the auction price.

glossary_terms.definition: A legally authorized delay in the payment of debts, or a period during which certain legal actions are suspended. In insolvency law, a moratorium prevents creditors from commencing or continuing proceedings against the debtor/company without court leave.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), s. 471; Insolvency Act 1967, s. 46
glossary_terms.example: Upon the winding up order being made against ABC Sdn Bhd, a moratorium automatically took effect — all creditors seeking to enforce judgment debts against the company required court leave under s. 471 of the Companies Act 2016.

glossary_terms.definition: In English law, the lender who holds a mortgage (security) over a borrower's property. In Malaysian land law under the NLC, the equivalent term is 'chargee' — the party in whose favour a charge (Form 16A) is registered.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965; Common law mortgage principles
glossary_terms.example: While the NLC uses the term 'chargee', in practice, Malaysian solicitors and bankers often use 'mortgagee' informally to refer to the bank holding a registered charge over the borrower's property.

glossary_terms.definition: An Islamic financing mode where the bank purchases an asset and sells it to the customer at a pre-agreed profit margin (cost + profit), with the customer paying the total price on a deferred basis. The bank discloses its cost price and profit margin to the customer.
glossary_terms.source: Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 (Act 759); BNM Shariah Standards on Murabahah
glossary_terms.example: Under the murabahah trade financing facility, the bank purchased raw materials costing RM100,000 and sold them to the manufacturer at RM115,000, payable in 90 days. The RM15,000 difference was the bank's profit.

glossary_terms.definition: The primary legislation (Act 56 of 1965) governing land tenure, administration, and registration in Peninsular Malaysia and the Federal Territory. The NLC establishes the Torrens System of registration and governs charges, transfers, caveats, and other land dealings.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965 (Act 56 of 1965)
glossary_terms.example: All banking security over land in Peninsular Malaysia is governed by the NLC. The NLC prescribes the forms for creating a charge (Form 16A), giving pre-foreclosure notices (Forms 16C and 16D), and discharging the charge (Form 16N).

glossary_terms.definition: A covenant in a loan agreement or debenture by which the borrower promises not to create any security interest over its assets in favour of any other creditor, without the lender's prior consent.
glossary_terms.source: Standard debenture terms; Contracts Act 1950; Common law
glossary_terms.example: The debenture contained a negative pledge clause prohibiting the borrower from charging, mortgaging, or creating any lien over its assets in favour of any other creditor without CIMB Bank's prior written consent.

glossary_terms.definition: A defence meaning 'it is not my deed'. A person who signs a document under a fundamental mistake as to the nature of the document (not merely its contents) may plead non est factum to avoid the document.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950; Common law; Saunders v Anglia Building Society [1971] AC 1004
glossary_terms.example: The elderly guarantor who was blind signed what she was told was a simple receipt document but was actually a guarantee for RM500,000. She successfully pleaded non est factum as she had no idea she was signing a guarantee.
glossary_terms.latinOrigin: Non est factum (Latin: it is not his/her deed)

glossary_terms.definition: In winding up proceedings, the Official Receiver is the officer of the court appointed as provisional liquidator upon the making of a winding up order, until a licensed insolvency practitioner is appointed as liquidator by the creditors.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), s. 471; Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972
glossary_terms.example: Upon the court making the winding up order against XYZ Sdn Bhd, the Official Receiver was appointed provisional liquidator. The Official Receiver called a creditors' meeting within 3 months to appoint a licensed liquidator.

glossary_terms.definition: A court order made under Section 256 of the NLC 1965 and Order 83 of the ROC 2012, directing the Land Administrator to sell charged land by public auction to satisfy the outstanding secured debt.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 256; Rules of Court 2012, Order 83
glossary_terms.example: The High Court granted an Order for Sale in favour of the chargee bank, specifying a reserved price of RM350,000 for the chargor's residential property, and directing the Kuala Lumpur Land Administrator to fix a date for the public auction.

glossary_terms.definition: A court process under Order 7 of the ROC 2012, used to commence legal proceedings where the primary questions are of law or the facts are not substantially in dispute. In banking litigation, it is used for Order for Sale applications (Order 83) and certain Originating Summons applications.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 7
glossary_terms.example: The bank filed an Originating Summons in the High Court (Shah Alam) for an Order for Sale of the chargor's property in Subang Jaya, supported by an affidavit and exhibits.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin for 'on an equal footing'. In insolvency law, the pari passu rule provides that unsecured creditors share equally in the assets available for distribution — no one unsecured creditor has priority over another.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777); Insolvency Act 1967
glossary_terms.example: After the bank (as secured creditor) received payment from the sale of the charged property, the remaining assets of the wound-up company were distributed pari passu among the unsecured trade creditors.
glossary_terms.latinOrigin: Pari passu (Latin: on an equal footing)

glossary_terms.definition: A bailment of personal property as security for a debt, with the creditor taking actual possession of the pledged asset. Unlike a lien, the pledgor (debtor) retains ownership but surrenders possession to the pledgee (creditor) until the debt is discharged.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), ss. 170-179
glossary_terms.example: The jeweller pledged his gold inventory (worth RM200,000) with the bank as security for a RM150,000 short-term working capital loan. The bank held physical possession of the gold in its vault.

glossary_terms.definition: The public notice issued by the Land Administrator advertising the sale of charged land by public auction. The Proclamation must be published in two Malaysian newspapers (one Bahasa Malaysia, one English) and posted at the Land Office. It specifies the date, time, reserved price, and conditions of sale.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 256; Land Administrator's auction rules
glossary_terms.example: The Proclamation of Sale was published in the New Straits Times and Utusan Malaysia on 1 September 2024, advertising the public auction of Lot 5678, Mukim Petaling, Kuala Lumpur (a terrace house) with a reserved price of RM420,000.

glossary_terms.definition: A document filed by a creditor in bankruptcy or winding up proceedings, proving the amount of the debt owed to them. The liquidator or Official Assignee adjudicates on the proof and admits or rejects it.
glossary_terms.source: Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972, r. 78; Insolvency Act 1967, s. 93
glossary_terms.example: The bank filed its Proof of Debt (Form 78) with the liquidator of the wound-up company, claiming RM3.5 million in outstanding term loan principal, interest, and legal costs, supported by the loan agreement and statement of account.

glossary_terms.definition: A person appointed (under a debenture or court order) to take control of a company's business and assets, manage the company's affairs, and realise its assets to repay the appointing chargee. Must be a licensed insolvency practitioner under the Companies Act 2016.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), Part IV, Division 8; Hong Leong Finance v Staghorn [2005]
glossary_terms.example: Upon the company's default under the debenture, AmBank appointed Encik Ali as Receiver and Manager of Daylight Construction Sdn Bhd. Ali immediately secured all bank accounts, inventories, and equipment, and began realising assets.

glossary_terms.definition: The minimum price below which the Land Administrator will not sell charged land at a public auction. The reserved price must reflect the current market value of the property, as evidenced by an independent valuation report.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965; Rules of Court 2012, Order 83; Perwira Affin Bank v Sardar Mohamed Hanif [2010]
glossary_terms.example: Based on the valuation report dated 15 August 2024, the bank proposed a reserved price of RM750,000 for the 3-storey shophouse. The court approved the reserved price in the Order for Sale.

glossary_terms.definition: The right of a guarantor (surety), upon paying the creditor, to stand in the creditor's shoes and exercise all rights the creditor had against the principal debtor, including enforcement of security.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, s. 92; Common law
glossary_terms.example: After paying RM200,000 to the bank under the guarantee, the guarantor exercised his right of subrogation — he was entitled to step into the bank's position and pursue the principal debtor for RM200,000, as well as enforce the bank's charge over the debtor's property.

glossary_terms.definition: The highest Shariah authority in Malaysia for Islamic finance matters, established under Section 52 of the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009. The SAC's rulings are binding on all courts and arbitrators in Islamic financial disputes (Section 57 CBA 2009).
glossary_terms.source: Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 (Act 701), ss. 52-58; Islamic Financial Services Act 2013
glossary_terms.example: The court referred the question of whether a specific Tawarruq structure was Shariah-compliant to the SAC. The SAC's ruling that the structure was permissible was binding on the court under s. 57 of the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009.

glossary_terms.definition: A tax imposed by the Stamp Act 1949 on specified instruments and documents. Key stamps in banking: 0.5% on loan agreements/charges, 1%-3% on memoranda of transfer (property), RM10 per RM1,000 on guarantees.
glossary_terms.source: Stamp Act 1949 (Act 378)
glossary_terms.example: The stamp duty on a RM500,000 housing loan was RM2,500 (0.5%), payable before presentation of the charge for registration at the Land Registry.

glossary_terms.definition: A formal written demand served on a company (under s. 466(1)(a) Companies Act 2016) or individual (under s. 3(1)(i) Insolvency Act 1967) requiring payment of the outstanding debt within a prescribed period (21 days for companies; 7 days for individuals — bankruptcy notice), failure of which constitutes grounds for winding up/bankruptcy.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016, s. 466; Insolvency Act 1967, s. 3(1)(i)
glossary_terms.example: The bank's solicitors served a statutory demand on the company's registered office, demanding payment of RM350,000 within 21 days. The company failed to pay and did not apply to set aside the demand.

glossary_terms.definition: The substitution of one party for another in respect of a claim or right. In insurance, when an insurer pays a claim, it is subrogated to the insured's rights against any third party responsible for the loss. In suretyship, a paying guarantor is subrogated to the creditor's rights.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, s. 92; Insurance law principles
glossary_terms.example: The bank's insurance company paid the fire insurance claim for the damaged factory. The insurer was then subrogated to the bank's rights and pursued the contractor whose negligence caused the fire.

glossary_terms.definition: A procedure under Order 14 of the ROC 2012 by which a plaintiff may obtain judgment without a trial, where the defendant's defence raises no genuine (bona fide) triable issue. Banks use this extensively in loan recovery cases.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 14
glossary_terms.example: The bank filed an Order 14 application for summary judgment supported by the loan agreement, statement of account, and demand letter. The court found the borrower's defence (that he never received the loan proceeds) was a sham and granted judgment for RM650,000.

glossary_terms.definition: A person (natural or legal) who undertakes secondary liability for another's debt by way of a guarantee. If the principal debtor defaults, the creditor may call on the surety to pay. 'Surety' and 'guarantor' are often used interchangeably.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, ss. 79-102
glossary_terms.example: Ibrahim acted as surety for his brother's company's bank loan. When the company failed to pay, the bank successfully sued Ibrahim as surety for the full outstanding amount of RM1.2 million.

glossary_terms.definition: A doctrine in equity by which a court may refuse to enforce a contract or order that is oppressive, grossly unfair, or involves unconscionable conduct — particularly where there is inequality of bargaining power, exploitation of vulnerability, or sharp practice.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, s. 24C (amendment); Equity principles; Tenaga Nasional v Duta Expressway [2003]
glossary_terms.example: The court refused to enforce a first demand performance bond where the beneficiary was attempting to call on it in circumstances that were clearly unconscionable — the call was made in bad faith and bore no relation to any actual breach.

glossary_terms.definition: An undertaking given by an applicant for an interlocutory injunction to compensate the respondent for any loss suffered if the injunction is later found to have been wrongly granted. It is a condition precedent to the grant of an ex parte injunction.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Common law
glossary_terms.example: Before granting the Mareva injunction, the court required the bank to give an undertaking in damages — promising to compensate the defendant if the injunction was later found to be unwarranted and had caused the defendant financial loss.

glossary_terms.definition: Influence exercised by one party over another to the extent that the latter's free will is overcome, resulting in a transaction that does not represent that party's free and voluntary choice. Undue influence may render a contract voidable.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, ss. 16-17; Arab-Malaysian Finance v Steven Phoa [2003] 1 MLJ 567
glossary_terms.example: The guarantor's wife demonstrated that she signed the guarantee under her husband's undue influence — he had pressured and threatened her over several days until she relented. The court set aside the guarantee.

glossary_terms.definition: A change to the terms of an existing contract agreed to by both parties. In guarantee law, a material variation of the principal contract without the guarantor's consent discharges the guarantor under s. 86 of the Contracts Act 1950.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950, ss. 62 and 86; Malaysia Discounts v Pesaka Astana [2008] 1 MLJ 214
glossary_terms.example: The bank unilaterally extended the loan tenure from 5 to 7 years and changed the interest rate without informing the guarantor. The Court held this was a material variation which discharged the guarantor under s. 86 of the Contracts Act 1950.

glossary_terms.definition: A contract that is valid and enforceable unless the innocent party elects to avoid it. A contract may be voidable for undue influence, misrepresentation, duress, or non est factum. The innocent party must elect to avoid within a reasonable time and restore the parties to their original position.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s. 19
glossary_terms.example: The guarantee was voidable (not void) for undue influence — it remained valid until the guarantor positively elected to avoid it by applying to court to set it aside. If he did not act promptly, the right to avoid may be lost.

glossary_terms.definition: The legal process of bringing a company's existence to an end by distributing its assets to creditors and, if any surplus remains, to contributories. May be voluntary (members' or creditors') or compulsory (court-ordered).
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), Part IV, Division 2; Companies (Winding Up) Rules 1972
glossary_terms.example: After unsuccessfully attempting to recover RM2 million from the company by garnishee and execution proceedings, the bank filed a winding up petition and the court made a winding up order against ABC Manufacturing Sdn Bhd.

glossary_terms.definition: A court order (execution process) under Order 45 of the ROC 2012 directing the bailiff to seize and sell the judgment debtor's movable and immovable property to satisfy an unpaid judgment debt.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 45
glossary_terms.example: After obtaining judgment for RM80,000, the bank filed a Writ of Seizure and Sale. The court bailiff attended the debtor's business premises and seized the company's delivery vehicles, which were subsequently sold at public auction for RM55,000.

glossary_terms.definition: The originating process in High Court or Sessions Court civil litigation under Order 6 of the ROC 2012, by which civil proceedings are commenced. It is served on the defendant who must enter an appearance within the prescribed time.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 6
glossary_terms.example: The bank's solicitors filed a Writ of Summons against the borrower and guarantor in the High Court for recovery of RM1,200,000 outstanding under a term loan facility.

glossary_terms.definition: Note: Malaysia abolished the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in 2018 and replaced it with the Sales and Service Tax (SST). Legal services are subject to 8% SST (from 2024) while certain instruments are exempt or zero-rated.
glossary_terms.source: Sales and Service Tax (SST) Act 2018; Customs Act 1967
glossary_terms.example: Legal services in banking transactions (loan documentation, conveyancing) are subject to 8% SST from 1 March 2024. Stamp duty is separate from SST and is governed solely by the Stamp Act 1949.

glossary_terms.definition: A prerogative remedy (now called a 'Quashing Order' in some jurisdictions) available in judicial review proceedings. It quashes a decision of an inferior court, tribunal, or public authority that was made illegally, irrationally, or in breach of natural justice.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53, r.2
glossary_terms.example: The High Court granted certiorari to quash the Industrial Court's award, finding that the Industrial Court had acted outside its jurisdiction by determining an issue not referred to it by the Director General of Industrial Relations.

glossary_terms.definition: A situation where an employee is forced to resign because the employer's conduct amounts to a fundamental breach of the employment contract. The employee's resignation is treated as a dismissal. Claimable under s.20 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967.
glossary_terms.source: Industrial Relations Act 1967 (Act 177), s.20; Quah Swee Khoon v Sime Darby Bhd [2000] 2 MLJ 600
glossary_terms.example: Siti was a manager earning RM15,000/month. Her employer unilaterally reduced her salary to RM8,000 and changed her job scope to clerical work without consent. She resigned and filed a constructive dismissal complaint with the Industrial Relations Department.

glossary_terms.definition: A conditional order of divorce pronounced by a court under s.51 of the Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976. The marriage is not yet dissolved. It becomes absolute after 3 months (unless the court orders otherwise). Ancillary orders (custody, maintenance, division of assets) are usually made at or after the decree nisi stage.
glossary_terms.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 (Act 164), ss.51, 55
glossary_terms.example: The court pronounced a Decree Nisi on 1 March 2025. The parties were still married. Three months later (on 1 June 2025), the petitioner applied for and obtained the Decree Absolute — the marriage was then formally dissolved.
glossary_terms.latinOrigin: Decree Nisi — Latin: 'unless' (the decree unless cause is shown to the contrary)

glossary_terms.definition: An internal inquiry conducted by an employer before dismissing an employee for misconduct. While not expressly mandated by statute, domestic inquiries are required as a matter of natural justice before an employee can be dismissed for misconduct. The DI must comply with the rules of natural justice: (1) adequate notice of the specific charges; (2) opportunity to be heard and to call witnesses; (3) impartial panel.
glossary_terms.source: Industrial Relations Act 1967; Dreamland Corporation (M) Sdn Bhd v Choong Chin Sooi [1988] 1 MLJ 111
glossary_terms.example: Ahmad was charged with misappropriating company petty cash. Before dismissal, the employer served a Notice of Charge, held a domestic inquiry where Ahmad was allowed to present his case, and only after the panel found him guilty was he dismissed.

glossary_terms.definition: A legal doctrine under s.57(2) of the Contracts Act 1950 whereby a contract becomes void if, after it is made, its performance becomes impossible or unlawful due to an event not within the parties' contemplation or control. The supervening event must make performance radically different from what was contracted for — mere hardship or increased cost is insufficient.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s.57(2); Guan Aik Moh (KL) Sdn Bhd v Selangor Properties Bhd [2007] 4 CLJ 427
glossary_terms.example: A concert promoter contracted to hire a venue. One week before the concert, the government issued a public health emergency order prohibiting all public gatherings. The contract was frustrated under s.57(2) — performance became unlawful, not merely inconvenient.

glossary_terms.definition: The principle under s.340 of the National Land Code 1965, as confirmed by the Federal Court in Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1, that a person who registers as a proprietor of land in good faith and for valuable consideration acquires an indefeasible title immediately upon registration — even if the instrument of transfer was obtained by fraud, forgery, or illegality affecting an earlier party in the chain.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965 (Act 56), s.340; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 FC
glossary_terms.example: A fraudster forged the landowner's signature and transferred the land to an innocent purchaser (James) who paid market value and registered the transfer. Even though the original transfer was forged, James's registered title is immediately indefeasible. The original landowner cannot recover the land from James — only a personal remedy in damages against the fraudster.

glossary_terms.definition: A corporate rescue mechanism under ss.403-430 of the Companies Act 2016 where an insolvent or potentially insolvent company is placed under the management of an independent judicial manager (a licensed insolvency practitioner) appointed by the court. During judicial management, there is a moratorium on legal proceedings and enforcement actions against the company, allowing time for a viable restructuring plan to be formulated and implemented.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), ss.403-430
glossary_terms.example: MegaCorp Sdn Bhd, an engineering company, became unable to service its RM80 million in bank loans due to cash flow difficulties. Its major shareholder applied for a judicial management order. The court appointed a judicial manager who negotiated a debt restructuring with creditors and returned the company to profitability within 18 months.

glossary_terms.definition: A public law principle in administrative law whereby a person who has been given a clear and unambiguous promise or established practice by a public authority may have a legitimate expectation that the promise or practice will be honoured. If the authority seeks to depart from it, the affected person must at minimum be given an opportunity to be heard (procedural legitimate expectation).
glossary_terms.source: Common law administrative law; adopted in Malaysia — Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim v Timbalan Perdana Menteri Malaysia [1992] 2 MLJ 23
glossary_terms.example: An applicant had followed a published government policy for 10 years when applying for an import licence. The government changed the policy without notice and rejected his application. He had a legitimate expectation that the published policy would be applied and was entitled to be heard before the policy was changed to his detriment.

glossary_terms.term: CIPAA (Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012)
glossary_terms.definition: A Malaysian statute (Act 746) that provides a fast-track statutory adjudication mechanism for resolution of payment disputes in the construction industry. CIPAA operates on a 'pay now, argue later' philosophy — an adjudication decision is interim binding and must be paid even if challenged, pending final resolution in arbitration or litigation.
glossary_terms.source: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012 (Act 746)
glossary_terms.example: A sub-contractor is owed RM500,000 for work done. The main contractor disputes RM200,000. The sub-contractor serves a Payment Claim under CIPAA. After adjudication, the adjudicator awards RM450,000. The main contractor must pay RM450,000 within 14 days and, if still disputing, must separately commence arbitration to recover any overpayment.

glossary_terms.definition: Under s.346 of the Companies Act 2016, a shareholder may petition the court for relief where the company's affairs are being conducted, or the powers of the directors are being exercised, in a manner oppressive to one or more of the shareholders. The test is whether the conduct is commercially unfair, not merely whether it is technically lawful.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), s.346; Re Kong Thai Sawmill (Miri) Sdn Bhd [1978] 2 MLJ 227; Sinnaiyah & Sons v Damai Setia [2015] 5 MLJ 1 FC
glossary_terms.example: Alex holds 40% of Company A. The majority shareholder (60%) diverts all company contracts to his own competing business, refuses to declare dividends, and removes Alex as director. Alex petitions under s.346 CA 2016 and the court orders the majority to buy out Alex's shares at fair value without minority discount.

glossary_terms.definition: The legal and mental capacity required to make a valid will. Under Malaysian law (applying the test from Banks v Goodfellow [1870]), the testator must: (1) understand the nature of making a will and its effects; (2) understand the extent of the property being disposed of; (3) comprehend the claims of persons who might expect to benefit; and (4) not be suffering from any disorder of the mind that affects the making of the will.
glossary_terms.source: Wills Act 1959 (Act 346); Banks v Goodfellow (1870) LR 5 QB 549 (applied in Malaysia)
glossary_terms.example: A 92-year-old testator made a will leaving his entire estate to a neighbour, cutting out his children. The children challenged the will on the ground that the testator was suffering from advanced dementia at the time of making the will. Medical records and expert psychiatric evidence were crucial in determining whether testamentary capacity existed.

glossary_terms.definition: A defence in tort law where the defendant proves that the plaintiff's own negligence contributed to the damage suffered. Under s.12 of the Civil Law Act 1956, the plaintiff's damages are reduced proportionately to the degree of their own negligence — the court apportions fault. Unlike the common law rule, contributory negligence does not completely defeat the plaintiff's claim in Malaysia.
glossary_terms.source: Civil Law Act 1956 (Act 67), s.12
glossary_terms.example: A motorcyclist was hit by a car that jumped a red light. However, the motorcyclist was also found to have been travelling at excessive speed. The court found 70% fault with the car driver and 30% with the motorcyclist. The total damages of RM200,000 were reduced by 30% — the motorcyclist was awarded RM140,000.

glossary_terms.definition: Property owned by either or both spouses that is subject to division by the court upon divorce under s.76 of the Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976. The court has a wide discretion and considers: the duration of the marriage, contributions of each party (financial and non-financial, including homemaking), and the needs of the parties.
glossary_terms.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 (Act 164), s.76
glossary_terms.example: After a 20-year marriage, the matrimonial home (RM800,000) and savings (RM200,000) were subject to division. The wife had worked throughout the marriage and also managed the household. The court ordered a 50-50 split of the matrimonial home and gave 60% of the savings to the wife, recognising her dual contribution.

glossary_terms.definition: A common law tort protecting unregistered trade marks and business goodwill. A claimant must prove: (1) goodwill or reputation attached to the goods or services; (2) a misrepresentation by the defendant (deliberately or innocently) likely to cause confusion; and (3) damage suffered or likely to be suffered as a result. The Jif Lemon test from Reckitt & Colman v Borden [1990] is widely applied.
glossary_terms.source: Common law; adopted in Malaysia under Civil Law Act 1956 (s.3); Trade Marks Act 2019 (s.2 for common law rights)
glossary_terms.example: A new restaurant began trading as 'Old Town Coffee' in the same vicinity as the famous 'OldTown White Coffee' chain. The chain brought a passing off action, proving goodwill in their name, the new restaurant's misrepresentation that it was associated with them, and actual loss of customers.

glossary_terms.definition: The cornerstone of the Malaysian Torrens system of land registration. Once a person is registered as the proprietor of land, their title is generally indefeasible (unassailable) and cannot be impeached except on the grounds specified in s.340 of the National Land Code 1965 (fraud, misrepresentation, insufficient consideration, or unlawful purpose affecting the registered proprietor directly).
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965 (Act 56), s.340; Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Kobchai Sosothikul [2005] 1 MLJ 586; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 FC
glossary_terms.example: A developer registers a transfer of land duly stamped and presented in proper form. Even if the underlying sale agreement is later found to be defective (e.g., for failure of a condition), the registered proprietor's title remains indefeasible unless the specific exceptions in s.340 NLC are made out.

glossary_terms.definition: A genuine pre-estimate of the loss likely to be suffered in the event of a specified breach of contract, agreed by the parties at the time of contracting and stipulated in the contract itself. In Malaysian construction contracts, LAD is typically expressed as a daily or weekly rate applicable from the agreed completion date until practical completion. LAD clauses are enforceable; penalty clauses (which are penal rather than compensatory) may not be.
glossary_terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s.75; Housing Development (Control and Licensing) Act 1966
glossary_terms.example: A property developer contracted to complete a housing unit by 30 June 2023. The SPA specified LAD at RM200 per day for late delivery. The developer only completed the unit on 31 December 2023 — 184 days late. The purchaser is entitled to claim LAD of RM200 × 184 = RM36,800.

glossary_terms.definition: A court action brought by a member (shareholder) of a company on behalf of the company where those in control of the company refuse to act to enforce the company's own rights. Leave of court is required under s.347 of the Companies Act 2016. The member must show: a prima facie case of wrong done to the company, those in control are unwilling to act, and the action is in the best interests of the company.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), s.347
glossary_terms.example: ABC Sdn Bhd's majority director misappropriated RM1 million of company funds. The company (controlled by the same director) refused to sue him. A minority shareholder applied for leave under s.347 CA 2016 to bring a derivative action on behalf of the company to recover the RM1 million.

glossary_terms.definition: A court order under s.256 of the National Land Code 1965 or Order 83 of the Rules of Court 2012 directing the sale of charged land to satisfy an outstanding loan debt. Chargees (banks) may apply for an order for sale when a chargor defaults on the secured loan. The land is sold by public auction and the proceeds are applied to discharge the debt.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965 (Act 56), s.256; Rules of Court 2012, Order 83
glossary_terms.example: A housing loan borrower defaulted on 12 consecutive monthly instalments. The bank served a Form 16C notice of demand and Form 16D notice of intended application. After waiting 1 month, the bank filed an Originating Summons under Order 83 ROC 2012 for an Order for Sale of the charged property.

glossary_terms.definition: Any application made to the court between commencement of the action and final judgment which does not finally dispose of the substantive rights of the parties. Includes applications for summary judgment, striking out, discovery, amendment of pleadings, interim injunctions, security for costs, and procedural directions. Heard in chambers before a Judge or Senior Assistant Registrar (SAR).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 32; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.68
glossary_terms.example: After the Defendant entered appearance, the Plaintiff filed an interlocutory application by way of Notice of Application (Form 57) for summary judgment under Order 14 of the Rules of Court 2012, supported by an Affidavit of the Plaintiff's recovery officer.

glossary_terms.definition: A court order which is temporary in nature, designed to preserve the status quo, protect rights, or hold the ring pending the full hearing of the dispute. Includes interim injunctions (prohibitory and mandatory), Mareva (freezing) orders, Anton Piller (search) orders, interim payment orders, and orders for preservation, detention, custody, or sale of property pending trial.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Specific Relief Act 1950, ss.50–55; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.25(2) & Schedule
glossary_terms.example: The Court granted an interim prohibitory injunction restraining the former employee from soliciting the Plaintiff company's clients pending the trial of the breach of restrictive covenant action.

glossary_terms.definition: An application made to the court in private session (not open court), heard before a Judge in Chambers or a Senior Assistant Registrar (SAR). Under Order 32 r 1 of the Rules of Court 2012, every application in chambers shall be made by Notice of Application (Form 57) supported by an Affidavit (Form 65). Chamber proceedings are informal — counsel make oral submissions, evidence is by affidavit, and the public is excluded.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 32
glossary_terms.example: The contested application for specific discovery under Order 24 r 7 was heard in chambers before the Senior Assistant Registrar at 9:30 a.m., with the Plaintiff's and Defendant's counsel making oral submissions on the relevance and necessity of the documents requested.

glossary_terms.definition: The current procedural mode (under the Rules of Court 2012) for initiating an interlocutory application in chambers. Form 57 of the ROC 2012. It identifies the parties, sets out the prayers (orders sought), states the date, time and place of hearing, and refers to the supporting affidavit. Under the previous Rules of the High Court 1980, the equivalent was called a 'Summons in Chambers' — practitioners often still use that term colloquially.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 32 r 1; Form 57
glossary_terms.example: The Defendant filed a Notice of Application (Form 57) seeking to strike out the Statement of Claim under Order 18 r 19 of the Rules of Court 2012 and the inherent jurisdiction of the Court (Order 92 r 4).

glossary_terms.definition: The pre-2012 term for a Notice of Application in chambers. Under the Rules of the High Court 1980, interlocutory applications were initiated by 'Summons in Chambers'. The Rules of Court 2012 replaced this with 'Notice of Application' (Form 57). The term continues in everyday practitioners' usage to refer generally to chamber applications, particularly an Order 14 summary judgment summons.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of the High Court 1980 (repealed); historical practice
glossary_terms.example: Counsel referred to her 'Order 14 summons in chambers' even though the form she filed was correctly titled 'Notice of Application'.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin for 'between the parties'. Refers to a proceeding or order made after notice has been given to all affected parties and they have had an opportunity to be heard. The default mode for interlocutory applications. Contrast with ex parte (without notice).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 32; common law procedure
glossary_terms.example: The interim injunction was granted ex parte but only until the inter partes hearing 14 days later, at which both parties would have the opportunity to argue whether it should be continued.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin for 'on the part of one only'. Refers to a proceeding or order made without notice to (and without the presence of) the other party. Reserved for cases of urgency or where notice would defeat the purpose of the order (e.g., Mareva freezing orders, Anton Piller search orders). The applicant on an ex parte application owes a duty of full and frank disclosure of all material facts, including those adverse to the applicant. Material non-disclosure is grounds for immediate discharge of the order.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 r 1; Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra [1988] 1 MLJ 97
glossary_terms.example: The Plaintiff applied ex parte for a Mareva injunction freezing the Defendant's bank accounts. The Court granted the injunction but required the Plaintiff to (a) give an undertaking as to damages and (b) come back inter partes within 14 days.
glossary_terms.latinOrigin: Ex parte (Latin: on the part of one only)

glossary_terms.definition: The duty owed by an applicant on any ex parte application to disclose to the court all material facts within the applicant's knowledge — including facts adverse to the applicant's case. The duty is non-delegable and absolute. Material non-disclosure (whether deliberate, reckless or innocent) is normally fatal: the order will be discharged and the applicant ordered to pay costs on the indemnity basis. The leading Malaysian authority is Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra [1988] 1 MLJ 97.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra Malaysia Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 97 (SC); Bank Mellat v Nikpour [1985] FSR 87
glossary_terms.example: The Defendant successfully applied to discharge the ex parte Mareva injunction on the basis that the Plaintiff had failed to disclose a strong arguable defence raised by the Defendant in pre-action correspondence — material non-disclosure.

glossary_terms.definition: A formal undertaking given by the applicant for an interim injunction (Order 29 r 2A ROC 2012) to abide by any order the court may make as to damages in the event the court is later of the opinion that the respondent has sustained damage by reason of the injunction which the applicant ought to pay. The undertaking is a non-negotiable precondition for the grant of an interim injunction. Where the applicant is impecunious or foreign, the court may require the undertaking to be fortified by security or a bank guarantee.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 r 2A
glossary_terms.example: The Plaintiff's counsel formally gave the usual undertaking as to damages, which was recorded in the sealed Order. When the injunction was later discharged at trial as wrongly granted, the Defendant successfully claimed RM250,000 in losses against the Plaintiff under the undertaking.

glossary_terms.definition: The classic three-stage test for the grant of an interim injunction, formulated by Lord Diplock in American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 and authoritatively adopted in Malaysia by the Court of Appeal in Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor [1995] 1 MLJ 193: (1) is there a serious question to be tried (a low threshold)? (2) would damages be an adequate remedy? (3) where does the balance of convenience lie (including preservation of the status quo)?
glossary_terms.source: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 (HL); Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor [1995] 1 MLJ 193 (CA)
glossary_terms.example: On the application for an interim injunction restraining the construction works pending trial of the trespass claim, the Judge applied the American Cyanamid test as restated in Keet Gerald: there was a serious question, damages would be an inadequate remedy for irreparable harm to ancient trees, and the balance of convenience favoured restraint pending trial.

glossary_terms.definition: An interim injunction restraining a defendant from disposing of, dealing with, or removing assets out of the jurisdiction (or within it) pending judgment, granted to prevent dissipation that would render any judgment unenforceable. Named after Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA [1975] 2 Lloyd's Rep 509. The applicant must show: a good arguable case on the merits; real risk of asset dissipation; balance of convenience favouring the order; and (on ex parte applications) full and frank disclosure.
glossary_terms.source: Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA [1975] 2 Lloyd's Rep 509; Aspatra Sdn Bhd v Bank Bumiputra [1988] 1 MLJ 97; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.25(2) & Schedule; Rules of Court 2012, Order 29
glossary_terms.example: The bank obtained an ex parte Mareva injunction freezing the borrower's three bank accounts and a property after evidence emerged that the borrower had begun transferring assets to family members in anticipation of judgment.

glossary_terms.definition: An exceptional ex parte interim order permitting the applicant (and supervising solicitor) to enter the respondent's premises to search for, inspect, copy and preserve specified documents or items which are evidence in the action. Three conditions per Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55 (adopted in Malaysia in Lian Keow v Paramjothy [1982] 1 MLJ 217): (1) extremely strong prima facie case; (2) very serious actual or potential damage; (3) clear evidence of incriminating items in the respondent's possession with real risk of destruction.
glossary_terms.source: Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55; Lian Keow Sdn Bhd v Paramjothy [1982] 1 MLJ 217 (FC); Rules of Court 2012, Order 29
glossary_terms.example: In the trade secrets misappropriation action, the Court granted an Anton Piller order permitting the Plaintiff (with an independent supervising solicitor) to enter the Defendant's office between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. on a working day to search for and image the laptops alleged to contain the misappropriated source code.

glossary_terms.definition: A formal warning endorsed prominently on a court order requiring a person to do or refrain from doing an act, stating that disobedience will render the person liable to be committed to prison for contempt of court (and/or to fine or sequestration of assets). Without a penal notice properly endorsed (Order 45 r 7 ROC 2012) and the order personally served, no contempt proceeding for breach can be founded. Standard text: 'If you, [Name], disobey this Order you will be liable to be committed to prison for contempt of court.'
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 45 r 7; Order 52 (committal)
glossary_terms.example: The sealed Mareva injunction was endorsed with a bold-typeface penal notice and was personally served on the Defendant by the bank's process server, who duly affirmed an Affidavit of Service.

glossary_terms.definition: A procedure under Order 14 of the Rules of Court 2012 by which a plaintiff may obtain judgment without a full trial where the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim and there is no other compelling reason why the case should go to trial. After the defendant enters appearance, the plaintiff files a Notice of Application + Affidavit. The defendant must 'show cause' (per National Co for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya [1984] 2 MLJ 300) by raising a bona fide triable issue. Particularly favoured by banks for liquidated debt claims.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 14; National Company for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya Sdn Bhd [1984] 2 MLJ 300 (FC)
glossary_terms.example: Within 14 days of the Defendant entering appearance, the Plaintiff bank filed an Order 14 application supported by an Affidavit exhibiting the loan agreement, statement of account, and demand letter. The Defendant could not raise any bona fide triable issue; summary judgment was entered for RM3.5 million.

glossary_terms.definition: A summary procedure under Order 18 r 19 of the Rules of Court 2012 (and the inherent jurisdiction preserved by Order 92 r 4) to strike out the whole or part of any pleading on the grounds that it: (a) discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence; (b) is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious; (c) may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the action; or (d) is otherwise an abuse of the process of the Court. The threshold is high — used only in 'plain and obvious' cases (Bandar Builder v UMBC [1993] 3 MLJ 36).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 18 r 19; Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v UMBC Bhd [1993] 3 MLJ 36 (SC)
glossary_terms.example: The Defendant applied to strike out the Statement of Claim on the basis that the cause of action was clearly time-barred under the Limitation Act 1953 — a plain and obvious bar appearing on the face of the pleading.

glossary_terms.definition: The Malaysian test for distinguishing a final order from an interlocutory order, important for determining the appellate route under s.68 of the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (which restricts appeals to the Court of Appeal in certain interlocutory categories without leave). The 'order test' (Asia Commercial Finance v Kawal Teliti [1995] 3 MLJ 189 (FC)) looks at the order actually made and asks whether it finally disposes of the rights of the parties. If yes — final; if no — interlocutory. Striking out granted = final; striking out refused = interlocutory.
glossary_terms.source: Asia Commercial Finance (M) Bhd v Kawal Teliti Sdn Bhd [1995] 3 MLJ 189 (FC); Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.68
glossary_terms.example: The High Court refused the Defendant's striking out application. As the refusal did not finally dispose of the parties' rights, it was an interlocutory order. The Defendant required leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal under s.68 CJA 1964.

glossary_terms.definition: Affidavits exchanged in the course of an interlocutory chamber application after the supporting affidavit. The respondent may file an Affidavit in Reply (or 'in Opposition') addressing the matters raised. The applicant may then file an Affidavit in Rejoinder responding to new matters. Further affidavits beyond the rejoinder require leave of the Court (Order 41 ROC 2012). Each affidavit must comply with Order 41 — sworn before a Commissioner for Oaths, with properly marked exhibits.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 41
glossary_terms.example: The Defendant's Affidavit in Reply alleged for the first time that the loan agreement was vitiated by misrepresentation. The Plaintiff filed an Affidavit in Rejoinder exhibiting contemporaneous correspondence rebutting the misrepresentation allegation.
