glossary_terms.definition: An order under Order 29 rr 10–18 of the Rules of Court 2012 requiring the defendant to make a payment on account of any damages, debt or other sum (excluding costs) which the defendant may be held liable to pay to the plaintiff. Available where: (a) the defendant has admitted liability; (b) the plaintiff has obtained judgment for damages to be assessed; or (c) on a balance of probabilities the plaintiff would succeed at trial for substantial damages or a substantial sum.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 rr 10–18
glossary_terms.example: In the personal injury action where liability was admitted, the Plaintiff obtained an Order for interim payment of RM50,000 to fund ongoing medical treatment pending the assessment of damages by the Sessions Court.

glossary_terms.definition: A Mareva (freezing order) of worldwide scope, restraining the respondent from dealing with assets anywhere in the world. Granted only on strong evidence of dissipation risk and significant assets outside Malaysia. The order incorporates standard 'Babanaft' and 'Derby & Co' carve-outs to protect third parties (banks, trustees) abroad and prevent the order being treated as penal extraterritorially.
glossary_terms.source: Babanaft International Co SA v Bassatne [1990] Ch 13; Derby & Co Ltd v Weldon (No 1) [1990] Ch 48; Aspatra v Bank Bumiputra [1988] 1 MLJ 97
glossary_terms.example: The bank obtained a worldwide Mareva freezing the borrower's assets in Malaysia, Singapore, Hong Kong and Switzerland, with Babanaft carve-outs protecting the foreign banks holding the accounts.

glossary_terms.definition: An undertaking given by an applicant for an interim injunction (or Mareva or Anton Piller) to compensate the respondent for any loss caused by the order if it later transpires that the order should not have been granted. Mandatory under Order 29 r 2A ROC 2012. The undertaking must be expressly recorded in the order. For impecunious or foreign applicants, the court may require fortification by bank guarantee, security, or payment into court.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 r 2A; F Hoffmann-La Roche & Co AG v Secretary of State for Trade and Industry [1975] AC 295
glossary_terms.example: The Applicant gave the standard undertaking that, if the Court should later find that the injunction has caused loss to the Respondent, the Applicant will pay such sum as the Court may consider just.

glossary_terms.definition: An order requiring the applicant for an interim injunction to back its cross-undertaking as to damages with security — typically a bank guarantee from a licensed Malaysian bank, payment into court, or a solicitor's undertaking. Ordered where the court considers the applicant may not be able to honour the undertaking (impecunious applicants, foreign applicants without local assets, or applications involving substantial potential damages).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29 r 2A; Aspatra v Bank Bumiputra [1988] 1 MLJ 97
glossary_terms.example: Because the Applicant was a foreign company with no Malaysian assets, the Court ordered fortification of the undertaking by a bank guarantee in the sum of RM500,000 from a licensed bank in Malaysia.

glossary_terms.definition: An injunction granted to preserve the status quo pending an appeal, after the substantive application has been refused or determined. Named after Erinford Properties Ltd v Cheshire CC [1974] Ch 261. Granted where a refusal of interim relief at first instance would render any successful appeal nugatory. The applicant must show that the appeal has reasonable prospects and that, without the injunction, the appeal would be rendered futile.
glossary_terms.source: Erinford Properties Ltd v Cheshire CC [1974] Ch 261; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s.44
glossary_terms.example: After the High Court refused the interim injunction restraining demolition, the Applicant obtained an Erinford injunction restraining demolition pending appeal to the Court of Appeal.

glossary_terms.definition: An injunction granted to restrain a wrong that has not yet occurred but is apprehended ('quia timet' — 'because he fears'). The applicant must show: (a) a strong probability that the apprehended wrong will occur; (b) imminent and substantial damage if it does. Used where awaiting the wrong to occur would be too late.
glossary_terms.source: Specific Relief Act 1950, s.54; Lemos v Kennedy Leigh Development [1961] 105 SJ 178
glossary_terms.example: The plaintiff obtained a quia timet injunction restraining the defendant from constructing the proposed wall which, once erected, would block ancient lights to the plaintiff's property.

glossary_terms.definition: A standard provision in court orders permitting the parties to return to court on short notice to seek variation, clarification, or further directions in respect of the order. Particularly common in Mareva, Anton Piller, and other complex interim orders where unforeseen circumstances may arise during execution.
glossary_terms.source: Practice; standard form order provisions
glossary_terms.example: The Mareva injunction included 'liberty to apply' on 24 hours' notice. When the Defendant required release of funds for medical expenses, an urgent application was made within the framework of the existing order.

glossary_terms.definition: An order that the costs of an interlocutory application will be costs in the substantive action — i.e., the eventual winner of the action will recover the costs of the application from the loser. Used where it is premature at the interlocutory stage to determine which party should bear costs (often because the merits will be tested at trial).
glossary_terms.source: Practice; Order 59 ROC 2012
glossary_terms.example: The Court refused the Defendant's striking out application but ordered 'costs in the cause' — meaning if the Defendant ultimately succeeds at trial, it will recover the costs of the failed striking out application.

glossary_terms.definition: An order that the question of costs of an interlocutory application is reserved to the trial judge or to a future hearing. Used where the court considers it premature to make a costs order at the time of disposing of the interlocutory application.
glossary_terms.source: Practice; Order 59 ROC 2012
glossary_terms.example: Costs of the discovery application were reserved to the trial judge, who would have a fuller picture of which party's conduct caused the dispute.

glossary_terms.definition: Costs which one party has already incurred but which have been wasted because of the other party's late amendment, late discovery, late evidence, or other procedural default. Typically ordered against the defaulting party in addition to (or in substitution for) ordinary costs of the application.
glossary_terms.source: Practice; Order 20 (amendment); Order 59 ROC 2012
glossary_terms.example: Because the Defendant amended its Defence on the eve of trial to introduce a new cause of action, the Court allowed the amendment but ordered the Defendant to pay 'costs thrown away' — including the Plaintiff's costs of preparing for the original trial.

glossary_terms.definition: An order that the legal representative (rather than the litigant) personally pays or forfeits costs which have been wasted by improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct of the litigation. Rarely made and only on serious facts. The legal representative must be given an opportunity to be heard before any such order is made.
glossary_terms.source: Order 59 r 8 ROC 2012; inherent jurisdiction; Ridehalgh v Horsefield [1994] Ch 205 (CA)
glossary_terms.example: The Court made a wasted costs order against the Plaintiff's solicitor personally, having found that an unmeritorious application had been pursued in disregard of clear authority.

glossary_terms.definition: A procedural directive requiring a party to demonstrate, by affidavit or argument, that the relief sought against it should not be granted. The classic example is Order 14 summary judgment: the plaintiff establishes a prima facie case, then the burden shifts to the defendant to 'show cause' why summary judgment should not be entered.
glossary_terms.source: Order 14 ROC 2012; National Co for Foreign Trade v Kayu Raya Sdn Bhd [1984] 2 MLJ 300 (FC)
glossary_terms.example: On the Order 14 application, the Defendant was required to 'show cause' by demonstrating either a bona fide triable issue or some other reason why the case should go to trial.

glossary_terms.definition: A bona fide issue of fact or law arising on the pleadings and the evidence which requires determination at trial. The threshold is more than a mere assertion or shadowy defence — the defendant must condescend to particulars supported by evidence. The presence of a triable issue defeats summary judgment under Order 14 and resists striking out under Order 18 r 19.
glossary_terms.source: Order 14 ROC 2012; Order 18 r 19 ROC 2012; Esso Standard Malaya Bhd v Southern Cross Airways [1972] 1 MLJ 168 (FC)
glossary_terms.example: The Defendant's affidavit raised a bona fide triable issue as to whether the loan agreement had been varied by an oral agreement during a meeting in 2024, supported by contemporaneous correspondence. Summary judgment was refused and the matter ordered to trial.

glossary_terms.definition: Summary determination under Order 14A ROC 2012 of a question of law or construction of any document, where the question is suitable for summary determination without full trial and the determination will dispose of the entire cause/matter or any substantial claim/issue. A faster route than full trial for cases turning on pure legal questions or document interpretation.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 14A
glossary_terms.example: The Court determined under Order 14A that the indemnity clause in the lease, on its proper construction, did not extend to consequential losses. This determination disposed of the principal claim without need for trial.

glossary_terms.definition: An order suspending the further conduct of proceedings, either temporarily or until a specified event. Common grounds: pending arbitration (s.10 Arbitration Act 2005 — mandatory if valid agreement and dispute within scope); pending appeal in related proceedings; forum non conveniens; lis alibi pendens; case management.
glossary_terms.source: Arbitration Act 2005, s.10; Order 32 ROC 2012; inherent jurisdiction
glossary_terms.example: The Court granted a mandatory stay of the High Court proceedings under s.10 of the Arbitration Act 2005, the dispute being within the scope of a valid arbitration agreement.

glossary_terms.definition: An order suspending enforcement of a judgment pending an appeal or pending some other condition (e.g., payment of costs). Granted under Order 55 r 16 (appeals from registrar) or Order 56 r 1(4) (appeals from Judge in Chambers) or Court of Appeal Rules. Test: whether enforcement would render any successful appeal nugatory; balance of injustice.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 55 r 16; Order 56 r 1(4); Court of Appeal Rules 1994, r.13
glossary_terms.example: Pending appeal of the summary judgment, the Defendant obtained a stay of execution conditional upon payment of half the judgment sum into court within 21 days.

glossary_terms.definition: A doctrine permitting the Malaysian court to stay or dismiss proceedings on the basis that another forum is clearly and distinctly more appropriate to determine the dispute. Test (Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460, applied in Malaysia): the defendant must identify another forum which is more appropriate; the court then considers connecting factors and the interests of justice.
glossary_terms.source: Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460 (HL); Malaysian application
glossary_terms.example: The Court stayed the Malaysian proceedings on forum non conveniens grounds, holding that Singapore was the clearly more appropriate forum given the place of contracting, place of performance, and governing law.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin for 'a lawsuit pending elsewhere'. The principle that, where the same dispute is already pending in another competent court, the second proceedings may be stayed (or struck out as abuse) to avoid duplication, conflicting judgments, and unnecessary costs.
glossary_terms.source: Common law; abuse of process doctrine; Henderson v Henderson principles
glossary_terms.example: The Court struck out the Malaysian action on the ground of lis alibi pendens, identical proceedings between the same parties already being pending in the Singapore High Court at a more advanced stage.

glossary_terms.definition: An order nisi (Latin: 'unless') is a provisional order which becomes absolute (final and enforceable) on a later date unless cause is shown why it should not. Common in garnishee proceedings (Order 49 ROC 2012) and certain contempt proceedings: garnishee order nisi → garnishee order absolute after the third party (garnishee) has been served and given an opportunity to dispute.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 49 (garnishee); Order 52 (committal)
glossary_terms.example: The bank obtained a garnishee order nisi attaching funds in the judgment debtor's bank account. Two weeks later, the bank served the garnishee bank, which did not dispute, and the order was made absolute, requiring payment over to the bank.

glossary_terms.definition: An order appointing a receiver to take control of property, an undertaking, or assets pending litigation or in execution of judgment. Equitable receivership is governed by Order 30 ROC 2012; statutory receivership by the security instrument (debenture) or statute (e.g., Companies Act 2016 for receivers and managers).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 30; Companies Act 2016, Part III, Division 8
glossary_terms.example: Pending determination of the partnership dispute, the Court appointed a receiver under Order 30 to take control of the partnership business and assets to preserve them for the parties.

glossary_terms.definition: A subpoena (writ of summons to attend court) requiring the recipient to attend and produce specified documents in their possession, custody or power. Distinguished from a subpoena ad testificandum (to give oral evidence). Issued under Order 38 r 14 ROC 2012.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 38 r 14
glossary_terms.example: The Plaintiff issued a subpoena duces tecum to the bank manager, requiring attendance at trial and production of all account opening documents and statements relating to the Defendant's accounts for the period 2020–2024.

glossary_terms.definition: An order under inherent jurisdiction restraining a defendant from leaving the jurisdiction pending compliance with an asset disclosure order ancillary to a Mareva injunction. Used to prevent the defendant from frustrating asset disclosure by departure. The defendant's passport may be ordered to be surrendered.
glossary_terms.source: Bayer AG v Winter [1986] 1 WLR 497 (CA); inherent jurisdiction
glossary_terms.example: Ancillary to the Mareva, the Court granted a Bayer order restraining the Defendant from leaving Malaysia pending compliance with the asset disclosure obligations, with the Defendant's passport to be lodged with the Defendant's solicitors.

glossary_terms.definition: A court order that has been formally entered (drawn up, settled, signed, and sealed by the registrar) and bears the court seal. Only sealed orders may be enforced or served for the purposes of contempt. The sealed order must be obtained from the court registry after lodgment of the draft.
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 42; Order 45
glossary_terms.example: The draft injunction order was lodged at the registry and emerged as a sealed order three days later. Only then could it be served personally on the Defendant for the purposes of enforcement.

glossary_terms.definition: The breach of a legal duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff resulting in damage. Requires four elements: duty, breach, causation, damage. Foundational tort governing personal injury, professional negligence, and most accident claims.
glossary_terms.source: Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562; Civil Law Act 1956
glossary_terms.example: The driver owed a duty of care to other road users, breached it by driving while distracted, causing the collision and the plaintiff's injuries — a textbook negligence claim.

glossary_terms.definition: A legal obligation imposed on an individual requiring adherence to a standard of reasonable care while performing acts that could foreseeably harm others. The first element of the tort of negligence; tested by the Caparo three-stage approach (foreseeability, proximity, fair/just/reasonable).
glossary_terms.source: Donoghue v Stevenson; Caparo v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605
glossary_terms.example: The Caparo test established that the auditors did not owe a duty of care to potential investors who relied on the published accounts to acquire shares.

glossary_terms.definition: The plaintiff's failure to take reasonable care for their own safety, contributing to the loss. Under s. 12 Civil Law Act 1956, damages are reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the plaintiff's share in the responsibility.
glossary_terms.source: Civil Law Act 1956, s. 12
glossary_terms.example: The Court found the plaintiff 25% contributorily negligent for failing to wear a seatbelt, reducing the damages award by that percentage.

glossary_terms.definition: The publication of a false statement that lowers the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society. Comprises libel (permanent form) and slander (transient form). Governed in Malaysia by the Defamation Act 1957.
glossary_terms.source: Defamation Act 1957; Sim v Stretch [1936]
glossary_terms.example: The newspaper article falsely accused the businessman of fraud, constituting libel actionable per se under the Defamation Act 1957.

glossary_terms.definition: Defamation in permanent form — writing, printing, broadcasting, or other permanent record. Actionable per se under s. 3 Defamation Act 1957 — no proof of special damage required.
glossary_terms.source: Defamation Act 1957, s. 3
glossary_terms.example: The defamatory blog post constituted libel and was actionable without proof of special damage.

glossary_terms.definition: Defamation in transient form — spoken word or gestures. Generally requires proof of special damage except in four cases actionable per se: imputation of crime, contagious disease, professional incompetence (s. 5 Defamation Act 1957), or unchastity in a woman (s. 4 Defamation Act 1957).
glossary_terms.source: Defamation Act 1957, ss. 4, 5
glossary_terms.example: The oral statement that the doctor was professionally incompetent fell within s. 5 and was actionable as slander per se.

glossary_terms.definition: A complete defence to defamation if the defendant proves the words complained of are substantially true. Statutory framework under s. 8 Defamation Act 1957 — defence does not fail merely because not every charge is proved if the unproven charges do not materially injure reputation given the truth of the rest.
glossary_terms.source: Defamation Act 1957, s. 8
glossary_terms.example: The newspaper relied on justification, proving the substantial truth of the allegations of corruption — defeating the defamation claim.

glossary_terms.definition: Defence to defamation for honest opinion (not statement of fact) on a matter of public interest based on true facts. Statutory under s. 9 Defamation Act 1957. Defeated by malice.
glossary_terms.source: Defamation Act 1957, s. 9
glossary_terms.example: The film critic's harsh review was protected as fair comment — opinion based on the true facts of the production, on a matter of public interest.

glossary_terms.definition: Defence to defamation for communications made in performance of a legal, social or moral duty to a person with a corresponding interest in receiving them. Defeated by express malice. Statutory categories listed in the Schedule to the Defamation Act 1957.
glossary_terms.source: Defamation Act 1957, Schedule
glossary_terms.example: The reference letter from a former employer to a prospective employer attracted qualified privilege — both had legitimate interest in the employee's character.

glossary_terms.definition: The 'responsible journalism' defence to defamation, derived from Reynolds v Times Newspapers Ltd [2001] 2 AC 127. Provides qualified privilege for publication of matters of public concern subject to factors including verification, urgency, and opportunity to comment.
glossary_terms.source: Reynolds v Times Newspapers Ltd [2001] 2 AC 127
glossary_terms.example: The newspaper successfully relied on the Reynolds defence — the article addressed a matter of significant public interest, sources were verified, and the claimant was afforded right of reply.

glossary_terms.definition: The principle that title or interest registered under the Torrens system is immune from challenge except on statutory exceptions (fraud, forgery, void instrument, unlawful acquisition). Codified in s. 340 NLC 1965 — interpreted as deferred indefeasibility post Tan Ying Hong [2010] 2 MLJ 1.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 340; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San
glossary_terms.example: The bona fide purchaser from the registered owner enjoyed deferred indefeasibility under s. 340(3) — but the immediate transferee from the forger did not, per Tan Ying Hong.

glossary_terms.definition: A caveat lodged by a person claiming title or interest in land under ss. 322-331 NLC 1965, preventing registration of dealings until the caveat is removed or lapses. Lapses after 6 years unless extended.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, ss. 322-331
glossary_terms.example: The purchaser lodged a private caveat against the property to protect his equitable interest pending completion of the sale and transfer of title.

glossary_terms.definition: A registrable interest in land sufficient to support the lodgement of a private caveat. The caveator must show a present, recognisable interest — speculative or contingent claims are insufficient.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 323; Damodaran v Choe Kuan Him [1979] 2 MLJ 267
glossary_terms.example: The purchaser under a sale and purchase agreement had a caveatable interest as equitable owner pending registration of transfer.

glossary_terms.definition: The acquisition of title to land by long, continuous, open and adverse possession. NOT recognised in Malaysia under s. 341 NLC 1965 — no title to State land or registered land may be acquired by adverse possession.
glossary_terms.source: National Land Code 1965, s. 341; Sidek bin Haji Muhamad v Government of the State of Perak [1982] 1 MLJ 313
glossary_terms.example: The squatters' 30-year occupation did not ripen into title — adverse possession is not recognised under the Malaysian Torrens system.

glossary_terms.definition: An equitable remedy compelling a contracting party to perform contractual obligations in specie. Governed by ss. 11-22 Specific Relief Act 1950. For sale of land, damages are presumed inadequate (s. 11(2)) — SP is the prima facie remedy.
glossary_terms.source: Specific Relief Act 1950, ss. 11-22; Bandar Builder Sdn Bhd v UMBC [1993] 3 MLJ 36
glossary_terms.example: The Court ordered specific performance of the sale and purchase agreement, directing the vendor to execute and register the Memorandum of Transfer.

glossary_terms.definition: An equitable remedy terminating a contract ab initio, restoring the parties to their pre-contractual position. Available for voidable contracts (consent vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, undue influence) under ss. 34-35 SRA 1950. Barred by affirmation, lapse of time, or impossibility of restitutio in integrum.
glossary_terms.source: Specific Relief Act 1950, ss. 34-35; Contracts Act 1950, s. 19
glossary_terms.example: On discovering the fraudulent misrepresentation, the buyer rescinded the contract and recovered the deposit, having promptly served notice of rescission.

glossary_terms.definition: A provisional divorce decree under s. 61 LRA 1976, made absolute after 3 months unless cause shown. The marriage is NOT dissolved by Decree Nisi — only by Decree Absolute.
glossary_terms.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s. 61
glossary_terms.example: The Court granted a Decree Nisi at the hearing; after the 3-month waiting period, the petitioner applied for and obtained the Decree Absolute, dissolving the marriage.

glossary_terms.definition: The final divorce decree under s. 61(2) LRA 1976, dissolving the marriage. Granted on application after 3 months from Decree Nisi unless cause shown.
glossary_terms.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s. 61(2)
glossary_terms.example: After 3 months from the Decree Nisi, the Decree Absolute was granted on motion — the parties were thereafter free to remarry.

glossary_terms.definition: The legal authority to care for and make decisions for a child. Under s. 88 LRA 1976, the welfare of the child is the paramount consideration. Children below 7 — rebuttable presumption in favour of mother. Joint custody with care and control to one parent is increasingly common.
glossary_terms.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s. 88; Guardianship of Infants Act 1961
glossary_terms.example: The Court awarded joint custody with care and control to the mother and reasonable access to the father, applying the welfare principle.

glossary_terms.definition: A court grant authorising a person to administer the estate of a deceased who died intestate. Granted under s. 30 PAA 1959 to those entitled in priority under the Distribution Act 1958 (spouse, children, parents, siblings).
glossary_terms.source: Probate and Administration Act 1959, s. 30; Distribution Act 1958
glossary_terms.example: The deceased left no will; her surviving spouse applied for and obtained Letters of Administration to administer the estate.

glossary_terms.definition: A court grant confirming the validity of a will and the authority of the executor to administer the estate. Granted under s. 3 PAA 1959 on application by the executor named in the will.
glossary_terms.source: Probate and Administration Act 1959, s. 3; Wills Act 1959
glossary_terms.example: The executor named in the testator's will applied for and obtained the Grant of Probate, then proceeded to gather and distribute the estate.

glossary_terms.definition: The state of dying without a valid will. The estate is distributed according to the statutory shares prescribed by s. 6 Distribution Act 1958 (for non-Muslims) — surviving spouse, issue, parents, etc., in fixed proportions.
glossary_terms.source: Distribution Act 1958, s. 6; Probate and Administration Act 1959
glossary_terms.example: The deceased died intestate; under s. 6 Distribution Act 1958, his surviving spouse received 1/3, his two children shared 2/3 of the estate equally.

glossary_terms.definition: The supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court over decisions of public bodies, exercised under Order 53 ROC 2012 and paragraph 1 of the Schedule to the Courts of Judicature Act 1964. Reviews legality, procedural propriety, irrationality (and increasingly proportionality).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53; Courts of Judicature Act 1964, Schedule paragraph 1
glossary_terms.example: The applicant filed for judicial review of the Minister's decision, on grounds of procedural impropriety and Wednesbury unreasonableness.

glossary_terms.definition: A prerogative writ to bring up and quash an unlawful decision of an inferior tribunal or public body. Most common remedy in judicial review. Issued under Order 53 ROC 2012 and the Schedule to the Courts of Judicature Act 1964.
glossary_terms.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964, Schedule; Rules of Court 2012, Order 53
glossary_terms.example: The High Court issued an order of certiorari quashing the Industrial Court's award, having found procedural impropriety in the conduct of proceedings.

glossary_terms.definition: A prerogative writ ordering a public officer or body to perform a specified public duty. Available where there is a clear public duty and no adequate alternative remedy.
glossary_terms.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964, Schedule; Rules of Court 2012, Order 53
glossary_terms.example: The Court issued mandamus compelling the local authority to consider the planning application that it had wrongfully refused to entertain.

glossary_terms.definition: A standard of judicial review that condemns a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it. From Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223. The 'irrationality' ground in the GCHQ taxonomy.
glossary_terms.source: Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223; GCHQ case
glossary_terms.example: The Minister's decision to revoke the licence on a single technicality was held to be Wednesbury unreasonable — no reasonable Minister could have so decided.

glossary_terms.definition: Standing to bring legal proceedings. In judicial review, a 'sufficient interest' is required under O 53 r 3. Originally restrictive (Lim Kit Siang v UEM [1988]), now broader for public interest cases (MTUC v Menteri Tenaga [2014]).
glossary_terms.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53; Lim Kit Siang v United Engineers
glossary_terms.example: The Federal Court held the public interest body had locus standi to challenge the energy policy decision affecting national interests.

glossary_terms.definition: Statutory remedy under s. 346 Companies Act 2016 for members and debenture holders against oppressive, prejudicial, or unfair conduct of company affairs. Wide range of relief available including buy-out at fair value (most common), regulation of affairs, and winding up.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016, s. 346; Pang Yong Hock v PKM Industries [2004] 3 MLJ 565
glossary_terms.example: The minority shareholder petitioned under s. 346 alleging oppression by the controlling family; the Court ordered a buy-out at fair value.

glossary_terms.definition: Action brought by a complainant in the name of the company under s. 347 Companies Act 2016, with leave of court. Pre-conditions: 30-day notice to directors, good faith, prima facie best interests of the company.
glossary_terms.source: Companies Act 2016, s. 347-348
glossary_terms.example: The director-shareholder, denied access to the boardroom, applied for and obtained leave to bring a statutory derivative action against the wrongdoing co-directors for breach of fiduciary duty to the company.

glossary_terms.definition: Statutory adjudication of payment disputes in construction contracts under the Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012. A right that cannot be ousted by contract; provides fast-track decision (45 working days from Adjudication Response) binding until set aside or finally determined.
glossary_terms.source: Construction Industry Payment and Adjudication Act 2012
glossary_terms.example: The unpaid subcontractor commenced CIPAA adjudication; the adjudicator's decision in its favour was enforced as a court judgment under s. 28.

glossary_terms.definition: Mandatory stay of court proceedings under s. 10 Arbitration Act 2005 where the matter falls within an arbitration agreement. Application must be made before substantive defence is filed. Confirmed mandatory by Press Metal Sarawak v Etiqa Takaful [2016].
glossary_terms.source: Arbitration Act 2005, s. 10; Press Metal Sarawak v Etiqa Takaful
glossary_terms.example: The Defendant successfully obtained a stay under s. 10 — the dispute fell within the arbitration clause and the application was filed prior to entering substantive defence.

glossary_terms.definition: Application under s. 37 Arbitration Act 2005 to set aside an arbitration award. Grounds mirror the New York Convention (incapacity, invalid agreement, lack of notice, beyond scope, irregular composition, non-arbitrable, public policy).
glossary_terms.source: Arbitration Act 2005, s. 37
glossary_terms.example: The respondent applied to set aside the award under s. 37(1)(b)(ii) (public policy), arguing the award was procured by fraud — the application was dismissed for failing to meet the high public policy threshold.

glossary_terms.term: Pain Suffering and Loss of Amenities (PSLA)
glossary_terms.definition: General damages awarded in personal injury cases for the pain and suffering and loss of amenities of life caused by the injury. Quantum guided by the Compendium of Personal Injury Awards (Malaysia) — tariffs for various injuries.
glossary_terms.source: Civil Law Act 1956; Compendium of Personal Injury Awards (Malaysia)
glossary_terms.example: For the spinal injury causing chronic pain and inability to engage in sports, the Court awarded RM120,000 PSLA, in line with the Compendium tariffs.

glossary_terms.definition: Damages for loss of income post-trial due to permanent or long-term incapacity. Calculated on the multiplier × multiplicand approach: net annual loss × number of remaining working years (capped). Codified in s. 28A Civil Law Act 1956.
glossary_terms.source: Civil Law Act 1956, s. 28A
glossary_terms.example: The Court awarded loss of future earnings of RM450,000 (multiplicand RM30,000 × multiplier 15 years) for the plaintiff's permanent incapacity.

glossary_terms.definition: The statutory test under s. 20 IRA 1967 for assessing whether an employer's dismissal of a workman was lawful. The employer bears the burden to prove (a) misconduct or other ground; and (b) proportionality of dismissal. Per Goon Kwee Phoy v J&P Coats [1981] 2 MLJ 129.
glossary_terms.source: Industrial Relations Act 1967, s. 20; Goon Kwee Phoy v J&P Coats
glossary_terms.example: The employer failed to prove just cause or excuse — the misconduct was unproven and dismissal was disproportionate to the alleged offence.

glossary_terms.definition: Where the employer's fundamental breach of the employment contract entitles the employee to treat the contract as repudiated and resign, treating the resignation as dismissal. The employee must resign promptly to claim constructive dismissal.
glossary_terms.source: Western Excavating (ECC) Ltd v Sharp [1978] QB 761; common law
glossary_terms.example: After his salary was unilaterally cut by 50% without consent, the senior manager resigned and successfully claimed constructive dismissal under s. 20 IRA 1967.

glossary_terms.definition: A trust imposed by equity (not by intention of the parties) to prevent unconscionable conduct. Common applications: secret commissions and bribes (FHR European Ventures); proceeds of breach of fiduciary duty; specifically performable contracts.
glossary_terms.source: FHR European Ventures LLP v Cedar Capital Partners LLC [2014] UKSC 45
glossary_terms.example: The director's secret commission from the seller was held on constructive trust for the company — the proprietary remedy gave priority over the director's other creditors on his subsequent insolvency.

glossary_terms.definition: The equitable process of identifying property in the hands of another by following its value through substituted assets. Distinct from following (which traces the same asset). Tracing rules: Re Hallett's Estate, Re Oatway, Re Diplock for mixed accounts.
glossary_terms.source: Foskett v McKeown [2001] 1 AC 102; Re Hallett's Estate (1880)
glossary_terms.example: Beneficiaries traced the misappropriated trust funds through the trustee's mixed bank account into the property he subsequently bought, claiming a proprietary interest in the property.

glossary_terms.definition: Personal liability of a third party who receives misapplied trust property with knowledge of the breach of trust. The standard for knowledge: 'such as to make it unconscionable for the recipient to retain the benefit' (BCCI v Akindele [2001] Ch 437).
glossary_terms.source: BCCI v Akindele [2001] Ch 437; common law
glossary_terms.example: The bank, with knowledge that the funds were misapplied trust money, was held liable for knowing receipt and ordered to account.

glossary_terms.definition: Personal liability of a third party who dishonestly assists in a breach of trust or fiduciary duty. The test is dishonesty assessed objectively — what an honest person would not have done in the circumstances (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan [1995] 2 AC 378).
glossary_terms.source: Royal Brunei Airlines Sdn Bhd v Tan [1995] 2 AC 378
glossary_terms.example: The director dishonestly assisted the trustee's breach by providing the misappropriated funds with a corporate vehicle to launder them — held personally liable for the resulting loss.

glossary_terms.definition: The period within which a cause of action must be commenced, beyond which the action is statute-barred. Under the Limitation Act 1953: contract and tort — including personal injury and running-down claims — 6 years from accrual (s.6(1)); recovery of land 12 years (s.9); actions to enforce a charge/mortgage 12 years. Malaysia has NO separate 3-year personal-injury period (unlike the UK). The Limitation (Amendment) Act 2018 inserted s.6A, a date-of-knowledge extension for latent (non-personal-injury) damage: 3 years from the date of knowledge, subject to a 15-year longstop. Suits against the Government or a public authority must be brought within 36 months (Public Authorities Protection Act 1948).
glossary_terms.source: Limitation Act 1953 (Act 254), ss.6, 6A, 9; Public Authorities Protection Act 1948 (Act 198)
glossary_terms.example: The plaintiff's contract claim, filed 7 years after breach, was statute-barred under s. 6(1)(a) Limitation Act 1953. A running-down claim, by contrast, must also be brought within 6 years of the accident — there is no shorter personal-injury period in Malaysia.

glossary_terms.definition: The doctrine that the appropriate forum for trial is the one with the most real and substantial connection to the action. Applied in O 11 leave applications and stay applications. Test in Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460.
glossary_terms.source: Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460
glossary_terms.example: The Court declined to grant leave to serve out of jurisdiction — England was the natural forum given the location of witnesses and governing law of the contract.

glossary_terms.definition: Use in the course of trade of a mark identical or similar to a registered trade mark in respect of identical or similar goods or services where likely to confuse. Statutory under s. 54 Trade Marks Act 2019.
glossary_terms.source: Trade Marks Act 2019, s. 54
glossary_terms.example: The Defendant's use of a confusingly similar logo on competing products constituted trade mark infringement, attracting damages and an injunction.

glossary_terms.definition: The common law tort of misrepresenting one's goods or business as those of another. Three elements (the 'classical trinity' from Reckitt & Colman v Borden [1990] 1 WLR 491): goodwill, misrepresentation, damage.
glossary_terms.source: Reckitt & Colman v Borden [1990] 1 WLR 491
glossary_terms.example: The Plaintiff's goodwill in the unregistered trade dress was protected by the tort of passing off — the Defendant's get-up amounted to actionable misrepresentation.

glossary_terms.definition: An invention that satisfies novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), and industrial application under the Patents Act 1983, ss. 11-16, and is not excluded subject matter (e.g. discoveries, mathematical methods, business schemes, methods of treatment).
glossary_terms.source: Patents Act 1983, ss. 11-16
glossary_terms.example: The novel pharmaceutical compound met the patentability requirements: novel, inventive, and industrially applicable — granted a patent valid for 20 years.

practice_directions.title: Mediation (Court-Annexed)
practice_directions.summary: Issued by the Chief Justice to govern court-annexed mediation. It superseded and revoked Practice Direction No. 5 of 2010, retaining its essence with more comprehensive features. Judges of the High Court and their Deputy Registrars, and Sessions Court Judges and Magistrates, are to direct parties to consider mediation in suitable civil and commercial matters.
practice_directions.practicalEffect: Expect the court to raise mediation at case management — attend with settlement instructions and authority. Where parties agree, the matter may be referred to judge-led mediation or the AIAC, and the trial timeline is managed pending the outcome.

practice_directions.title: Electronic Filing System (EFS) under the Case Management System (CMS)
practice_directions.summary: Filing of cause papers in the major court registries is conducted electronically through the Electronic Filing System — a component of the Judiciary's Case Management System, which also includes e-Review and Court Recording & Transcription (CRT).
practice_directions.practicalEffect: Register for an EFS account and file through a licensed service bureau or the e-filing portal. Documents must be in the prescribed PDF format with correct document-type tagging; filing fees are paid electronically. Physical filing is accepted only at registries not yet gazetted for EFS.

practice_directions.title: Pre-Trial Case Management & e-Review
practice_directions.summary: Pre-trial case management is mandatory under Order 34. Courts conduct case management — increasingly by e-Review (online) — to fix timelines for pleadings, discovery, bundles, witness statements and the trial date.
practice_directions.practicalEffect: Diarise every case-management and e-Review date; non-attendance or non-compliance with directions can lead to the action being struck out or judgment entered. File the pre-trial case management checklist and dispose of all interlocutory matters before the trial date is fixed.

practice_directions.title: Common Bundle of Documents (Parts A / B / C)
practice_directions.summary: Parties are to agree a common bundle of documents organised into Part A (authenticity and contents agreed), Part B (authenticity agreed, contents disputed) and Part C (authenticity disputed).
practice_directions.practicalEffect: Agree the bundle and its Part A/B/C categorisation at case management. Part A documents are admitted without further proof; Parts B and C must be proved through witnesses. Paginate and index the bundle as directed before trial.

practice_directions.title: Federal Court — Leave to Appeal in Civil Matters
practice_directions.summary: An appeal to the Federal Court from a civil decision of the Court of Appeal lies only with leave of the Federal Court — generally on a question of general principle decided for the first time, or a question of importance on which a decision would be to public advantage.
practice_directions.practicalEffect: File a Notice of Motion for leave to appeal within one month of the Court of Appeal decision, supported by affidavit and the proposed questions of law. Only if leave is granted do you proceed to the Notice and Memorandum of Appeal. Frame the leave questions tightly against the s.96 threshold.

practice_directions.title: e-Arahan Amalan — Authoritative Register of Practice Directions & Circulars
practice_directions.refNo: Office of the Chief Registrar, Federal Court
practice_directions.summary: e-Arahan Amalan is the official, searchable register of all practice directions and circulars issued by the Judiciary, maintained by the Office of the Chief Registrar of the Federal Court. It is the single source of truth for the current text and status of every practice direction.
practice_directions.practicalEffect: Before relying on any practice direction or circular, confirm its current version and status on e-Arahan Amalan — directions are amended, superseded and revoked frequently, and registry-specific circulars vary between courts.

bar_council_rulings.title: Advertising, Publicity & Soliciting of Work
bar_council_rulings.ruling: An advocate and solicitor shall not solicit work or advertise, directly or indirectly, in a manner that is false, misleading, or outside the permitted forms of publicity. Permitted publicity (firm website, approved directory entries and announcements) is regulated and must preserve the dignity of the profession.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.57 LPA 1976; Legal Profession (Publicity) Rules 2001; Legal Profession (Practice & Etiquette) Rules 1978
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Keep firm websites, social media, brochures and announcements within the permitted categories of publicity. Do not tout for work, pay referral fees for clients, or make comparative or self-laudatory claims.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and lead to disciplinary proceedings.

bar_council_rulings.title: Conflict of Interest
bar_council_rulings.ruling: An advocate and solicitor shall not act where there is a conflict, or a real risk of conflict, between the interests of two clients, or between a client's interest and the solicitor's own interest, unless the position is properly managed and informed consent is obtained where permissible.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.57 LPA 1976; Legal Profession (Practice & Etiquette) Rules 1978; common law fiduciary duties
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Run a conflict check before accepting every retainer. Decline or cease acting where you hold a former client's confidential information relevant to the new matter, or where you would be acting for both sides of a transaction or dispute.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and lead to disciplinary proceedings.

bar_council_rulings.title: Clients' Accounts & Handling of Client Money
bar_council_rulings.ruling: Client money must be kept in a separate client account, distinct from the firm's office account, and dealt with strictly in accordance with the Solicitors' Accounts Rules. Firms must keep proper books of account and submit an annual Accountant's Report.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.57 LPA 1976; Solicitors' Accounts Rules 1990; Accountant's Report Rules 1990
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Bank client money into the client account without delay, never use it to fund the firm or other clients, reconcile the client account regularly, and file the Accountant's Report on time as a condition of the practising certificate.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and lead to disciplinary proceedings.

bar_council_rulings.title: Contingency & Conditional Fees
bar_council_rulings.ruling: An advocate and solicitor shall not enter into a contingency or conditional fee arrangement for contentious proceedings — i.e., a fee payable only on success or calculated as a share of the sum recovered. Such arrangements offend the doctrines of champerty and maintenance.
bar_council_rulings.basis: Legal Profession Act 1976; Legal Profession (Practice & Etiquette) Rules 1978; common law (champerty & maintenance)
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Charge on a proper basis (scale, hourly or agreed fees) and document the retainer. Do not promise 'no win, no fee' or take a percentage of the damages in litigation.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and lead to disciplinary proceedings.

bar_council_rulings.title: Sharing of Fees & Touting
bar_council_rulings.ruling: An advocate and solicitor shall not share professional fees with, or pay a commission to, any unqualified person for introducing or referring clients, nor permit any person to tout for work on the firm's behalf.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.37 & s.57 LPA 1976; Legal Profession (Practice & Etiquette) Rules 1978
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Do not pay 'agents', runners or introducers for clients, and do not split fees with non-lawyers. Reserved legal work must be carried out by, and fees retained within, the profession.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and lead to disciplinary proceedings.

bar_council_rulings.title: Solicitors' Remuneration for Conveyancing & Non-Contentious Work
bar_council_rulings.ruling: Remuneration for conveyancing and certain non-contentious matters is governed by the prescribed scale under the Solicitors' Remuneration Order. Scale fees are mandatory and may not be discounted save as permitted.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.57 LPA 1976; Solicitors' Remuneration Order 2005 (as amended)
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Apply the prescribed scale to sale-and-purchase, charge/loan and tenancy documentation; do not offer unauthorised discounts or rebates to win conveyancing work. Confirm the current scale and any amendments before quoting.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and lead to disciplinary proceedings.

bar_council_rulings.title: Firm Name, Nameplate, Letterhead & Name Cards
bar_council_rulings.ruling: The firm name, nameplate, signboard, letterhead, stationery and name cards must comply with the Rulings as to form and content, and must not amount to advertising or be undignified or misleading.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.57 LPA 1976; Bar Council Rules & Rulings (Firm Name, Nameplate, Letterhead chapters)
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Ensure signage and stationery state only permitted particulars, use an approved firm name, and avoid logos or wording that cross into prohibited advertising.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and lead to disciplinary proceedings.

bar_council_rulings.title: Anti-Money Laundering Obligations of Legal Practitioners
bar_council_rulings.ruling: When carrying on prescribed activities (such as handling client funds or dealing in real property on a client's behalf), an advocate and solicitor is a reporting institution and must observe customer due diligence, record-keeping and suspicious-transaction reporting obligations.
bar_council_rulings.basis: Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 (Act 613); Bar Council AML/CFT Guidelines
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Conduct client identification/CDD before acting, keep records for the prescribed period, watch for red flags, and file suspicious-transaction reports where required — without 'tipping off' the client.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Non-compliance carries statutory penalties under AMLA 2001 and may also constitute professional misconduct.

bar_council_rulings.title: Pupillage (Chambering)
bar_council_rulings.ruling: The Rulings govern the conduct of pupillage, including the master's responsibilities, the pupil's permitted scope of work, and the requirements to be satisfied before a pupil may be called to the Bar.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.57 LPA 1976; Legal Profession Act 1976 (admission provisions); Bar Council Pupillage Rulings
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: Masters must properly supervise pupils and only permit work allowed during the reading period; pupils must satisfy the attendance and competency requirements before petitioning for admission.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Breach may amount to 'misconduct' under s.94(3) LPA 1976 and may affect admission to the Bar.

bar_council_rulings.title: Cessation, Change in Practice & Disciplinary Proceedings
bar_council_rulings.ruling: The Rulings prescribe the steps on cessation of practice or a change in a firm's constitution (notice, handling of files and client money) and recognise that breaches of the Rules and Rulings may be referred to the Disciplinary Board.
bar_council_rulings.basis: s.57 & ss.93–103 LPA 1976; Bar Council Rulings (Cessation / Change in Practice)
bar_council_rulings.practicalEffect: On dissolution, retirement or merger, give the required notices, account to clients for money and documents, and arrange for ongoing matters to be handed over. Co-operate with any disciplinary inquiry.
bar_council_rulings.consequence: Misconduct is dealt with by the Advocates and Solicitors Disciplinary Board under Part VII of the LPA 1976.
